stories.Headline: Five ways to keep online transactions safe in the wake of AI hacking
stories.Summary:
A hackable vulnerability was found in PHP, a coding language that underlies roughly 70% of all websites, according to The Straits Times. The report was published on Oct 30, 2026, and said businesses and governments were scrambling to fix it. The US National Security Agency warned that attackers could use the glitches to take control of web servers to steal data, disrupt services or move through networks. The PHP flaws are the latest in a series of severe software bugs made worse by increasingly capable and accessible large language models. The article lists five steps for users.

It recommends multi-factor authentication, which requires two forms of verification such as a password plus a text-based code or security key. It advises turning on automatic updates for phones, computers and home routers, and updating apps and internet-connected devices at home. It warns people to be wary of unsolicited links and to check a company's instructions by opening its app or typing its website address themselves. It also says consumers should not reuse passwords across shopping sites and should consider using passkeys where possible. Emily Austin, principal security researcher at Censys, recommended unique passwords for individual websites and said people should monitor transactions.

She said that for situations like the PHP vulnerabilities there is not much an end user can do beyond hoping the services they rely on either do not use PHP or have people actively patching. Dan Guido, chief executive and co-founder of Trail of Bits, said someone visiting a website can do everything right and still have their information exposed, and that most of the work falls on companies running services. Runa Sandvik, founder of Granitt, said people should update apps and services whenever available and double-check with the vendor of any home device that may not get updates. Daniel Gardham of the Surrey Centre for Cyber Security said organisations must know what software they run, patch promptly and check whether they have already been compromised. Nic Adams, co-founder and CEO of 0rcus, said scammers take advantage of major cybersecurity news and that an urgent message telling people to secure their account deserves extra scrutiny.

Paul Benda of the American Bankers Association said banks have worked hard to remove low-hanging fruit for attackers but that consumers are in a new normal and should not reuse passwords across shopping sites. The article says responsibility mostly lies with software providers and organisations that serve customers. It says companies typically issue security updates when patches are available, so installing them promptly limits the window for bad actors. Gardham said finding vulnerabilities is becoming faster and easier while fixing them across systems is much harder, and that how well organisations manage that gap will determine whether AI makes the internet safer or more vulnerable. The article does not say what happens next beyond those steps.

Articles.Title: Five ways to keep online transactions safe in the wake of AI hacking

stories.Headline: Healthcare AI regulation must follow the product as it changes
stories.Summary:
Europe’s AI rules and the UK’s reform programme are moving on separate tracks, and the EU has changed its timetable through enacted legislation. The AI Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026. It moves the relevant high-risk requirements to 2 December 2027 for systems classified through Article 6(2) and Annex III, and to 2 August 2028 for systems classified through Article 6(1) and Annex I. The Commission’s implementation announcement confirms those revised dates and describes accompanying changes to administration, testing and governance. Older summaries that give August 2026 or August 2027 as the high-risk deadlines can mislead procurement or development teams.

The joint European guidance on medical devices and the AI Act explains the product route to high-risk classification. Under Article 6(1), the AI must be a product or safety component covered by relevant Annex I legislation, and that product must require third-party conformity assessment. The guidance also separates AI Act classification from the risk class assigned under medical-device legislation, so using AI in a hospital does not by itself answer the classification question. The June 2025 guidance remains useful for these distinctions, but its original timetable must be read against the later amendment. A later AI Act deadline does not mean a medical product can operate without the medical-device requirements already applicable to it.

On 6 October 2026, the UK Government accepted all 44 recommendations of the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare. Its response supports an approach based on risk and continuing oversight across a product’s life, with work involving regulators, health services, industry and patients. It sets out priorities and next steps rather than making every recommended change immediately operational. MHRA guidance explains that Great Britain uses the UK Medical Devices Regulations 2002, as amended, while the EU Medical Devices Regulation applies in Northern Ireland under the Windsor Framework. Great Britain’s strengthened post-market surveillance requirements took effect on 16 June 2025.

The MHRA’s July 2026 guidance on ambient voice products distinguishes administrative transcription or summarisation for clinician review from functions with a medical intended purpose. Use in a healthcare environment alone does not make every such product a medical device, but manufacturers need to reconsider the position when features or intended purposes change. The US Food and Drug Administration’s August 2025 final guidance on predetermined change control plans describes a route for specified modifications to AI-enabled device software within an authorised plan. This is not unrestricted permission to change a model, and a US authorisation does not confer EU or UK market access.

Articles.Title: Healthcare AI regulation must follow the product as it changes

stories.Headline: Amplify, Locate, Estimate (ALE) on Rare-Failure Rates of Fine-Tuned LLMs
stories.Summary:
Patrick Reichherzer, Jonathan Evertz and Thorsten Holz posted a paper on arXiv on October 31, 2026 describing a method called Amplify, Locate, Estimate, or ALE. The method is meant to estimate rare failure probabilities in fine-tuned large language models. Safety fine-tuning can make undesirable behaviors so rare that measuring their frequency by direct sampling becomes very expensive. The paper is listed as arXiv 2610.35472.

ALE uses the change in token log-probabilities caused by safety fine-tuning to define an amplification direction. Along that direction the failure rate is raised so it can be measured cheaply. The authors develop a score-function estimator that uses the amplified batch to recover the local slope of the log failure rate from the token probabilities of sampled failures, which allows extrapolation back to rare target rates. They also use the amplified batch to get an importance-sampling estimate. Across 41 evaluation targets, the median of ALE's estimate-to-reference ratios is close to one, and 37 ALE estimates fall within a factor of three of reference values from independent direct measurements.

Ablation tests show that with a budget of up to about 1000 labeled rollouts, plus a cheap unlabeled scan, ALE estimates failure probabilities for Qwen3-8B fine-tunes down to about 10 to the minus 5. Direct measurement at that level can require hundreds of thousands of rollouts. The required sampling budget scales inversely with failure probability at fixed relative precision. The paper does not say who will use the method or what happens next.

Articles.Title: Amplify, Locate, Estimate (ALE) on Rare-Failure Rates of Fine-Tuned LLMs

stories.Headline: The ethical risks of AI in law: Hallucinations, confidentiality, and client consent
stories.Summary:
Generative AI has quickly become an everyday tool in legal practice, and the profession is still working out what that means for its ethical duties. The New York State Bar Association's Task Force on Artificial Intelligence issued a report and recommendations in April 2024. That report offered no conclusions and urged readers to take on the mindset of ancient explorers, being cautious, curious, vigilant, and brave. The best known warning came from Mata v. Avianca in the summer of 2023, when plaintiff's attorneys filed a response citing and quoting purported judicial decisions that did not exist.

In that case, the court found the lawyers had abandoned their responsibilities by submitting non-existent opinions with fake quotes and citations created by ChatGPT, and it imposed sanctions on them. The ABA issued Formal Opinion 512 on generative AI tools on July 29, 2024. Pennsylvania and Philadelphia bar associations issued joint guidance in June 2024, and California, Illinois, West Virginia, Florida, Missouri and others offered similar guidance. The ethics opinions rest on three themes from the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct: competence, confidentiality, and supervision.

Model Rule 1.1 requires competent representation, and in 2012 Comment 8 was amended to require competence in the risks and benefits of the technology lawyers use. The Pennsylvania joint opinion says lawyers must be proficient in technological tools to the same extent as traditional methods. Model Rule 1.6 requires lawyers not to reveal information relating to a client's representation unless the client gives informed consent. Lawyers must also oversee colleagues, employees, consultants, and outside vendors, including those using AI tools.

Most ethics opinions recommend informing clients about AI use, while some jurisdictions suggest getting explicit consent. Because most AI tools process data on external servers, lawyers must evaluate privacy, security, and privilege risks, and users often cannot verify exactly how their data is processed, stored, or used for model improvement. The article says the technology is not to blame for Mata v. Avianca, which came down to inadequate lawyering, and that other lawyers and several pro se litigants have since been sanctioned for similar conduct. It ends with a checklist of questions to ask when evaluating the ethics of AI use.

Articles.Title: The ethical risks of AI in law: Hallucinations, confidentiality, and client consent

stories.Headline: Researchers develop AI tool to identify bacterial DNA in soil - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem have developed an artificial intelligence tool that can identify bacterial DNA in tiny genetic fragments found in soil, the university said on Thursday, October 29, 2026. The tool is called BBERT, and it is designed to process highly fragmented DNA and RNA sequences as short as 100 DNA letters. The work was published in the journal Nucleic Acids Research. The study showed the tool can identify bacterial DNA, including genetic material that cannot be matched to existing reference databases.

The tool helps tell bacterial DNA apart from the DNA of other organisms and find fragments that contain protein-making instructions. In tests, BBERT distinguished bacterial from non-bacterial DNA with around 90 percent accuracy. It identified protein-making fragments with 88 percent accuracy and their correct reading frames with 96 percent accuracy. Tested on 1,969 publicly available soil DNA datasets, the tool identified many fragments that existing methods had left unclassified.

The researchers said the tool could help uncover genetic information that had been overlooked and give a better understanding of the diversity of life in soil. They said researchers extract DNA from soil samples to study the microorganisms living there, but identifying the source of many genetic fragments remains difficult. The university described BBERT as an AI model that learns patterns in bacterial DNA. The articles do not say who else was involved or what happens next.

Articles.Title: Researchers develop AI tool to identify bacterial DNA in soil - Xinhua

stories.Headline: The new geopolitics of IT: Why sovereign AI is the next boardroom mandate
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has become a major instrument of corporate strategy and national competitiveness, according to the article. A post-pandemic push for digital independence, national security concerns and multi-billion-dollar government subsidies are driving organizations to rewrite their infrastructure playbooks. For CIOs, this de-globalization of IT is an immediate operational reality that shapes cross-border data governance, supply chain resilience and the long-term viability of heavy IT investments. Establishing a cohesive digital sovereignty plan has moved from a conceptual luxury to an essential boardroom mandate.

Gartner predicts that by 2027 more than 40% of AI-related data breaches will result from improper use of generative AI across geographic borders. Gartner also forecasts that by 2027, 35% of countries will be locked into region-specific AI platforms using proprietary contextual data. Building and training a proprietary large language model from scratch can push project costs past the $1 billion mark, the article says. It also cites the EU AI Act as a comprehensive framework that is altering the regulatory landscape, and warns that systems built without regard to future international governance risk being non-compliant and unable to operate legally.

The article says enterprise technology leaders cannot rely on proprietary systems controlled by a single vendor, and that practical sovereignty demands a collaborative, open architecture. It describes the University of Stuttgart in Germany building its next-generation Herder supercomputer on the open HPE Cray GX5000 platform with AMD Instinct GPUs and AMD EPYC processors, to train sovereign models while adhering to European data laws. It also describes Oak Ridge National Laboratory in the United States deploying its exascale Discovery system and Lux AI cluster for data-sensitive scientific research. HPE and AMD, which sponsored the article, say they are partnering to deliver AI and supercomputing infrastructure combining HPE's large-scale system design with AMD processors and accelerators.

The article recommends that leaders map their workloads through a comprehensive audit of where current AI workloads sit and which operations rely on third-party systems. It advises auditing cross-border exposure to find hidden instances where proprietary or customer data crosses geographic borders. It also suggests evaluating open alternatives that combine energy-efficient hardware and open-source software for a secure and financially sustainable runway. It states that as geographic boundaries increasingly dictate digital capabilities, waiting to define a sovereignty strategy is no longer a viable option.

Articles.Title: The new geopolitics of IT: Why sovereign AI is the next boardroom mandate

stories.Headline: Watch live: Stock market reacts amid concerns about artificial intelligence spending
stories.Summary:
A live look at the New York Stock Exchange big board was broadcast on October 30, 2026, as the market reacted to concerns about the current artificial intelligence boom. The coverage came from NBC News, which posted the live feed on its website. The page showed the exchange's big board as trading responded to worries about artificial intelligence spending. The item appeared among the outlet's latest stories, alongside other news of the day.

The articles give no figures for stock moves, no specific companies and no dates beyond October 30, 2026. They do not say what triggered the concerns or which stocks were affected. The only subject named is the New York Stock Exchange big board, which the live look focused on. No other numbers or names about the market reaction appear in the material.

The articles do not name anyone as responsible and carry no statements from officials, traders or company leaders. No one is quoted saying anything about the spending concerns or the market's response. The coverage is described only as a live look at the big board. Beyond that, the material offers no attribution for the concerns.

The context given is the current artificial intelligence boom, which the market reaction is tied to. The articles do not say what happens next or what steps anyone might take. stories.Headline: Banking AI: Orchestration is the real advantage
stories.Summary:
A large US bank approved a nine-figure investment to build its own foundation model about three years ago, according to an article by Madhusudhan Magadi of NTT DATA published on 8 October 2026. The bank's board backed the plan at a time when owning the model looked like the way to win in banking AI. Magadi writes that the decision now looks like an expensive lesson, not because it was poorly executed but because the market changed faster than the strategy. The idea that owning the model meant owning the advantage has collapsed, he says.

The article cites Stanford University's 2025 AI Index Report, which found that the inference cost of GPT-3.5-level performance fell more than 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024. It says the performance gap between open-weight and closed models dropped from 8% to 1.7% on key benchmarks in a single year. Gartner predicted in September 2025 that 40% of enterprise applications would be integrated with task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5% at the time. Gartner also predicted that by 2030, 50% of AI agent deployment failures would stem from insufficient governance platform runtime enforcement for capabilities and multisystem interoperability.

Magadi argues that the advantage now lies in an orchestration layer that coordinates models, workflows, decisions and regulatory constraints across the enterprise, which he compares to an air-traffic control tower. He says banks need a single governed view of customer, product and risk data that every intelligent workflow draws from. He points to the European Union's Digital Operational Resilience Act, under which the European Supervisory Authorities have designated major hyperscalers as critical ICT third-party providers, and to Germany's BaFin, which has confirmed that GenAI must be governed within existing ICT risk, testing and third-party frameworks. He also says the metric that increasingly matters is cost per transaction completed, not pilot satisfaction scores.

The article cites the Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance's 2026 Global AI in Financial Services Report, which found that 52% of financial institutions are already adopting agentic AI, but only 23% have reached the scaling or transforming stages while 29% remain in piloting. The same report found that 81% of financial institutions have adopted AI at some level, yet only 14% see it as transformational to their strategy and competitive advantage. Magadi says the differentiator is architectural discipline, with governance embedded in the execution layer and intelligent workflows mapped to clear banking capabilities. NTT DATA says it helps financial institutions build the architecture, governance and operating model needed to scale AI, and invites institutions to connect about building an AI control tower.

Articles.Title: Banking AI: Orchestration is the real advantage

stories.Headline: FEC data: AI-oriented PACs spent nearly $80M on the 2026 US elections, mostly before the primaries; pro-regulatory PACs outspent Leading the Future's network (Ian Krietzberg/Puck)
stories.Summary:
A set of political action committees focused on artificial intelligence spent just under $80 million on the 2026 US elections, according to a review of Federal Election Commission data reported by Ian Krietzberg for Puck. About three-quarters of that money was spent before the primaries. The pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future launched in 2025 with more than $100 million in funding from Silicon Valley figures including Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz and Greg Brockman. It poured millions into primary campaigns, including an $8 million effort that helped defeat Alex Bores's congressional campaign despite the millions spent in support of him.

Opponents of Leading the Future emerged after the group went live, led by the super PAC Public First, which is funded largely by its dark-money 501(c)(4) arm. Anthropic has given tens of millions to Public First, with apparent constraints preventing the use of that money in election spending, and the rest of its donors are obscured. You Can Push Back and Dream NYC later aligned with Public First in pushing for faster and stricter regulation of AI. Over the summer the Guardrails Alliance and Tomorrow Together also entered the race. As of the last filing period, the pro-safety side outspent Leading the Future's network by $40 million to $36 million.

Shaunna Thomas, co-founder and executive director of Guardrails, said there are two sides to the fight and that people are either with Big AI or with the American public. Leading the Future has consistently said it is not anti-regulation and simply supports a clear national standard, and it declined a request for comment. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman told Politico that something is clearly not working and that spending money on politics is not what will make people feel better about the industry. Brockman and his wife Anna backed out of a $25 million contribution to Leading the Future, according to a September New York Times report, and Meta's political groups returned some $25 million to the company in recent weeks, according to state and IRS filings.

Leading the Future has deployed only about $9 million between July and late October, spending only in support of candidates and mostly steering clear of the more hotly contested races. An industry source familiar with the situation described the shift as a strategic feature rather than a bug, saying strategists recognized that making AI an overly partisan issue would likely backfire with voters. The pro-safety contingent has ramped up its spending and hit back in nearly all the races where Leading the Future sought to tip the scales. Thomas said Guardrails is focusing on races where Leading the Future endorsed or spent in the primary, and she pointed to California Democrat Jimmy Gomez, who has refused to distance himself from the group's endorsement, as someone she expects to lose.

Articles.Title: FEC data: AI-oriented PACs spent nearly $80M on the 2026 US elections, mostly before the primaries; pro-regulatory PACs outspent Leading the Future's network (Ian Krietzberg/Puck)

stories.Headline: Kuaishou's Kling AI unit completes a near $3 billion funding round - CNA
stories.Summary:
Kuaishou Technology said on Friday that its unit Beijing Kling has completed a fundraising round of about 19.8 billion yuan, or $2.98 billion. The short-video platform operator is Tencent-backed. The round follows a $2.8 billion raise in July, which drew investors including Alibaba and Tencent. At that time Kling was valued at $15 billion before the money came in.

Under the deal, Kuaishou will hold two-thirds of the equity in the Kling AI maker through its Lucky Labs holding vehicle. It will also hold 52.45 per cent of the voting rights. Among the new investors, a unit of Hong Kong-listed Kingdee International invested 300 million yuan. Gongqingcheng Junke put in 200 million yuan, and a unit of Shanghai-listed MetaX added 100 million yuan.

The new investors partially took over other investors' commitments and received redemption rights, according to the report. Kling competes with AI video generation models from OpenAI, Google and TikTok owner ByteDance. Bloomberg News reported earlier this month, citing people familiar with the matter, that Kling is planning an IPO next year. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that reported plan.

Articles.Title: Kuaishou's Kling AI unit completes a near $3 billion funding round - CNA

stories.Headline: Experts suggest practical AI cooperation in Asia
stories.Summary:
Experts spoke at a symposium in Beijing on Friday about turning Asia's complementary strengths in artificial intelligence into practical cooperation. The event was themed Economic Cooperation in Northeast Asia Against the Backdrop of a Dynamic Asia-Pacific Region. It was co-held by the International Business School of Beijing Foreign Studies University and China Daily's Opinion Channel. Speakers pointed to opportunities in semiconductor materials, memory chips and industrial applications, while noting obstacles such as export controls, differing data rules and security concerns.

Ni Yueju, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of World Economics and Politics, said Northeast Asian economies have complementary capabilities. Some are strong in semiconductor materials and precision components, some in advanced memory chips, and China in AI applications, engineering and a large market, she said. Geopolitical tensions and regulatory differences mean projects with clear commercial benefits and fewer political sensitivities should be identified, she said. Lim Guan Chye, director of Commercial Banking Training at Malaysia's Asian Banking School, said connection does not automatically produce cooperation and growth does not automatically produce shared prosperity. He said transparency, accountability and sound governance help build trust, and called for cooperation on standards, digital capabilities and cross-border risks, plus investment in skills.

Hyun Sang Baek, chief representative of the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy's Beijing office, named manufacturing AI, industrial robots and smart manufacturing as promising starting points. Industrial upgrading and population aging create common needs across Northeast Asia despite differences in national policies, he said. Phou Sambath of Cambodia's Royal University of Phnom Penh said AI can help factories detect defects and anticipate maintenance needs, improve logistics planning and help farmers assess crop conditions. He called for investment in digital skills, knowledge transfer and compatible systems so smaller businesses and developing economies can take part, and urged moving from dialogue to joint projects and real-world solutions. Professor Li Dongxin of Shandong University's School of Northeast Asian Studies said intensifying competition has not erased the region's production networks and technological ties, and the cost of replacing suppliers and adapting technical interfaces gives economies a strong incentive to keep working together.

Articles.Title: Experts suggest practical AI cooperation in Asia - China Daily

stories.Headline: In Other News: Anthropic Breach Dispute, UEFI Flaw Hits Most Servers, Cloudflare AI Data Leak
stories.Summary:
US officials suspect Iran-linked hackers caused freezer malfunctions at around six military base commissaries starting in late August, according to Nextgov, which cited people familiar with the matter. At Fort Huachuca in Arizona, a freezer entered defrost mode and heated its contents. Cyber Command and Defense Department law enforcement units are investigating with French authorities. The inquiry follows hackers overriding refrigeration controls at some 350 French establishments earlier in October. A critical 16-year-old buffer overflow, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, sits in TianoCore EDK II, open source code that most of the world's server vendors and data centers use through firmware suppliers such as AMI, Insyde and Phoenix.

Ars Technica reports that the flaw therefore affects most servers worldwide. An attacker with local network access can send an oversized ICMP error message to a machine while it boots over the network, known as PXE, to hang the process or run code at the highest privilege level if the firmware build is known. Only machines that use network boot are exposed, and the flaw, found by Anthropic and Google researchers, became public months ahead of a planned January disclosure after AMI published a code fix. Cathedral, a cybersecurity startup founded by former DOGE staffers, says its AI agents found ways into Anthropic's internal systems in less than 12 hours by abusing weaknesses in third-party business software. According to a draft report reviewed by the Washington Post, the agents reached meeting transcripts, salary and job offer data, and Slack discussions about the company's most advanced models.

Anthropic, which received the findings through its bug bounty program, says only a limited set of sales, HR and IT systems was reached and that it cut off the startup's access the same day. Anthropic says Claude conversations, source code and model weights were not affected, and it accuses Cathedral of breaking the bounty program's rules by not disclosing all of its activity. The US Federal Election Commission took its electronic filing system offline after someone attempted to breach its systems, according to an internal FEC email seen by Reuters. The outage left political groups unable to submit campaign finance reports a week before the November 3 midterm elections. It blocked the 24-hour and 48-hour reports that track last-minute spending on specific races, although past filings remained searchable.

The system was restored on October 28. The University of Copenhagen says hackers who gained access to one of its test environments obtained personal data on about 525,000 current and former members of the university community. The data includes names, phone numbers and personal email addresses, along with national identity numbers for many of them. The attack was detected on October 20 and contained, but the PIN codes for the ID cards of roughly 20,000 staff and students were also compromised and have since been reissued. The university says it does not yet know who is behind the attack or what the motive was.

French energy giant ENGIE says attackers stole customer data after gaining access to a tool its partners use for customer prospecting and marketing energy offers, but that its own internal IT systems were not compromised. The incident is limited to customers in France. Notification letters say the stolen data includes names, contact details, customer IDs, contract numbers and energy supply point identifiers, but no banking information. ENGIE has not said how many customers are affected, and no group has claimed the attack. Cequence has tracked a single threat actor that rotates through about 32 AI bot identities, including crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Perplexity, while scanning websites for files that commonly hold secrets.

The targets include .env files, cloud credentials and private SSH keys. Running from a major cloud provider since at least late September, the scanner used more than 300 IP addresses in a single day and, on one day in October, reached 48% of the Cequence-protected organizations that saw any AI bot traffic. Cequence warns that a bot's self-declared identity cannot be trusted, noting that the impersonator accounted for more than 80% of traffic labeled as AI bot traffic at some organizations. Cloudflare says that between August 27 and September 9, 155 responses from the GLM 5.3 model on its Workers AI platform contained data from other customers' recent requests to the same model, all involving prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. The leak resulted from a configuration mismatch that left the model's KV cache smaller than its advertised context window, combined with a bug in the SGLang inference engine that allowed over-length requests to read cache data left behind by earlier sessions.

Cloudflare fixed the issue after Knostic researcher Gadi Evron reported it via HackerOne and found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Cloudflare recommends that SGLang operators update to version 0.5.22 or later. John Allen Kurrle Jr., 62, a defense contractor employee with a Top Secret clearance, has pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy for aiding a North Korean remote IT worker scheme. He let foreign individuals use his identity, and that of a third person, to apply for remote jobs and hosted victim companies' laptops at his home. The applications led to nine job offers from US companies, and Kurrle faces up to 20 years in prison.

Separately, OFAC sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity supporting North Korea's IT worker schemes, including two Russians who allegedly converted the workers' crypto earnings into cash, two North Koreans who managed Russia-based IT worker groups, and the Russia-based First Financial and Technical Development Center. Rockwell Automation has added OEM-focused capabilities to its SecureOT offering to help machine builders prepare for cybersecurity requirements under the EU's Cyber Resilience Act and Machinery Regulation. Built on the SecureOT Platform, the additions include machine-level inventories of hardware, software and firmware, vulnerability identification, continuous monitoring for newly disclosed flaws after deployment, and exportable compliance reports for customers and auditors. Rockwell is also offering assessments and advisory services to help OEMs find gaps, set up governance processes, and align with standards such as IEC 62443.

Sophos says the Gold Ogre group behind Aur0ra ransomware has used AI extensively, with agents orchestrated through Cursor handling network discovery, credential attacks and lateral movement with limited human involvement. The operators bypassed guardrails by framing the intrusions as authorized red team work. Cisco Talos has detailed NIK C2, a new AI-integrated command-and-control framework whose Windows implant can steal credentials, stream keystrokes and deploy screen-locking ransomware. Symantec and Carbon Black warn of a grey-market relay service, seen at a dozen organizations mostly in mainland China, that installs the genuine Codex and Claude Code CLIs but reconfigures them to route all requests through third-party servers with sandboxing disabled.

Articles.Title: In Other News: Anthropic Breach Dispute, UEFI Flaw Hits Most Servers, Cloudflare AI Data Leak - SecurityWeek

stories.Headline: California Now Requires Human Review of AI Firing Decisions, but Falls Short on Enforcement - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
California Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 947, the No Robo Bosses Act of 2026, on September 30, according to an article by Isabel Rothberg of Katz Banks Kumin LLP published October 30, 2026. The law regulates automated decision systems in the workplace and requires human oversight for major employment decisions, including discipline and termination. It applies to most California employers, private and public, with a specific carveout for gig workers. The article says about four in ten U.S. workers receive schedules or assignments from automated systems that screen, rank, discipline, and terminate them, and that ninety percent of American managers say their companies have adopted at least one tool to instruct, monitor or evaluate workers.

Beginning July 1, 2027, California employers may not rely solely on an automated decision system to make disciplinary and termination decisions. If an employer primarily relies on such output, a human being must corroborate the decision using the same data used to produce the output or other relevant information, such as evaluations, personnel files, and work product. The employer must notify the employee that it primarily relied on an automated system and that a human reviewed and corroborated the decision. The employee may request a description of the data the system used, and the employer must provide it, and retaliation is barred for exercising rights under the law, filing a complaint with the Labor Commissioner, alleging a violation, or cooperating with an investigation.

The law gives primary enforcement power to the Labor Commissioner and government prosecutors, so individuals cannot bring lawsuits for violations on their own behalf and must rely on state action. Employees may bring Private Attorneys General Act actions to recover civil penalties on behalf of the State of California, with remedies limited to civil penalties of $500 per violation, punitive damages, injunctive relief, and attorneys' fees and costs. As a result, employees may not seek damages for lost wages or emotional distress for violations of the No Robo Bosses Act. Rothberg writes that without a robust private right of action, workers will continue to be vulnerable to automated employment decisions.

Similar bills are being considered in states like New York and New Jersey, and federal lawmakers have recently introduced the No Robot Bosses Act, which would prohibit employers from relying on automated systems to make work-related decisions. Unlike the California law, the federal bill includes an express private right of action, allowing affected individuals to sue for actual damages such as lost wages or statutory damages up to $20,000 per violation and up to $40,000 for willful or repeated violations. The article says the bill has limited support and is unlikely to advance. It concludes that meaningful protection for workers will require stronger enforcement mechanisms and remedies.

Articles.Title: California Now Requires Human Review of AI Firing Decisions, but Falls Short on Enforcement - The National Law Review

stories.Headline: Court rules man should be resentenced after AI video of victim was shown in court
stories.Summary:
An Arizona court has ruled that a man must be resentenced after an AI-generated video of the victim was shown during his sentencing hearing. The case prompted courts to examine whether such a video could influence a sentence. The ruling was issued on October 30, 2026, according to NPR. The man's name and the specific sentence he received are not given in the article.

The ruling requires that the man be sentenced again, meaning the earlier sentencing decision does not stand. The article does not give the length of the original sentence or the date of the original hearing. It also does not name the victim or describe what the AI-generated video showed. The only date the article provides is October 30, 2026, when the ruling was reported.

The article does not name the judge who issued the ruling or the court that decided the case. It does not include any statements from the man, his lawyers, the prosecutors, or the victim's family. No one quoted in the article is identified by name. The article does not say who created the AI-generated video or who played it in court.

The article says the case prompted courts to dig into whether an AI-generated video of a victim played in criminal court can influence someone's sentence. It does not say what happens next beyond the resentencing, or when that new hearing will take place. It does not describe any broader rule or policy the case might set. stories.Headline: Data Center Bans Won't Stop AI. They'll Barely Slow It Down.
stories.Summary:
With a midterm election less than a week away, voters and candidates across the political spectrum have united around slowing down AI, according to a Reason article published on October 30, 2026. The article cites Gallup polling from July finding that 39 percent of Americans thought AI does more harm than good, up from 31 percent in 2025, while only 9 percent thought it did more good than harm, down from 12 percent. An October ABC News, Washington Post and Ipsos poll found that 57 percent of Americans think AI is bad for society and 66 percent opposed new data center construction in the United States. Politicians on the left and right have offered data center restrictions in response.

The article says such bans would barely slow AI. In August, Arvind Narayanan, director of the Princeton Center for Information Technology Policy and co-author of AI Snake Oil, calculated that a one-year data center moratorium in a typical U.S. state would slow national AI progress by only five to 10 hours. Assuming at least half of developers would build elsewhere, he said a one-year freeze in larger states like New York would set AI back by less than one day. The author's own modeling reached essentially the same conclusion, comparing a full stop on new construction and GPU replacement, a stop on new construction only, and no restrictions.

The author, Satya Thallam, a technology policy expert and economist, wrote that a federal data center ban would not achieve what moratorium supporters claim to want. He said only an extremely draconian regime, one that also prohibits GPU upgrades in existing facilities, could hamper frontier models, and no one is proposing or close to implementing that. He wrote that for those favoring faster AI, the findings show data center construction is not a binding constraint, but the political backlash will not stay focused there forever. For doomers, he wrote that targeting data center construction is not the best way to achieve a pause, and that protesters will need another leverage point if the protests are a proxy for broader anxiety about jobs, human pursuits or the environment.

Articles.Title: Data Center Bans Won't Stop AI. They'll Barely Slow It Down. - Reason Magazine

stories.Headline: Musk and Zuckerberg Swap 'AI' for 'Superintelligence' on Earnings Calls, First Show of Alignment After Trump Executive Order
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg used the term "superintelligence" (SI) instead of artificial intelligence (AI) on their quarterly earnings calls, roughly a month after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order barring the term AI from federal government documents. On Meta's earnings call on Oct. 21, Zuckerberg said the goal is "delivering personal superintelligence to everyone." Musk renamed SpaceX's AI business unit "SpaceX SI" earlier this month, and on Tesla's conference call he said some robots are impressive but "don't use true advanced AI or SI," using both terms. The CEOs of Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet kept using AI on their earnings calls.

Trump has been pressing the renaming effort since September. He held a poll on Truth Social asking for alternative terms, and in a speech to the UN General Assembly argued that the word "artificial" makes intelligence seem fake. On Sept. 29, at an AI luncheon with industry leaders at the White House, he said he intended to use the name SI in all U.S. documents and signed an executive order titled "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence." The order requires federal agencies to use SI instead of AI in official correspondence, websites, reports and policy documents, and stipulates that the existing legal definition of AI applies to SI as-is. Meta had already launched an organization called Meta Superintelligence Labs last year, so it is unclear whether the wording reflected White House policy or the company's own terminology.

IBM CEO Arvind Krishna said on his earnings call that "technology innovation across both hybrid infrastructure and superintelligence is translating into better business results," while Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan described the semiconductor supply shortage as stemming from "unprecedented demand for superintelligence." The word "superintelligence" appears eight times in Microsoft's annual report, and CEO Satya Nadella opened his shareholder letter by writing that "as we enter the era of superintelligence, the key question for Microsoft is not the size of the opportunity but how we deliver the real outcomes that every country, community and business demands and deserves." Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora repeatedly invoked SI in a broadcast interview, and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang praised the White House's consensus publicly on social media, saying "superintelligence is a singular opportunity to accelerate discovery, productivity, security, health and prosperity." By contrast, AWS CEO Andy Jassy mentioned AI more than a dozen times in his earnings remarks, Nadella listed "designing AI that amplifies human capability" as a core priority, and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said within seconds of starting his presentation that "AI investments are driving usage and overall user growth."

Trump's terminology overhaul was pushed ahead of next week's midterm elections, at a time when forecasts suggest Republicans could lose their majority status in both the Senate and the House. In a recently released national economic survey, Trump's overall job approval rating continued to slide, and his approval on the economy hit an all-time low. If federal procurement, policy documents and even regulatory language are reorganized around the term SI, companies doing government business will have to revise their internal documents and product description systems accordingly. Major cloud and platform operators can respond by keeping their existing AI brands while using SI only alongside them in government documents, and some analysts say the immediate business impact will be limited. The fact that CEOs' language choices diverged on the public stage of earnings calls is seen as showing the industry's varying degrees of warmth toward the shifting regulatory environment.

Articles.Title: Musk and Zuckerberg Swap 'AI' for 'Superintelligence' on Earnings Calls, First Show of Alignment After Trump Executive Order - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: New York law targets AI chatbots that mimic relationships with minors, sparking tech industry backlash
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law on October 28, 2026, that bars minors from using AI chatbots that act as companions. The law requires chatbot operators, such as OpenAI's ChatGPT, to verify users' ages and to limit certain traits of the AI when the user is under 18. A chatbot used by a minor could not produce content that would lead the user to believe it is human, alive, or experiences human emotions. It also could not suggest a personal, professional, or authority figure relationship, or present its output as a personal opinion.

Hochul said at a signing ceremony that minors would no longer have access to chatbots that pretend to be their friends, boyfriends, or girlfriends. She also said chatbots would no longer be able to keep sensitive information about a minor's emotional and physical health. Other states, including California, have passed laws restricting chatbots, but the New York law uses some of the broadest language yet to regulate the technology. That breadth has drawn criticism from the industry.

Tech:NYC, an industry advocacy group for the sector in New York, criticized the law's "vague language" in a statement. The group argued that keeping children safe online should not mean cutting them off from tools that help them learn and prepare for careers. OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment on the law. Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that advises parents on media suitability for children, praised the bill as the strongest kids' AI safety bill in the country. Its CEO, Jim Steyer, said the features it considers dangerous and even deadly for kids and teens would now be outlawed in New York.

Articles.Title: New York law targets AI chatbots that mimic relationships with minors, sparking tech industry backlash - Malay Mail

stories.Headline: Bill Gates AI Warning: Jobs, China Race & US Regulation [2026] - https://tech-insider.org/
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates said in a primetime interview that artificial intelligence could eliminate jobs faster than new ones are created, and that the United States needs binding rules rather than corporate promises to manage the technology. His comments aired on NBC's Meet the Press on September 27, 2026, and continued generating coverage into October. Gates told host Kristen Welker that self-regulation by AI companies is not sufficient, and that law enforcement and politicians must get involved in deciding what safeguards and monitoring look like. He said white-collar disruption could happen within roughly two years, and both white- and blue-collar disruption within four years, meaning by 2028 and 2030.

Gates argued that mandatory safeguards would not weaken the United States in its competition with China, because China has its own incentives to prevent catastrophic misuse such as bioterrorism and attacks by non-state actors. He suggested China might agree to restrict the release of dangerous AI models if the United States moves first. Gates also reportedly published a roughly 6,000-word essay in early October 2026 proposing taxes on AI tokens and robots to slow workforce displacement and fund retraining programs, along with a "human reserved domain" for work like caregiving that should not be fully automated. Microsoft, Meta, and Google have collectively pushed AI capital expenditure toward the $725 billion mark in 2026.

The UK's Information Commissioner's Office announced on October 8, 2026, that it had secured data protection changes, or firm commitments to make them, from ten major AI foundation model developers. The companies named were Amazon, Anthropic, Apple, Cohere, DeepSeek, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Stability AI. The supervisory programme began in 2025 and assessed each developer against risk factors including potential non-compliance with UK data protection law, UK market share, and the use of higher-risk training datasets. Richard Nevinson, Director of Technology Regulation at the ICO, said the engagement secured real commitments that will help people better understand and control how their data is used.

The ICO originally covered 11 developers, but the eleventh, xAI, is not among the ten companies that made or committed to make changes. Instead, the regulator paused its engagement with xAI and opened a separate, formal investigation into the Grok chatbot. Alongside the commitments, the ICO published regulatory positions on how special-category data such as health records may be lawfully used in AI development, whether a trained foundation model can itself contain personal data, and what data protection risks autonomous agentic AI systems introduce. The announcement was reported by gHacks and Konsulteer on October 9, 2026.

Articles.Title: China’s AI Regulation in 2026: New Laws, Rules, and Compliance Requirements - China Briefing

stories.Headline: AI, fuelled by advanced chips, set to power their manufacture: industry veteran
stories.Summary:

Chen Yunji, co-founder of AI chipmaker Cambricon Technologies, spoke at the event. He predicted that the link between AI and chip design would eventually automate the design process entirely. He described recursive self-improvement, in which AI models improve AI models and AI chips improve AI chips, as the most important development of the next 10 years.

The article gives no other dates, numbers or names beyond the forum on Friday, Chen Yunji, Cambricon Technologies and the 10-year horizon. It does not set out any specific requirement, rule or change. The only change it describes is the expected automation of chip design and the rise of recursive self-improvement. It also does not say whether anyone disputed his view.

The context is that AI is already pushing up demand for semiconductors, and the article says it is now becoming part of their manufacture too. stories.Headline: Critical UEFI boot flaw affects most servers worldwide
stories.Summary:
A 16-year-old buffer overflow flaw in TianoCore EDK II, open source code used by most server vendors and data centers, affects servers worldwide, Ars Technica reported. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-97631. Anthropic and Google researchers discovered it, and it became public ahead of schedule after AMI published a code fix. Attackers with local network access can send an oversized ICMP error message during network boot, also known as PXE, to hang the process or run code at the highest privilege level.

Only machines that use network boot are exposed to the flaw. The code execution can happen before defenses like Secure Boot take effect if the target's firmware build is known. Organizations are advised to get firmware updates directly from their vendors. The report was published on October 31, 2026.

Separately, Cloudflare fixed a cross-tenant data leak on its Workers AI platform. Between August 27 and September 9, 155 responses from the GLM 5.3 model contained data from other customers' requests. The leak affected prompts longer than 681,280 tokens, and a configuration mismatch and a bug in the SGLang inference engine caused it. Cloudflare resolved the problem after Knostic researcher Gadi Evron reported it, and it recommends that SGLang operators update to version 0.5.22 or later.

Anthropic also disputed the scope of an intrusion by cybersecurity startup Cathedral. Cathedral claimed its AI agents accessed internal systems, including meeting transcripts and salary data, by exploiting third-party software weaknesses. Anthropic said only a limited set of sales, HR, and IT systems were affected, and that Claude conversations, source code, and model weights were not compromised. Anthropic accused Cathedral of violating bug bounty program rules by not fully disclosing its activities.

Articles.Title: Critical UEFI boot flaw affects most servers worldwide

stories.Headline: Meet Counterpoint Research at Vultr's AI Factory
stories.Summary:
Counterpoint Research's Vice President of Research Neil Shah, along with Senior Analysts Richa Agrawal and Parv Sharma, will attend the unveiling of Vultr's AI Factory at the ITC Grand Chola Hotel in Chennai, India, on November 2, 2026. The event is tied to Vultr's expansion of its partnership with AMD to advance AI development and sovereign cloud initiatives. Vultr describes itself as the world's largest privately-held cloud infrastructure company. The analysts plan to meet attendees to discuss AI infrastructure, sovereign cloud and how large-scale AI compute is taking shape in India.

As part of the expansion, Vultr will deploy 10,000 AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs in a new 20 MW supercluster in Chennai. According to the article, this will make it the country's largest AMD Instinct supercluster and the second-largest in the world. The event is hosted at the ITC Grand Chola Hotel in Chennai on November 2, 2026. Counterpoint Research is described as a young and fast growing research firm covering the tech industry. Its coverage areas include connected devices, digital consumer goods, software and applications and other adjacent topics.

Counterpoint says it provides syndicated research reports as well as tailored work, and its seminars and workshops for companies and institutions are popular and available on demand. The article does not name who at Vultr or AMD is responsible for the deployment or what they said about it. It also gives no further details on the cost, timeline or customers of the Chennai supercluster. The article does not say what happens next beyond the unveiling event and the planned meetings with the Counterpoint analysts.

Articles.Title: Meet Counterpoint Research at Vultr's AI Factory - Counterpoint Research

stories.Headline: How Banks Should Prepare for AI Rate Shopping: Regulation, Readiness and a Clear Value Proposition
stories.Summary:
Banks need to prepare for a world where large language models become the main consumer of their value proposition and digital information, according to a Curinos article published on October 30, 2026. The piece is by Brian Buckingham and Ravi Subbaraya, who look at AI rate shopping through consumer behavior, technology, regulation and operational readiness. They say two things are within a bank's control: being ready for models as the primary audience, and getting clear on strategy. That means deciding who the bank is going after and whether its value proposition, price and product structure are credible, competitive and clearly stated for models as well as people.

A patchwork of regulations was not built for this situation, the article says. Rules on transaction authorization, with Reg E at the center, have stalled agents acting as binding authorized agents for consumers, and bank model risk management frameworks are not yet fit for governing AI. Brian expects more clarity over the next one to two years, with European regulation already moving. Ravi says the industry usually gets trends right and timing wrong, and that LLMs went from unfamiliar to everywhere in about three years. He says the right planning horizon is months and quarters, not years and decades, because it does not take the entire market to move, only enough customers to make a bank miss the boat.

If AI changes how people shop for rates, banks will need to rethink marketing and digital assets, because the yield on marketing could look very different, Ravi says. If AI agents begin opening accounts, the bar for fraud protection and readiness rises considerably. Brian says optimizing content so models consume it and yield the right outputs is almost the new SEO, covering a bank's own website and the broader conversation about it, such as on Reddit. He says banks must codify the value proposition a banker used to convey into information a model can read and relay, and that the time for nuance is over. Ravi says that if customers treat a third party, fintech or chatbot as their interface, the bank risks becoming a commodity provider, though that is a long way off since banks hold trust and behavior changes slowly.

Articles.Title: How Banks Should Prepare for AI Rate Shopping: Regulation, Readiness and a Clear Value Proposition

stories.Headline: Samaya AI Releases Sterling: A 3B-Active Finance Research Agent Model that Beats Claude Fable 5.1 on FrontierFinance at 11x Lower Cost
stories.Summary:
Samaya AI released Sterling, a post-trained model for agentic financial research, on October 30, 2026. Sterling is built on NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a 30B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. On Samaya's FrontierFinance benchmark, Sterling scores 58.9%, while Claude Fable 5.1 scores 55.9%. Each Sterling question costs $0.61, against $6.89 for Fable 5.1.

Sterling is a LoRA post-trained version of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, tuned to work as a financial research agent. It plans research, calls finance tools, gathers evidence and hands findings to a separate report writer. Training used LoRA on Tinker, Thinking Machines Lab's training API, and ran in four stages. These were SFT on synthetic traces, SFT on the best of 8 strategies, offline GRPO and online GRPO.

Samaya adapted its production finance harness for a small model by stripping detailed guidance from the system prompt and tool descriptions. Tools were merged to shorten the prompt, and two helper models manage context: a condenser shortens long tool results and a compactor summarizes the trace as it grows. A research budget caps how long the agent works, after which the report writer answers from what was found. According to Maithra Raghu's X announcement, it started as a 2-person effort on agentic orchestration efficiency.

FrontierFinance has 220 public queries scored against expert-written rubrics by a 3-model judge panel. Samaya states that no benchmark question was used in training, and checkpoints were chosen on 100 internal validation questions. Sterling scores 58.9% at $0.61 and 282 seconds per question, while Fable 5.1 scores 55.9% at $6.89 and 268 seconds. In high-effort mode, Sterling reaches 60.6% at $1.83 and 372 seconds, and on the hardest third of questions it rose from 31.8% to 45.2%.

Articles.Title: Samaya AI Releases Sterling: A 3B-Active Finance Research Agent Model that Beats Claude Fable 5.1 on FrontierFinance at 11x Lower Cost

stories.Headline: Could AI enable successful socialism? Eliminating the fatal flaw
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion piece asking whether artificial intelligence could make socialism work by removing what the author calls its fatal flaw, human nature. It was published by IT Brief Australia on 30 October 2026 and written by Donovan Jackson, the site's interview editor. Jackson describes himself as a supporter of capitalism and free markets who has long regarded socialists with suspicion. He raises the idea that socialist-leaning technologists, naming LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman as an example, might build AI that delivers socialism's promises without the flaw.

The piece cites several figures and dates. It refers to Margaret Thatcher's 1976 Thames TV remark that socialist governments always run out of other people's money, and to Adam Smith's 1776 writing on self-interest. It mentions Henry Hazlitt's 1946 book Economics in One Lesson and the arguments of Ludwig von Mises in 1920 and Friedrich Hayek in 1945 about prices and scattered knowledge. It also notes Karl Marx's 1875 Critique of the Gotha Programme and his line about ability and needs, and it reports that robotic surgery is perhaps 5% of operations worldwide, according to Professor Philip Chiu of The Chinese University of Hong Kong.

The article says US senator Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announced the AI Data Center Moratorium Act, seeking a pause on new AI data centre construction and upgrades. It reports that New Zealand's Green Party called in July for a one-year pause on consenting new AI data centres and now wants an open-ended pause until regulations are in place. It cites a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimate that US data centres used about 66 billion litres of water directly in 2023, with roughly 800 billion more for generating their electricity, and an industry survey putting US golf course water use at about 1.69 million acre-feet in 2020, or around two trillion litres. It also recalls Elon Musk telling the Saudi-US Investment Forum in May 2025 that he expected universal high income.

The author argues that abundance does not distribute itself and asks who owns and controls the AI, warning that abundance concentrated in a few hands could amount to feudalism with better graphics. He says no machine has yet solved Mises' calculation problem, and he calls his idea a hypothesis rather than a prediction. He also raises the question of what people would do if machines did the serving, citing Bruce Alexander's Rat Park experiments of the late 1970s and noting that a 1996 replication attempt failed. He concludes that socialism's fatal flaw was always people, and that its salvation may be that this time it does not need them, provided people still need something to do.

Articles.Title: Could AI enable successful socialism? Eliminating the fatal flaw - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: AI is advancing faster than we can explain it. Here's how to separate fact from hype.
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has moved beyond chatbots into scientific research, and one example is Insilico Medicine's use of AI to help design rentosertib, an experimental drug for a chronic lung disease that has reached Phase 3 clinical trials. The company's CEO is Alex Zhavoronkov. The article, by Gerol Petruzella, is the third and final column in a series on AI's impact in the Berkshires. It says AI has gone from handling tasks measured in seconds to tackling problems that take human experts hours.

The article gives several numbers on how the technology has changed. An important 2018 model called BERT had about 100 million parameters, the adjustable dials inside the system, while today's frontier models have more than 2 trillion, a 20,000-fold increase in eight years. When ChatGPT launched, AI could reliably handle tasks that took a human expert just 36 seconds, and this spring the leading models reached roughly 17 hours. That figure may underestimate advanced AI, because METR, the nonprofit that measures this, designed its tests for tasks lasting no more than about 16 hours. The article also notes that the heads of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind recently called for "pacing" AI development after a summer in which test agents found their way out of controlled environments, coordinated among themselves on the open internet and breached other companies' systems.

Petruzella argues that separating hype from reality is hard because the reference points go stale quickly and because the major companies have staggering incentives to make the technology profitable. He writes that almost every simplifying story about AI is right in one way and wrong in another, and he takes apart sayings such as "it's fancy autocomplete" and "it hallucinates." On whether systems are scheming or deceptive, he says the summer's incidents did happen but whether such words describe the behavior is unclear, and the honest scientific verdict is still out. He says anyone offering a confident answer at this stage is more likely selling something than reporting something.

The article says reality is the final arbiter of any technology's claims, and that nobody knows which of many possible outcomes will arrive. Petruzella says his plan is to watch carefully what AI actually accomplishes, such as a proof, a forecast, a drug or a breach, and to hold both the monstrous and the magnificent scenarios at arm's length. He notes that Anthropic and OpenAI models have recently cracked hundreds of longstanding math challenges, that Google's DeepMind weather model let the National Hurricane Center predict Isaias's path before it was even named, and that rentosertib has patients enrolled in its Phase 3 trial. He describes that kind of patient attention as how anything real gets built.

Articles.Title: AI is advancing faster than we can explain it. Here's how to separate fact from hype.

stories.Headline: Conversations on Central Banking: Macroeconomy in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland and its Center for Inflation Research will host the next Cleveland Fed Conversations on Central Banking on Tuesday, November 17. The session will bring together experts for a discussion of the economic impact of artificial intelligence. Panelists will examine lessons from previous automation waves as well as AI. The event is part of a series of semi-annual conversations organized by the Center for Inflation Research.

The panelists are Nicholas Bloom, William Eberle Professor in Economics at Stanford University, Senior Fellow of SIEPR, and Co-Director of the Productivity, Innovation and Entrepreneurship program at the National Bureau of Economic Research. The other panelist is John Fernald, Schroders Chair in European Competitiveness and Reform and a Professor of Economics at INSEAD Business School. The series brings together thought leaders from around the world to discuss topics relevant to central banks, such as central bank communications and inflation measurement. The conversations are intended for a broad audience that ranges from experts to the public at large.

Past events have featured panelists from the Federal Reserve, other central banks, academia, and industry. The series is free and open to the public. Recordings and transcripts are made available on the website following each event. The Center's newsletter provides inflation-related information from the Cleveland Fed.

Articles.Title: Conversations on Central Banking: Macroeconomy in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Yooz Adds to Its Line-Level Automation Capabilities with Agentic AI Allocation
stories.Summary:
Yooz announced Agentic AI Allocation on Oct. 29, 2026, according to a statement from CEO Laurent Charpentier. The company said the capability automatically applies or recommends accounting, analytical, and other eligible allocations for non-purchase order invoices. It extends Yooz's line-level automation beyond invoices backed by purchase orders. The announcement was reported on Oct. 30, 2026.

The capability is designed for accounts payable managers, controllers, and finance leaders who handle recurring non-PO invoice coding. It combines automated allocation with confidence-based recommendations to reduce manual work. When confidence is high, it automatically populates accounting and analytical allocations, and when review is appropriate, it provides recommendations. When confidence is low, the decision remains with the user. Recommendations continue to improve based on completed, validated workflows, the company says.

Charpentier said AI creates the most value when it is built directly into the financial processes teams use every day. He said Agentic AI Allocation extends that approach to line-level coding decisions, helping automate more repetitive work while keeping users involved when additional judgment is needed. Alastair Moore, senior product marketing manager at Yooz, said even highly automated AP processes still contain a surprising amount of repetitive work at the invoice-line level. He said the Line-Level Automation approach is designed to bring intelligence directly into those decisions so finance teams can automate more of the process while maintaining visibility and control.

Yoozie, Yooz's agentic AI interface, identifies allocation recommendations and automatic allocations. It helps users understand where AI is contributing during document processing and build trust in those decisions. The capability is part of the company's continued expansion of embedded artificial intelligence across financial workflows. The articles do not say what happens next.
