Companies with significant market positions should assess their distribution practices, pricing policies, and contractual arrangements for potential competition law risks. The court also issued new guidance on AI disputes, addressing deepfakes, voice cloning, AI-generated hallucinations, online doxxing, big-data price discrimination, autonomous driving, and model training. The guidance is particularly relevant to foreign AI developers training models on Chinese-language content or deploying AI systems in China.

The Supreme People’s Court also issued nine typical unfair-competition cases covering trade secrets, commercial disparagement, false advertising, passing off, and online competition. These cases set guidance for lower courts handling such disputes. China’s Supreme People’s Procuratorate published five typical cases on the use of technical expertise in IP enforcement, addressing patent infringement, trade-secret protection, copyright technical protection measures, and unauthorized deep linking. For foreign rights holders, the cases show how Chinese prosecutors assess technically complex IP disputes, particularly trade-secret theft and whether confidential information qualifies as a trade secret. The developments highlight the importance of monitoring China’s evolving judicial interpretations and enforcement practices across IP, competition, and AI regulation.

Articles.Title: CPI | China IP Update: AI Disputes & Competition Cases

stories.Headline: Democrats Are Playing With the AI Fire - Byline Times | Substack
stories.Summary:
Crypto and AI companies have been putting more than $520 million into a political influence campaign for the 2026 midterms, according to Byline Times. The money goes through Political Action Committees, which can raise unlimited funds. Crypto spending has leaned toward Republicans at 62 to 38 percent, while AI spending has leaned toward Democrats at 61 to 39 percent. The FairShake crypto PAC network spent $40 million to help defeat Democrat Sherrod Brown in 2024 and has dropped at least another $30 million this cycle to fight his return to Congress.

In 2025, 18 Senate Democrats crossed the aisle to help Donald Trump pass the GENIUS Act, a regulatory package friendly to stablecoins such as Tether, and almost all of them had benefited from crypto SuperPAC spending. Leading the Future, a pro-AI PAC network that has taken cash from OpenAI's Greg Brockman, is modelled on FairShake, and the two share donors including Andreessen Horowitz and personnel including Josh Vlasto. The Public First Action PAC network has taken more than $40 million from Anthropic, the maker of Claude. Politico reported that Democratic consultants have urged candidates in competitive seats to stay quiet on AI for fear of being targeted by the PACs.

Thomas Ferguson of the Institute for New Economic Thinking, who co-wrote a recent paper, said most ordinary people are really unhappy, frightened and squeezed, especially on healthcare. He described the Democratic Party as a split-level show, contrasting an affordability-minded grassroots wing with old guard Democrats tied to corporate America and Silicon Valley. He said crypto had bought a powerful position within the Democratic Party, and that a past Democratic elite with a questionable record on financial reform is re-emerging with tech industry support, offering a weak, industry-friendly regulatory settlement. He warned that the same Democrats who coddled the banks after 2008 are now offering to do the same for tech, with money as their big weapon.

Barack Obama and Kamala Harris have publicly backed Project Blueprint, which aims to put AI executives in the room with the politicians writing the industry's rules. It sits inside the venture firm of Democratic mega-donor Ron Conway, who has also backed Leading the Future with $100 million, and is led by former Obama press secretary Jay Carney. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has launched a commission designing the Democrats' AI safety policy in partnership with the innovation community, stacked with representatives who have benefited from PAC spending. Ferguson warned that if both parties patronise Silicon Valley and fail to curb its excesses, there is a real risk that history repeats itself.

Articles.Title: Democrats Are Playing With the AI Fire - Byline Times | Substack

stories.Headline: New Framework Puts Ransomware Resilience for AI Systems in Focus
stories.Summary:
Behnaz Karimi, co-lead of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project’s AI Bill of Materials initiative, developed a new framework called the Ransomware Assessment and Incident Defense Framework for AI Systems, or RAID-AI, over the past two years with help from Yuvaraj Govindarajulu, also a co-lead at OWASP AIBOM. The tool is available online for free to anyone who wants to use it. The two had planned to introduce it at the ISC2 Security Congress in Denver, Colorado, held between October 26 and 28, but visa issues stopped Karimi from attending. Karimi told Infosecurity that RAID-AI focuses on ransomware attacks against AI systems, whether or not an attacker uses AI.

The framework asks security teams to assess their own controls by hand rather than connecting to or scanning their systems. Users select maturity levels on a scale from zero to five, and the controls are grouped into general and AI-specific categories with levels such as basic, advanced and high. General controls cover recovery, training and sensitive-data protection, while AI-specific areas include data, tools and runtime. RAID-AI maps controls to NIST’s Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 and CISA’s Cybersecurity Performance Goals 2.0, and it lets users map adversarial attacks through MITRE ATT&CK, MITRE ATLAS and NIST Adversarial. Organizations do not need to connect internal systems or upload company documents to complete the assessment.

Karimi said ransomware attacks targeting AI systems are slowly being seen now. She pointed to an April 2025 report by Zoran Mitrovic, head of engineering at Kintra Health, which detailed how ransomware actors used data poisoning techniques, and to an alleged cyber-attack on Novo Nordisk in June 2026 where hackers claimed to have stolen AI models used by the pharmaceutical company. She said the assessment is not an automated audit, so results depend on users’ evaluations and the tool does not independently verify an organization’s security posture. She told Infosecurity that teams should ideally bring security managers, engineers and AI-security specialists together in workshops.

The console shows results in dashboards, including maturity views and mappings to other frameworks, and users can download PDF reports that highlight weaknesses and help teams set priorities. Karimi said the dashboard can give senior leaders a high-level overview while technical teams use the underlying controls to guide more detailed discussions. Karimi and Govindarajulu have provided documentation covering guidelines for using the tool and how it was developed and how maturity levels and security scores are calculated. In the future, Karimi hopes to provide practical implementation resources, including videos and blueprints to help security engineers apply individual controls, and to develop a similar tool for ransomware threats targeting agentic AI systems.

Articles.Title: New Framework Puts Ransomware Resilience for AI Systems in Focus

stories.Headline: Float’s Rob Khazzam on how Canadian companies should rethink AI spending
stories.Summary:
Rob Khazzam, co-founder and CEO of the Toronto-based startup Float, discovered a few months ago that his own AI usage was costing $2,364 a day. He had selected an expensive model without realizing it would stay the default for new conversations, so even routine prompts ran up the bill. He shared the story in a recent interview with BetaKit as a lesson for other business leaders. Float builds what it describes as Canada's intelligent financial operating system and serves nearly 10,000 customers.

AI spending on Float grew twelve-fold over two years and more than four-fold in the past year alone, Khazzam said. In the past year, seventy percent of customers had a month when their AI bill jumped 50 percent. At Float itself, token spend rose from the equivalent of 0.1 percent of payroll a year earlier to about five to six percent in October. Khazzam now looks at payroll and token spend together as a share of revenue, expecting the business to grow alongside the combined expense.

Khazzam said leaders should understand how AI spending helps teams accomplish more while catching costly habits like his own. He argued the right frame is to view payroll and token spend together as a human capital investment, rather than treating AI as a software expense to cut whenever it climbs. Before posting a role, managers at Float must email and explain why the role is needed and how AI can support the work, though hiring may still go ahead and Float is hiring now more than ever. He also said the marginal benefit of a frontier model is not needed in most use cases, and he favors giving data scientists and principal engineers more discretion over access to powerful models.

Khazzam recommended setting spending thresholds and assigning someone to flag when usage crosses them, investigate the causes, and recommend adjustments. Letting employees try different AI tools helped Float find useful applications, but people sometimes solved the same problem with different products, and he said 20 people were once trying to solve the same problem using five different tools. Monthly adoption reports showed who was using which products and consuming the most tokens, and Float eventually consolidated its tools. Standardizing made it easier to manage permissions and protect, according to the article, which ends there.

Articles.Title: Float’s Rob Khazzam on how Canadian companies should rethink AI spending

stories.Headline: CFTC chair calls for financial rules redesign for autonomous AI agents
stories.Summary:
Michael Selig, a commissioner at the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, called for financial regulation to be redesigned for a world in which autonomous artificial intelligence agents can hold assets and trade directly. He spoke on Oct. 29 at the first Frontier Forum in Washington, according to a Cointelegraph report cited by DigitalToday. Selig said existing regulatory systems assume that human traders are the ones carrying out financial activity. He said regulators must now address situations in which AI agents act independently in financial markets.

Selig said it is now possible to imagine a refrigerator staking ether and using the proceeds to buy groceries automatically, or even issuing its own meme coin. He said regulators must answer how they would supervise such activity. He described AI as a technology as real as the printing press, the steam engine and the internet. He said the core issue is who bears responsibility when an agent slips beyond control. He also said regulators may need an agent verification system, separate from existing know-your-customer systems, to identify on whose behalf multiple agents are trading.

Selig said AI could give individual investors and small businesses risk-management capabilities that were previously available only to large institutions. He warned that as AI becomes more autonomous, unexpected market reactions could emerge. He said trades could become one-sided if agents using similar models make similar decisions, and that ultra-high-speed automated trading could make market surveillance and risk management harder. The Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee warned last year that widespread use of similar models could amplify market shocks. Animoca Brands Chairman Yat Siu also said that if many users ask AI the same trading question, they could all get similar answers.

Crypto trading infrastructure is rapidly adopting autonomous trading tools. Coinbase unveiled an agentic wallet in February that lets AI agents execute spending and trading within user-set limits. Binance introduced features for AI agents in March and began supporting market data and spot order placement and management functions. In a survey released by eToro in September, 79 percent of U.S. millennial investors and 77 percent of Gen Z investors said they already use AI or are willing to use it to choose investments or adjust portfolios. The report says the CFTC's concerns are not limited to crypto, and that as asset holding, order execution and risk management shift to AI agents, regulators face the task of redefining registration requirements, assignment of responsibility, monitoring methods and verification procedures.

Articles.Title: CFTC chair calls for financial rules redesign for autonomous AI agents

stories.Headline: Sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
stories.Summary:
Google Research researchers Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni introduced a sleep framework for continual learning in large language models, announced in a blog post dated October 27, 2026. The work was conducted by Behrouz of Google and Cornell University, Farnoosh Hashemi of Cornell University, Adel Javanmard of Google and the University of Southern California, and Mirrokni. The framework adds a sleep phase so a deployed model can keep learning new facts and improve reasoning without catastrophic forgetting or a fixed knowledge cutoff. The post says the approach lets models retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens.

The framework alternates an active wake phase, where the model processes inputs and stores temporary information in short-term memory, with an offline sleep phase for memory consolidation and self-improvement. During sleep, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts memory blocks and updates its weights using self-generated practice examples, while its core codebase and design stay unchanged. Consolidation uses parameter expansion with the Hope architecture, Generalized Knowledge Distillation, reinforcement learning-based imitation learning and Levenshtein distance, then resets high-frequency temporary parameters through synaptic pruning. A dreaming stage randomly activates non-standard experts, filters synthetic samples with gradient-based data selection, and refines the model with supervised fine-tuning. The post says the framework operates within a fixed architecture and human-defined training rules.

In results, the sleep method had a near-zero performance drop in multi-stage continual translation for unseen languages such as Manchu and Kalamang, where in-context learning, Cartridges and supervised fine-tuning suffered severe forgetting. On the BABILong long-context benchmark it showed near-perfect scaling up to 10M tokens, outperforming GPT-4 and Titans. For factual knowledge incorporation on SQuAD and continued pre-training it reached 48.9% on single-task and 46.2% on CPT evaluations, beating the base model, SFT and Self-Adapting Language Models. On AIME 24/25 and HMMT 25 math benchmarks, a sleep-enhanced base model scored 79.2%, 69.0% and 46.1%, above SFT, group relative policy optimization and on-policy self-distillation.

The post presents the paradigm as a path toward autonomous, continually learning AI systems that move beyond static pre-training and fragile context windows. It says alternating active learning and offline rest lets models retain short-term memories, abstract new skills into long-term parameters and keep self-improving without catastrophic forgetting. The authors ground the two stages in a theory: consolidation works as structured low-rank compression, and dreaming diversifies and selects updates to give a more balanced optimization landscape. The post does not say when the framework might be deployed in products or what further work is planned.

Articles.Title: Sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning

stories.Headline: Best smart AI glasses in 2026: Features for different lifestyles
stories.Summary:
Meta published a guide on October 30, 2026, describing its lineup of smart AI glasses for 2026. The article presents several models, including Meta Glasses, Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3), Meta Ray-Ban Display, Oakley Meta HSTN and Oakley Meta Vanguard. It frames the glasses as lightweight frames that give hands-free access to calls, texts, photos and real-time AI support. The guide says the right pair depends on a person's lifestyle and how they plan to use the glasses.

The article describes features rather than announcing a single product or price. Meta Glasses come in five frames, Meta Fury, Meta Starfire, Meta Adventurer, Meta Nova and Meta Capri, and support prescription lenses. Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) comes in Wayfarer, Aviator and Zena, with a 12 MP front-facing camera and open-ear speakers. Meta Ray-Ban Display shows directions and translations in a private in-lens display and comes with the Meta Neural Band on the wrist. Oakley Meta HSTN has an ultra-wide 12 MP camera and Transitions lenses, and Oakley Meta Vanguard has an IPX4 rating and a 9-hour battery life.

The article presents the guidance as Meta's own advice on choosing a pair. It says buyers should weigh prescription compatibility, battery life, audio design, camera quality, AI assistant capabilities, display versus no display, comfort, app compatibility, privacy controls, and price and value. It notes that battery life depends on how often the camera, display or AI assistant is used. It also says visible LED and capture indicators matter for signaling when recording, and that respecting nearby people's privacy is part of responsible use.

The article gives no release dates, prices or availability details beyond the lineup itself. It says Meta AI responds quickly and handles navigation, messages and contextual information, with some features running locally and others relying on a phone connection. It adds that Ray-Ban Meta Blayzer Optics and Scriber Optics are built specifically for prescription wearers. The article does not say what happens next beyond directing readers to compare models and choose based on their routine.

Articles.Title: Best smart AI glasses in 2026: Features for different lifestyles

stories.Headline: Estée Lauder expands AI across its vast beauty business
stories.Summary:
Estée Lauder Companies announced on Friday, October 30, 2026, that it is expanding its use of Microsoft cloud and AI tools across its business. The New York-based company is one of the world's biggest makers of skin care, makeup, fragrance and hair care products. Its brands include Estée Lauder, Clinique, Origins, M·A·C, La Mer, Bobbi Brown Cosmetics and Aveda. Its products are sold in 150 countries and territories.

At the center of the effort is the company's Unified Data Platform, built on Microsoft technology. It connects 80 years of consumer insights across the company's brands, regions, channels and functions. The goal is to speed up product innovation and produce sharper data-driven insights. The expanded use of the tools will touch almost every part of the business, from marketing to operations to research and development. The company has also expanded Copilot access across its office-based global workforce of more than 14,000.

Brian Franz, Chief Technology and Transformation Officer at The Estée Lauder Companies, commented on the partnership in a press release. He said the partnership with Microsoft, along with other strategic partners in what the company calls its One Operating Ecosystem, is powering its teams. He said this gives them the capabilities to ultimately deliver more relevant, personalized experiences. Those experiences are meant to meet consumers' evolving needs, he said.

The company's scientists have decades of product data to draw on. Having that data in one place on the Unified Data Platform could make it easier to use as they develop new products and internal solutions. The company described the global beauty market as increasingly competitive. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the announced expansion.

Articles.Title: Estée Lauder expands AI across its vast beauty business

stories.Headline: VAPOR PANDA Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Scale a Global Espionage Campaign
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike's OverWatch team reported on October 29, 2026 that a China-linked group it calls VAPOR PANDA ran a global espionage campaign using an AI-driven framework named ARTEX. The activity began on October 17, 2026, when a single ARTEX controller was used against more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries over an 11-day window. Targets included foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia and the Middle East, a Middle East interior ministry, semiconductor, defense and think tank organizations in the U.S., and telecommunications providers in several regions. CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organizations, where the adversary deployed the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor and carried out credential spraying, network scanning and reconnaissance, and it also ran password spraying against at least 12 more organizations.

The operation relied mainly on the Chinese-developed DeepSeek large language model plus a second subscription-based commercial model that CrowdStrike could not confirm. In one intrusion alone, the planning agents consumed about 1.4 billion input tokens. ARTEX coordinates a main agent with planner and worker agents over a shared graph of facts and goals, moving each engagement from initial access through host reconnaissance and lateral movement. A human stayed in the loop, with recovered transcripts showing an operator issuing instructions in Chinese, labeled as a human instruction and timestamped in China Standard Time, directing the agents to write web shells, extract domain administrator passwords and inventory endpoint sensor coverage, including finding hosts without the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor.

CrowdStrike said the campaign marks an escalation in China-nexus use of AI agents, from single intrusions to multiple simultaneous engagements steered by a human operator. It described the adversary as pairing AI-driven workflow with established tradecraft, citing cases at two U.S. pharmaceutical organizations and a Greek government entity. CrowdStrike noted the campaign is separate from ARTEX activity recently reported by industry sources under the Storm-0940 designation, and that it had previously documented ARTEX and similar frameworks used by financially motivated and unattributed actors. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: VAPOR PANDA Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Scale a Global Espionage Campaign

stories.Headline: As festive online shopping surges, how are e-commerce firms using AI to detect fake orders, prevent fraudulent refunds?
stories.Summary:
India’s festive e-commerce season is expected to bring a surge in fake orders, account misuse and fraudulent refund claims, according to a Livemint report published on 30 October 2026. Datum Intelligence expects festive order volumes to rise from 760 million in 2025 to 966 million in 2026, a 27.1% increase. The number of festive shoppers is projected to grow 14.5%, and each shopper is expected to place 11% more orders. The average order value is expected to fall slightly, from ₹1,578 to ₹1,554.

The report says platforms face risks including suspicious cash-on-delivery bookings, fake customer identities, offer abuse, account takeovers, fraudulent return requests and delivery tampering. TransUnion’s H1 2026 report found that 7.1% of attempted digital transactions involving consumers in India in 2025 were suspected to be fraudulent, against a global average of 3.8%. In India’s logistics sector, 16.3% of attempted digital transactions were suspected of fraud in 2025, the highest rate among sectors analysed, and suspected fraud attempts there rose 31% year on year. Suspected fraud was highest at the account-login stage at 3.9%, followed by account creation at 3.1% and financial transactions at 1.2%.

Krishna Gupta, CEO of logistics platform ShipMaxx360, said festive sales push up risks related to fake orders, COD fraud and returns. He said this is complicated because customer, order, payment and delivery data may be spread across multiple platforms and service providers. Gupta said this lack of integration makes anomalies hard to detect, so fraud may be found only later. He said AI can analyse purchase patterns, order history, delivery patterns and refund requests to detect early risk, but this relies on integration between different parts of a business.

The report says AI can support automated risk scoring, which separates potentially high-risk orders for manual review. Machine learning can assess order history, account details, order value, device information, delivery experience and shipping addresses. A transaction may look legitimate on its own but be flagged when viewed alongside related patterns across multiple orders, according to Shipmaxx. The report says traditional rule-based checks may not be enough during the festive rush, when genuine customers may also place multiple or high-value orders.

Articles.Title: As festive online shopping surges, how are e-commerce firms using AI to detect fake orders, prevent fraudulent refunds?

stories.Headline: AMD Is Chasing Nvidia in AI, but Investors Could Win Either Way
stories.Summary:
AMD reported second quarter Data Center revenue of $6.72B, up 107%, and that segment now makes up 58% of total revenue. CEO Lisa Su said AMD enters the second half with strong momentum as EPYC demand accelerates, Instinct deployments scale and Helios begins to ramp. Shares are up 164.77% year-to-date at $567.04, even after a 10.08% decline over the past month. Helios racks are shipping and AMD has gigawatt-scale deals with OpenAI, Meta Platforms and Anthropic.

Analysts expect 2026 EPS of $7.5884 to rise to $15.7629 in 2027, growth of 108%, with revenue projected to climb 75%. The 2027 EPS consensus stood at $13.4921 three months ago, meaning estimates have climbed 17% in a single quarter. AMD has beaten EPS and revenue estimates in each of its last four quarters. At today's price, AMD trades at 36x 2027 estimates, and at $1,000 the multiple would be 63x.

Su told analysts AMD expects to significantly exceed its prior $20 annual EPS target, and if 2027 earnings reach the high estimate of $20.25, $1,000 works out to about 49x. Management expects Data Center revenue to more than double year-over-year in 2027, with server revenue growing more than 70%. AMD raised its forecast for the data center AI accelerator market to $1.4 trillion by 2030. Nvidia chief Jensen Huang said in August that demand is much higher than 70% while supply allows the company to confidently deliver 70%, and demand Nvidia's supply cannot cover gives AMD room to grow.

Reaching $1,000 requires a 76% gain, and since 2000 AMD has beaten that mark in eight calendar years, including rises of 348% in 2009, 295% in 2016, 148% in 2019 and 128% in 2023. With a market cap near $925.8B, gains like that get harder to repeat, though 2026 has already delivered more than double the needed return. The main hurdles are Helios yields, data center power availability and export controls, and a 63x multiple would leave little margin if the broader market turns down. Nvidia trades at 23x fiscal 2027 estimates and 14x fiscal 2028 estimates, so both stocks benefit if AI spending remains strong.

Articles.Title: AMD Is Chasing Nvidia in AI, but Investors Could Win Either Way

stories.Headline: How AI is transforming U.S. military industrial complex
stories.Summary:
The core of the U.S. Military Industrial Complex is shifting from traditional hardware manufacturers to algorithm and AI companies, according to The Hindu. This shift was formally marked on September 29, 2026, when U.S. President Donald Trump convened the CEOs of the world's most powerful AI companies to sign the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The article describes the Accord as a voluntary framework that symbolically integrated AI firms into the national security architecture. It says the military implications of the Accord are unmissable.

The article says substantive developments had already occurred months earlier in the military domain. In May 2026, the U.S. Department of War announced agreements with eight AI companies to deploy their capabilities on classified networks at impact levels 6 and 7. The companies named are SpaceX, OpenAI, Google, Nvidia, Reflection, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, and Oracle. The article describes those levels as the highest classification tiers for sensitive military operations.

The article attributes the shift to three interlocking attributes: the inversion of war economics, the restructuring of procurement and capital logic, and the software-defined transformation of the military technology stack. It says the core of the MIC has moved from the factory to the server because of the arithmetic of cost-imposition, the venture-velocity logic of capital, and the architectural revolution of software-defined warfare. It adds that this will lead to an obvious fallout across the global defence industrial base. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: How AI is transforming U.S. military industrial complex

stories.Headline: Google parent Alphabet’s shares plunge 12.6% as investors question returns from AI spending
stories.Summary:
Alphabet’s shares fell 12.64% on the Nasdaq on Thursday, October 29, 2026, closing at $283.82. The drop wiped out about $482 billion in market value and was the company’s worst one-day fall since it began trading in 2004. The sell-off followed quarterly results that renewed concerns about whether Alphabet’s heavy AI investments will generate enough returns. In pre-market trading on Friday, October 30, 2026, the shares slipped a further 0.42% to $282.64.

Revenue grew 25% year-on-year to $127.6 billion in the quarter ended September 30, while net profit fell to $26.5 billion from $35 billion a year earlier. Earnings from business operations rose 30% to $40.6 billion, and Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion. Alphabet spent $51.4 billion on capital expenditure in the quarter, mainly on data centres, servers and networking equipment. Because this exceeded the $42.3 billion in cash generated from operations, the company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion.

Chief financial officer Anat Ashkenazi said infrastructure spending was a major reason for the negative free cash flow. She also cited inventory being built up for sales of Google’s own AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units, and a $5.2-billion payment relating to a European Commission fine. She said capital expenditure would increase significantly in 2027. Alphabet kept its capital expenditure guidance of $195 billion to $205 billion for 2026.

Revenue from Google Search and related advertising grew 12% to $63.35 billion, slower than the 17% growth in the previous quarter. Philipp Schindler, Google’s senior vice-president and chief business officer, said growing queries through AI Mode were affecting advertising revenue because Google earns less from these queries than from traditional Search. He said Google was experimenting with advertisements in AI-powered Search features and that foreign exchange movements were the biggest factor behind the slowdown. Chief executive Sundar Pichai said year-on-year growth in Search queries was the highest in five years.

Articles.Title: Google parent Alphabet’s shares plunge 12.6% as investors question returns from AI spending

stories.Headline: ‘Anchor the ground’: Canada, EU launch new alliance with deals on Ukraine, minerals, AI
stories.Summary:
Canada and the European Union announced a closer alliance at a summit in Montreal on Oct 30, 2026. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the two sides were anchoring the ground to protect shared values. He spoke at a press conference with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa. The move comes as both Canada and the EU have faced US tariffs and territorial threats since Donald Trump returned to power.

Canada agreed to join the EU's €90 billion support loan for Ukraine with an initial €500 million. The two sides also agreed to work more closely on critical minerals, artificial intelligence, trade and economic security. They signed a digital trade deal and a separate pact allowing the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects. Talks also opened on Canada joining EU programmes including Erasmus and Galileo, and Europe opened its supercomputing infrastructure to Canadian researchers, industry and start-ups.

Von der Leyen said the partnership was not against anyone else but for common strength. She called Canada the EU's first associate member, a label Germany and a handful of other EU states opposed and had dropped from a joint summit statement. Carney backed the title and said its substance would be determined in the coming months. He said Canada's contribution to the Ukraine loan was a powerful message of support to Kyiv, according to von der Leyen.

Carney will take part in an EU leaders summit in June, and European commissioners and Canadian ministers will hold a separate meeting in the spring, Costa said. Von der Leyen said the two would form the nucleus of a larger alliance for the future open to other partners. A senior EU official said a key part would be coordinating economic security measures, like tariffs, so they do not inadvertently harm group members. Canada is rich in rare earths and critical minerals Europe mostly sources from China but needs major infrastructure investment to jump-start its mining industry.

Articles.Title: ‘Anchor the ground’: Canada, EU launch new alliance with deals on Ukraine, minerals, AI

stories.Headline: AI is changing motherhood for the worse
stories.Summary:
A commentary published by The Japan Times on October 30, 2026, argues that artificial intelligence is changing motherhood for the worse. The piece was written by Abby McCloskey for Bloomberg. It says recent books and studies have begun to highlight the risks AI poses to children, and it calls that a good thing. The author says mothers are affected too, not just kids. The commentary states that 81% of parents use AI for parenting support, and the author says she is one of them.

She appreciates the technology managing her grocery list but worries it could make parenting harder. She asked Google's Gemini how AI might go about dismantling American motherhood. The answer warned that AI could encourage what it called hyperindividualized isolation, intensify perfectionism and make every parenting decision seem to carry a risk of permanent, catastrophic consequences. The author is responsible for the argument, which appears as a commentary in the newspaper. She writes that she is among the parents using AI and that she worries about its effect on parenting.

She describes Gemini's answer as ringing eerily true. The piece says we may be realizing we should not wait a decade after a new technology emerges before sounding the alarm, as she says happened with social media. The commentary does not say what happens next. It offers no study results, no policy proposal and no response from Google. It does not name any regulator or say whether any rules are planned.

Articles.Title: AI is changing motherhood for the worse

stories.Headline: AI giants promise publishers new way to block some scraping
stories.Summary:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic pledged on Oct 30 to give media outlets and other websites a single way to stop their content being scraped to train artificial intelligence models. The promise came after growing criticism and legal battles from news publishers. The announcement comes as publishers face a surge in bots that scrape their articles to feed AI models. Some, like the New York Times, have taken the matter to court.

The new solution will let publishers enter one standardised instruction that any AI company adopting the protocol recognises and honours. It will not fully take effect for months: Microsoft will implement it beginning Feb 1, 2027, and Google sometime in 2027. OpenAI said it will roll it out in the coming months, while Anthropic said it has already started. The setting applies only to future training of models and does not prevent bots from crawling otherwise, and scraping is allowed by default until a publisher changes the setting, Microsoft said in a blog post.

In December 2023, the Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft for allegedly using millions of its articles without authorisation or payment to train ChatGPT, and the two companies are invoking an exception to copyright law known as fair use. Microsoft and Google said in separate blog posts that opting out of AI training could reduce the chances a publisher's content surfaces in AI apps and experiences. Meta spokesman Andy Stone wrote on X that he supported the effort, saying a common signal conveying such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step. Internet infrastructure provider Cloudflare has blocked AI bots by default on new customer sites since July 2025, and a standard called Really Simple Licensing already lets publishers charge bots that visit their pages.

Articles.Title: AI giants promise publishers new way to block some scraping

stories.Headline: Chinese AI optical suppliers slump despite upbeat third-quarter earnings
stories.Summary:
Shares of major Chinese optical communications suppliers fell on Friday, extending a two-day sell-off despite strong third-quarter earnings. Chengdu-based Eoptolink Technology closed 14.2 per cent lower at 196.00 yuan in Shenzhen. Suzhou TFC Communication slid 8.4 per cent to 148.00 yuan, and industry leader Zhongji Innolight fell 5 per cent to 553.00 yuan. The losses followed steep declines on Thursday, when TFC plunged 19.8 per cent, Eoptolink tumbled 11.1 per cent and Innolight fell 8.5 per cent.

Innolight on Thursday posted a 174 per cent surge in third-quarter net profit to US$1.29 billion, as revenue jumped 172 per cent. Innolight and Eoptolink make optical transceivers, hardware that converts electrical signals into pulses of light to carry data across fibre networks in AI data centres. TFC produces optical components used in communications equipment. The article attributes the sell-off to fears of slower AI growth outweighing the upbeat earnings.

The article names no individual executives and carries no statements from company officials or regulators. It gives no one as responsible for the declines beyond the market reaction to fears of slower AI growth. No company comment is included in the report. The only explanation offered is that those fears trumped the strong results.

The report does not say what happens next for the three companies. It describes the slump as extending a two-day sell-off and notes that shares clawed back some losses on Friday. No further dates, targets or guidance are given. The article provides no additional context beyond the earnings figures and the price moves.

Articles.Title: Chinese AI optical suppliers slump despite upbeat third-quarter earnings

stories.Headline: Can AI teach kids to think? Malaysia’s classroom tech push faces a reality check
stories.Summary:
Malaysia is pushing artificial intelligence into classrooms, and the South China Morning Post reported on the debate on 30 October 2026. The article opened with Pravin Ganesan, a 42-year-old tech worker in Kuala Lumpur, who taught his eight-year-old daughter a few basic prompts for homework. He checked her answers closely and said generative AI is good at breaking difficult concepts into child-friendly terms. He said it helped her learn and understand things better, and that he sometimes finds it hard to explain things the way an eight-year-old can follow.

The article says Malaysia is accelerating AI in classrooms, and it reports fears that students will trade genuine understanding and values for easy answers. It does not give specific policies, dates or figures for the push. The piece is framed as a reality check on whether AI can teach children to think. It presents the parent's experience alongside those concerns rather than resolving them.

Responsibility is described mainly at the level of parents and the wider classroom push. Pravin is shown taking responsibility by teaching basic prompts and checking the answers closely. The article does not name officials or agencies, and it does not quote them. The concerns it reports are attributed generally to fears that are mounting, not to a named person.

The context is a growing debate over children's access to AI, which the article says many parents still question. It sets one family's practical use against worries about easy answers. The article does not say what happens next, and it gives no timeline for the classroom push. It ends on the open question of whether AI can teach kids to think.

Articles.Title: Can AI teach kids to think? Malaysia’s classroom tech push faces a reality check

stories.Headline: Crypto expert warns of looming 'AI hacking bloodbath' after massive Binance breach
stories.Summary:
A massive breach hit Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange, and Eric Schiffer, chairman of Patriarch and Reputation Management Consultants, spoke about it in a Fox Business video. The video was published on October 31, 2026, and the breach was valued at $6.3 billion. Schiffer warned that the hack could signal a wave of cyberattacks fueled by artificial intelligence. He also offered advice to cryptocurrency investors on protecting their assets.

The articles give few further details about the breach itself, such as how it happened or who carried it out. The $6.3 billion figure is the only loss amount the articles state, and the only date given is the October 31, 2026 video publication. The articles do not describe any new rules, requirements or policy changes in response to the hack. They also do not name any other people or give any other numbers.

Schiffer is the person the articles hold out as the expert voice on the breach. He said the Binance hack could be a sign of a coming wave of cyberattacks driven by artificial intelligence. He also gave advice to cryptocurrency investors about protecting their assets, though the articles do not spell out what that advice was. The articles do not attribute any other statements to him or to anyone else.

The context the articles provide is a warning about artificial intelligence being used to fuel more cyberattacks after this breach. The articles do not say what Binance has done or plans to do in response. They also do not say what regulators or authorities might do next. No further steps or timeline are given beyond Schiffer's warning and his advice to investors.

Articles.Title: Crypto expert warns of looming 'AI hacking bloodbath' after massive Binance breach

stories.Headline: In the Age of AI, Curiosity Is Our Greatest Creative Tool
stories.Summary:
The article is a first-person reflection by a Canadian designer living in New York who returned to Toronto for the Registered Graphic Designers' annual DesignThinkers conference on October 20 to 21. The writer describes reconnecting with familiar faces and meeting first-time attendees, and calls the event a creative homecoming. The conference theme was Out of Office, created by the Calgary-based studio Daughter. The writer says the theme celebrates stepping away from screens, trusting instincts, and making space for creativity beyond everyday work.

The piece does not report a news event or a change to any policy. It says the writer considers themselves an AI optimist and sees exciting work in tools applied to problems needing new ways of thinking, including briefs on AI's potential in sustainability. It says optimism means being curious enough to explore potential, thoughtful enough to question limitations, and willing to take responsibility for use. It says design understanding is critical because generating an image or concept has become increasingly accessible, and the harder question is what to do with that capability.

The writer credits designer Valentina D'Efilippo, whose talk was titled Let's Speak Data, with the principle to design for understanding and follow your curiosity. The writer says D'Efilippo works at the intersection of data and storytelling, where the challenge is helping people make sense of information rather than simply presenting it. The writer says that idea resonated beyond information design, whether the work is a brand identity, a campaign, or an experiment with new technology. The job, the writer says, is to make meaning, not merely something that looks good.

The writer argues curiosity takes us beyond the obvious answer, prompting a closer look, a question about the reference everyone else uses, or pursuit of an idea that does not immediately fit the brief. The writer says this can lead to an unexpected connection or reveal that an original assumption was wrong. The writer notes the temptation to follow familiar visual conventions can be difficult to resist in design. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: In the Age of AI, Curiosity Is Our Greatest Creative Tool

stories.Headline: US economy powers ahead as AI boom, shoppers defy oil shock
stories.Summary:
The US economy grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter of 2026, the Bureau of Economic Analysis said on Oct 29. That was faster than the 2.2% rate in the second quarter and the fastest growth in a year. Strong consumer spending and AI-driven business investment outweighed higher oil prices tied to the conflict in the Middle East. The report came less than a week before the midterm elections on Nov 3, which will determine control of Congress.

Consumer spending, which makes up more than two-thirds of the economy, rose at a 3.8% pace, the same as in the second quarter. Consumer prices were up 3.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier, and average gasoline prices were still above US$4 a gallon. The Federal Reserve on Oct 28 kept its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75% to 4% range and said inflation remains elevated. Economists expected the Fed to raise rates in December.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh told reporters that economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. He said domestic spending has been resilient while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments. Aditya Bhave, head of US economics for Bank of America, said this is a hot economy and that inflation is the price paid for it. He said inflation is going to remain elevated.

Some economists said the strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy because of the growing dominance of AI-related spending. Investors are focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects with uncertain payoffs, and tech firms have borrowed huge sums for AI spending over the past year. Households have also been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. Economists anticipated a slowdown in consumer spending as gas costs stay high.

Articles.Title: US economy powers ahead as AI boom, shoppers defy oil shock

stories.Headline: Tencent’s cloud boss plays long game to patch ‘leaky’ AI ship
stories.Summary:
When Pony Ma called Tencent's artificial intelligence effort "a leaky ship" in the summer of 2026, the company was struggling to catch rivals such as DeepSeek in the post-ChatGPT era. One of his key lieutenants, Dowson Tong, responded by proposing a retooling to focus on businesses. The turnaround effort centered on WorkBuddy, which had been considered a side project within Tencent's internet portfolio. By the fall, the Claude Cowork-style AI assistant served 32 million monthly users, more than its rivals combined.

WorkBuddy combined Tencent's existing messaging and office tools with AI agents that can take data and produce reports. Its rise launched Tencent into a lucrative segment of AI, described as an important first step toward regaining its tech credibility. Tong, a Hong Kong native and Silicon Valley veteran, is now one of a handful of key Tencent executives leading the push to close the gap with ByteDance, the parent of TikTok, and longstanding rival Alibaba Group Holding. At stake is Tencent's future industry standing against fast-rising AI-native firms from DeepSeek to Moonshot AI, which the article says have propelled China to the forefront of the global AI race.

Tong said in Shenzhen this week that WorkBuddy's ascent signals a shift by Tencent toward enterprise agents rather than consumer chatbots, at least in the early phases, so the company can better monetize the emerging technology. The article does not give further direct comments from Tong or from Pony Ma beyond Ma's "leaky ship" remark. It also does not assign responsibility for the company's earlier struggles to any named individual. The push is described as high-stakes for Tencent's standing in the industry.

The article frames the effort as Tencent's attempt to recover its position in AI after falling behind in the post-ChatGPT period. It says the focus on enterprise agents is meant to help Tencent monetize the technology more effectively in its early phases. The piece does not say what specific next steps Tencent plans, nor does it give a timeline beyond the fall of 2026. It also does not state how the competition with ByteDance, Alibaba, DeepSeek or Moonshot AI will develop.

Articles.Title: Tencent’s cloud boss plays long game to patch ‘leaky’ AI ship

stories.Headline: Foxconn chief downplays AI bubble concerns, sees strong 2027 growth
stories.Summary:
Foxconn Chairman Young Liu spoke on Friday at the company's annual tech day in Taipei and downplayed concerns about a possible artificial intelligence bubble. He said demand from the key Nvidia server supplier was clear and strong. He also said sales growth was expected to be double-digit in 2027. The event was reported by Nikkei Asia on October 30, 2026.

Liu said Foxconn is not just an assembler "moving boxes around" but can build state-of-the-art equipment such as Nvidia's DSX POD, a modular container-sized AI factory. The company plans a major supply chain expansion in Texas. The articles give no further figures or dates for that expansion. They also give no other names beyond Liu and Nvidia.

Liu is the chairman of Foxconn and made the comments at the tech day. He downplayed the bubble concerns and pointed to clear and strong demand. He described the company's manufacturing role in his own terms. The articles do not quote anyone else.

The context is concern about a possible AI bubble and questions over AI demand. The articles say Foxconn expects double-digit sales growth in 2027. They do not say what happens next beyond the Texas expansion plan. They give no further details on timing or scale.

Articles.Title: Foxconn chief downplays AI bubble concerns, sees strong 2027 growth

stories.Headline: AI as a New Tribe: Professor Alan Macfarlane on what makes us human
stories.Summary:
Professor Alan Macfarlane, an emeritus professor of anthropological science at the University of Cambridge and a Life Fellow of King’s College, spoke at an SCMP Plus fireside chat at The Center in Central, Hong Kong, on October 26, 2026. The event was published by the South China Morning Post on October 30, 2026. He was interviewed by SCMP senior AI technology reporter Vincent Chow. The discussion asked what an anthropologist might make of artificial intelligence if he approached it as an unfamiliar tribe.

Macfarlane invited the audience to consider AI as an unfamiliar culture, looking at its origins, how it operates and its place in society. He placed AI within a series of communication revolutions, from speech and writing to printing and computing, and argued it represents another major shift in how knowledge is created, preserved and transmitted. He emphasised that despite being digital, AI depends on resource-intensive physical infrastructure, including data centres, electricity supplies and semiconductor manufacturing. He also distinguished between processing information and experiencing the world, questioning whether discussing death, beauty or pain amounts to understanding them, and said AI’s apparent intelligence comes from sophisticated pattern recognition and the human knowledge used in its training rather than conscious experience.

Chow noted that much of the US debate on AI focuses on consciousness and new forms of intelligence, while in China the emphasis is often on practical applications and everyday problem-solving. Macfarlane suggested that cultural and philosophical traditions help shape these perspectives. During the audience Q&A, discussion turned to education, employment and digital technology’s impact on younger generations, and Macfarlane stressed the importance of helping children understand both AI’s opportunities and risks while preserving time for creativity and human interaction. He offered a cautiously optimistic view that, if managed thoughtfully, automation could relieve people of repetitive labour and create more time for civic life, leisure and creative pursuits. The event was supported by Huatai International.

Articles.Title: AI as a New Tribe: Professor Alan Macfarlane on what makes us human

stories.Headline: Japan asks Anthropic, OpenAI for more access to advanced models
stories.Summary:
Japan has asked the U.S. artificial intelligence developers Anthropic and OpenAI to give it greater access to advanced models used to find cybersecurity weaknesses, Nikkei has learned. The request came from the Japanese government, which reported the move on October 31, 2026, Tokyo time. The government also said it will encourage operators of essential infrastructure to use these models. The step is meant to bolster the nation's cyber defenses as attacks mount.

The articles give no further numbers, dates or names beyond Anthropic, OpenAI, Japan and the October 31, 2026 report date. They do not say what specific access the government wants or what the models would be used for in detail. They also do not say whether the two companies have responded to the request. No timeline is given for when expanded access might arrive.

Responsibility for the request rests with the Japanese government, which made the call to the two U.S. developers. The articles do not include direct statements from government officials or from either company. They describe the aim as strengthening cyber defenses and widening use of the models by essential infrastructure operators. No one is quoted on what the companies said in reply.

The context is a rise in cyber attacks against Japan, which the articles describe as mounting. The request fits a wider push by Tokyo to shore up its cyber defenses, including reported plans to reorganize defense research around AI and cyber. The articles do not say what happens next, such as any talks or deadlines. They also do not say whether the companies have agreed to anything.

Articles.Title: Japan asks Anthropic, OpenAI for more access to advanced models

stories.Headline: Nearly half of S’pore employers who use AI in HR do so for recruitment: SNEF survey
stories.Summary:
A survey of 1,000 employers in Singapore, conducted in June and July, found that 740 of them use artificial intelligence in human resources, according to the Singapore National Employers Federation. The findings were released on Oct 30 at the first SNEF Employers’ Summit at Grand Hyatt Singapore, which more than 300 business leaders, senior HR practitioners and trade association leaders attended. The technology is used most in recruitment, at 49%, and in managing employee performance, at 45%, and less in deciding compensation, at 26%, and managing employee exits, at 15%. Larger firms with more than 200 employees are more likely to use tools such as Workday and SAP SuccessFactors, while small and medium-sized enterprises rely more on all-purpose tools like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot.

Out of nearly 3,000 HR use cases reported by 655 employers, 85% still require human confirmation or sign-off for AI-automated processes. Nearly all employers, at 97%, have designated someone with authority, such as a supervisor or hiring manager, to intervene and change decisions if needed. The top three concerns among employers using AI were over-reliance that could erode HR capabilities, knowing when to trust AI over professional judgment, and accountability when AI makes errors. The survey also found that 84% of employers using AI in HR said they were very or extremely familiar with at least one framework covered in the poll, including the Workplace Fairness Act and the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices.

SNEF president Kuah Boon Wee said the level of oversight should match the stakes, lighter for routine tasks and closer for decisions that affect people’s livelihoods. He said AI should enable people to contribute at a higher level, not weaken the capability that businesses depend on. Singtel group chief executive Yuen Kuan Moon said in his keynote address that all AI-related projects at the company are put through three lenses on investment returns, covering customers, employees and future growth. He encouraged employers to start with value from the customer and employee standpoints rather than from technology, and to redesign the flow of work before selecting tools.

Acting Manpower Minister Jasmin Lau highlighted a recently launched HR playbook that brings together AI starter kits for selected HR uses and training to build AI fluency among HR professionals. She also urged employers to include their unions and employees when redesigning jobs, saying people are more likely to contribute to change when they have helped shape it. At the summit, Kuah launched an AI-HR pre-scoped solution, a paid package with workplace planning advisory support, workforce diagnostics and skills analytics, and AI solutions. SNEF is starting with a pilot and a preliminary group of consultants supported under the Workforce Development Grant (Job Redesign+), including BDO Singapore and Elitez Group, and eligible employers can access funding of up to $150,000 for each company’s job redesign projects.

Articles.Title: Nearly half of S’pore employers who use AI in HR do so for recruitment: SNEF survey

stories.Headline: Copilots are now coworkers: What happens next with AI
stories.Summary:
NTT DATA published an article by Sandeep Kaushik on 21 August 2026 about AI agents moving from experiments into everyday enterprise work. The article says agents are becoming part of the enterprise operating fabric, helping employees and increasingly performing work on their behalf across productivity tools, enterprise data, business applications, workflows and customer-facing processes. It describes Microsoft tools including Copilot Chat, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Microsoft Copilot Cowork and Microsoft Scout, which it says can coordinate multistep work and track progress behind the scenes. The article frames the next phase of AI transformation as a combination of intelligence and trust.

The article says agents need identities, defined access, governance, policies, observability, accountability and lifecycle management, much like employees. It draws a distinction between an agent that borrows a person's identity and permissions and one with its own enterprise-managed identity and purpose-built access, saying the difference determines how accountability, auditing, governance and risk are managed. It lists questions for CIOs, CISOs and other business leaders, including who owns an agent, what data it can access, what actions it can take, how it is monitored and how its behavior is stopped or modified. It recommends extending existing trusted infrastructure to agents, citing Microsoft Entra for identity and access, Microsoft Defender for threat protection, Microsoft Purview for governance and compliance, the Microsoft 365 admin center for management and Microsoft Agent 365 as a control plane.

The article attributes the guidance to NTT DATA and its author, Sandeep Kaushik, a Senior Director and Strategic Advisor at the company's Microsoft Center of Excellence for Digital Workplace Services. It says organizations should assess AI and agent readiness beyond technology, including licensing, data readiness, security posture, shadow agents, operating model, skills and readiness for change. It advises prioritizing use cases with repetitive effort, fragmented information, high coordination costs, decision bottlenecks or significant business impact, and building a secure foundation with least-privilege principles, conditional access, sensitivity labels, agent identities and registries, onboarding processes and responsible AI guardrails. It also recommends a repeatable process for discovering, designing, building, testing, publishing, monitoring and improving agents, using tools such as Microsoft Copilot Studio, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Graph.

The article describes NTT DATA's Workplace Frontier Transformation with Microsoft, which it says starts with Frontier Immersion and Value Discovery, followed by a Frontier Readiness Assessment with 30-, 60- and 90-day roadmaps. It then lists the Frontier Foundation Accelerator, which establishes a secure landing zone, governance model, tenant readiness, identity controls, Microsoft Purview and Defender policies, Agent 365 controls, adoption playbooks and a pilot operating model, and the Frontier Scale Accelerator, which builds and deploys agents across business functions and integrates platforms such as SAP, ServiceNow, Salesforce and Jira. It ends with Embrace and Lead Frontier, a long-term operating model to govern, optimize and scale an agentic workforce. The article says the value of the approach is moving forward with purpose and control, and that only by redesigning how work is done and building trust into the operating model will AI become an intelligence multiplier.

Articles.Title: Copilots are now coworkers: What happens next with AI

stories.Headline: Japan's Marubeni looks to profit from bottlenecks arising from AI boom
stories.Summary:
Marubeni, one of Japan's five big trading houses, is betting on physical bottlenecks such as demand for energy and natural resources stemming from the artificial intelligence boom to drive its growth. The company is expanding its exposure to businesses that supply and manage the power, metals and communications infrastructure needed to support rising demand for computing power. Its CEO said energy and resource constraints can be a source of growth for the trading house. The report was published by Nikkei Asia on October 30, 2026, with the interview dated the same day in Tokyo.

The articles give no further numbers, dates or names beyond Marubeni, its CEO and the October 30, 2026 report. They do not say how much the company is investing or which specific projects it will take on. The stated change is a shift toward supplying and managing power, metals and communications infrastructure tied to computing demand. No financial targets or timelines are given.

Responsibility for the strategy rests with Marubeni and its CEO, who framed energy and resource constraints as a source of growth rather than a risk. The articles do not name the CEO or give further direct comments. They also do not say which parts of the company will carry out the expansion. No other officials or outside parties are cited on the plan.

The context is the wider AI boom and the strain it puts on energy, resources and communications capacity. The articles note related industry concerns, including a talent shortage described as tech's biggest bottleneck in AI expansion. They do not say what specific steps Marubeni will take next or when results are expected. No further details on the plan are provided.

Articles.Title: Japan's Marubeni looks to profit from bottlenecks arising from AI boom

stories.Headline: Chinese shipping, coal stocks outperform AI as earnings outlooks diverge
stories.Summary:
Chinese shipping and coal stocks outperformed artificial intelligence shares this week as a market selloff hit AI suppliers, Nikkei Asia reported on October 30, 2026. COSCO's profit jumped 80% in the third quarter, helped in part by higher freight rates. The gains came partly from side effects of the Iran war, which caused a prolonged fuel crunch and supply chain disruptions. The report described the contrast as a tech rout.

The article gives few further details on the numbers behind the moves. It does not name the size of the selloff or the specific coal companies involved. It also does not give dates for the third quarter results beyond the October 30 report. No other figures or names are provided in the article.

The article attributes the shipping gains to higher freight rates and the coal gains to the fuel crunch and supply disruptions. It does not quote any executives or officials by name. No one is described as responsible for the market moves. The report presents the earnings outlooks as diverging between the sectors.

The context is a bruising selloff of AI suppliers this week, set against a prolonged fuel crunch and supply chain disruptions. The article does not say what happens next for either sector. It offers no forecasts beyond the earnings outlooks it describes. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Chinese shipping, coal stocks outperform AI as earnings outlooks diverge

stories.Headline: Memory chip makers outearn Alphabet, other tech giants on AI demand
stories.Summary:
Five leading global memory chip suppliers together reported higher total operating and net profits than five big U.S. tech companies last quarter, Nikkei Asia reported. It was the first time that had happened, and the report linked it to artificial intelligence investment driving chip demand that is currently outpacing supply. The article was published on October 31, 2026, Japan time, and was written by Kyohei Suga. It named Kioxia and Samsung among the memory makers reaping the benefits of a spending surge. The report gave several figures on the memory makers' results.

It said Kioxia's net profit is set to surge 15-fold to $8.7 billion this quarter. Related Nikkei headlines cited in the article said SK Hynix's quarterly profit soared sevenfold to $63 billion on strong memory demand, and that Samsung posted tech's biggest ever profit with a blockbuster third quarter. The article also said AI demand and soaring memory prices lifted Japan's chip exports by 41 percent. The article said investors are starting to doubt the staying power of the memory makers' gains. It did not name the five U.S. tech companies or give their profit figures.

Alphabet was mentioned in the headline, but the article text did not give its results or any comment from the companies involved. No responsible official was named and no direct statements were paraphrased in the article. The context given is a broad AI investment boom in data centers, which the article said is fueling demand for memory chips. It also pointed to related coverage, including a Foxconn chief downplaying AI bubble concerns while expecting strong growth in 2027, and warnings that Asia's AI data center boom faces a reality check from public markets. The article did not say what happens next for the memory makers' profits.

Articles.Title: Memory chip makers outearn Alphabet, other tech giants on AI demand

stories.Headline: LG CNS Q3 operating profit up 15 pct led by AI, cloud biz growth
stories.Summary:
LG CNS Co., the information technology affiliate of LG Group, reported on Friday that its operating profit rose 15 percent from a year earlier, led by growth in its artificial intelligence and cloud businesses. The company said in a regulatory filing that operating profit was 138.2 billion won, or about US$103.2 million, in the July-September period. Sales rose 9.3 percent from a year earlier to 1.66 trillion won. Net profit fell 21.1 percent on-year to 83 billion won, mainly because of unfavorable exchange rates.

LG CNS said its AI and cloud businesses led the overall growth in operating profits, and it plans to keep its agentic AI service and AI infrastructure businesses as the two main pillars for competitiveness. The company acquired tangible assets worth around 380 billion won to secure graphic processing units needed to run and build AI factories. It also partnered with the New York-based venture fund General Atlantic to jointly invest in ventures involving corporate software and AI. In physical AI, LG CNS said it is running on-site tests of its robot training and operation platform, PhysicalWorks, and plans to strengthen cooperation with global big tech companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and Amazon Web Services.

The articles do not name individual executives or include direct comments from company officials, so responsibility is attributed to LG CNS as the company that issued the filing and announced the results and plans. The reported figures, including the 15 percent operating profit rise, the 9.3 percent sales growth and the 21.1 percent net profit decline, come from the company's regulatory filing. LG CNS also described its own plans for AI and cloud businesses, the asset purchase and the General Atlantic partnership. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the company's stated plans.

Articles.Title: LG CNS Q3 operating profit up 15 pct led by AI, cloud biz growth

stories.Headline: 2026 Global AI Report: A Playbook for Private and Sovereign AI
stories.Summary:
The 2026 Global AI Report: A Playbook for Private and Sovereign AI was published by NTT DATA on October 30, 2026. The report says AI progress is now limited less by models than by the infrastructure underneath them. Systems built for centralized, borderless data flows are struggling to support AI that must run in controlled and localized environments. Data jurisdiction is becoming an architectural constraint, and the report says everyone sees the shift but few are acting on it.

The report draws on insights from nearly 5,000 senior executives across more than 30 markets and more than a dozen industries, including automotive, manufacturing, banking and insurance. It says 37% see sovereign AI as driving competitive advantage. Leaders who redesign early and move decisively are creating competitive divergence, according to the report. It also says private and sovereign AI sound like independence but are built on tightly orchestrated ecosystems, and that legacy infrastructure remains the greatest barrier to deploying AI at scale.

The report says leaders treat sovereignty as a core design principle and have stronger revenue and growth margins. It says success depends on designing localized AI environments with rapid, secure data flows and on complex, tightly orchestrated multiprovider AI ecosystems. It adds that building private and sovereign AI is more than assembling technologies and requires outside assistance. The playbook covers geopolitics and the need for greater data control, factors in organizations' AI infrastructure choices, and why legacy infrastructure is an ever-present constraint.

The report examines challenges and opportunities for private and sovereign AI across regions and industries. It says sensitive data must be put in the right place and intelligence kept secure and controlled. It notes that private and sovereign AI overlap territory, operations, technology, and legal and regulatory requirements. The playbook is available by completing a form on the NTT DATA site.

Articles.Title: 2026 Global AI Report: A Playbook for Private and Sovereign AI

stories.Headline: Sejong University professor to co-organize int'l workshop on AI chip technologies in Athens
stories.Summary:
Park Gi-ho, a professor in the Department of Computer Sciences and Engineering at Sejong University, will co-organize the Eighth International Workshop on Domain Specific System Architecture in Athens, Greece, on Sunday. The workshop is part of the 59th IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture, known as MICRO 2026, which is scheduled to run from Oct. 31 to Nov. 4 in Athens. The event aims to share the latest research advances in artificial intelligence semiconductors and domain-specific system architecture. It also aims to promote research collaboration among experts from academia and industry worldwide.

Key topics will include systematic design methodologies for AI accelerators, programming environments for next-generation neural processing units and memory technologies for robotic foundation models. The workshop is co-organized by Park, professor Sim Jae-woong of Seoul National University and professor Kim Hye-soon of the Georgia Institute of Technology. The International Symposium on Microarchitecture is a conference with a 59-year history in computer systems and processor architecture design. Experts from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Nvidia, Korean AI chipmaker FuriosaAI and the Institute of Science Tokyo will deliver invited talks at the workshop.

MIT professor Joel Emer, who also serves as a senior distinguished research scientist at Nvidia, will discuss a systematic approach to AI accelerator design that takes into account the characteristics of AI models. He will explain how linking AI models' computational characteristics with hardware architectures can help improve accelerator efficiency. Kang Jee-hoon, chief research officer at FuriosaAI, will discuss the programming environment for the company's latest AI accelerator, the RNGD neural processing unit. His talk will cover software development tools, including compilers, as well as techniques for making effective use of AI accelerators.

Professor Daichi Fujiki of the Institute of Science Tokyo will discuss memory mechanisms in AI models. He will introduce techniques for generating certain AI model parameters during hardware execution, as well as approaches to data storage and generation. Researchers from the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya in Spain and the University of Texas at San Antonio will present their findings during the technical paper sessions. Topics will include scheduling techniques for efficiently processing graphics workloads and methods that leverage cache locality to accelerate graph neural network computations on graphics processing units.

Articles.Title: Sejong University professor to co-organize int'l workshop on AI chip technologies in Athens

stories.Headline: Hyundai Motor advances $6.3 bil. AI hub in Saemangeum
stories.Summary:
Hyundai Motor Group said on Friday, October 30, 2026, that it will set up two special purpose companies next month for a 9 trillion won, or $6.3 billion, AI data center project in Saemangeum, North Jeolla Province. Five group affiliates, Hyundai Motor, Kia, Hyundai Mobis, Hyundai Engineering & Construction and Hyundai AutoEver, have approved investments in the project. Hyundai AutoEver approved its participation through a board resolution. Construction is scheduled to begin in March 2027, with operations targeted for early 2030.

One of the new companies will build the hyperscale data center and its infrastructure, and the other will purchase high-performance graphics processing units and provide computing services. The center will support self-driving software, robot training and vehicle research as the group develops physical AI, which refers to AI that controls machines such as cars and robots in the real world. The group is also discussing technical cooperation with global companies and financing with the state-run Korea Development Bank and other lenders. The wider Saemangeum AI Valley is also planned to include a robot manufacturing cluster, solar power, a hydrogen production plant and an AI hydrogen city.

On Friday the group opened an on-site project office in Gunsan to handle permits, construction and discussions with government agencies. About 30 people attended the ceremony, including Saemangeum Development and Investment Agency Commissioner Moon Sung-yo and Jeonbuk State Gov. Lee Won-taek. Hyundai Motor Group Vice President Shin Seung-kyu said the office is a symbol of the group's will to push ahead with the project without wavering. Saemangeum is a large reclaimed coastal zone in North Jeolla Province, roughly 200 kilometers south of Seoul, that is being developed as a strategic enclave for high-tech industry, green energy and tourism.

Articles.Title: Hyundai Motor advances $6.3 bil. AI hub in Saemangeum

stories.Headline: Korea's medical AI advances, but clinical adoption remains slow
stories.Summary:
Experts discussed the slow clinical adoption of medical AI in Korea at a symposium hosted by Eulji University Medical Center to mark its 70th anniversary, held in Seoul under the theme "Future Healthcare with AI." The Korea Times reported the event on Oct. 30, 2026, in an article by Kim Bo-kyoung. The article said AI has improved public access to medical information and helped physicians at primary and secondary institutions keep up with research. Despite this, adoption in clinical settings remains slow.

According to Ministry of Food and Drug Safety data cited by the article, 549 AI medical devices received regulatory approval through the first half of this year, but only 49 are covered by national health insurance. Seo Joon-beom, a professor at Asan Medical Center, said regulatory approval does not necessarily mean a technology is needed in clinical practice. He said Korea has yet to address its longstanding reimbursement issue, including whether hospitals should be paid more for technologies. Park Jung-hwan of the health ministry's Medical AI and Data Policy Division pointed to regional disparities, saying new AI technologies are concentrated in the capital region.

The Presidential Council on National Artificial Intelligence Strategy established a national AI health care strategy in August, aiming to build digital health care infrastructure within the current administration's term. Park said AI-powered services could overcome geographical barriers and narrow regional gaps, citing uses such as analyzing patient transfer and emergency room data during the golden hour. Seo called for Korea to develop its own health care foundation models rather than rely on foreign technologies, and for greater access to research data. Kim Hyeon-chang, director of the Yonsei Institute for Digital Health, said the goal is not simply high-performance AI but better disease prevention, treatment and health management.

Articles.Title: Korea's medical AI advances, but clinical adoption remains slow

stories.Headline: Dongwon launches AI-powered tuna vessel with drone technology
stories.Summary:
Dongwon Industries launched the Danuri, a 2,000-ton tuna vessel, at Dadae Port in Busan on Thursday afternoon. The launch ceremony drew about 200 attendees, including Oceans and Fisheries Minister Hwang Jong-woo, Dongwon Group Chairman Kim Nam-jung and Dongwon Industries CEO Park Sang-jin. Captain Kim Min-sung and about 30 crew members departed on an approximately yearlong tuna fishing operation in the South Pacific. The vessel is equipped with AI, drones and remote monitoring for fishing and crew safety. Dongwon invested more than 50 billion won, or about $35 million, in the Danuri.

The vessel carries two fish-detection drones that can take off and land automatically while it is moving and fly at up to 120 kilometers per hour. Drone footage is analyzed in real time by AI systems in the control room, while three-dimensional sonar and radar help crews identify fish schools.
