stories.Headline: APEC tourism seminar highlights AI's influence on international tourism industry
stories.Summary:
The APEC Smart Tourism Seminar took place on Thursday in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, as an official project of the APEC Tourism Working Group. It focused on how AI will influence travel services. Zhang Xu, chair of the World Tourism Alliance, told the seminar that AI is driving a profound transformation of tourism and will be pivotal to the recovery of international travel. He said digital technologies are reshaping the entire process of tourism services, from smart destinations and personalized itineraries to multilingual services and cross-border visitor flow forecasting.

UN Tourism's World Tourism Barometer estimates that 1.52 billion international tourist trips were recorded in 2025, almost 60 million more than in 2024, with Asia-Pacific and China in particular leading the growth. According to China's National Immigration Administration, foreign nationals made 22.91 million inbound trips to China in the first half of 2026, up 20.4 percent year-on-year. Cihan Cobanoglu, a professor of AI business at Virscend University in Irvine, California, said China provides an excellent example of how AI and digital technologies can improve tourist services. He said that in 15 years of traveling to China he has seen huge changes, and that apps such as Didi and Alipay now offer multilingual services that let him get to the airport, check into his hotel and book train tickets without any help.

Hangzhou has long been at the forefront of smart tourism in China. Ahead of the 2025 Spring Festival, the city introduced the "Easy Go" luggage service, one of China's first, which lets travelers book luggage transfers through a mobile app. The service ensures their belongings are transported anywhere within the city while they move freely between attractions and shopping areas. The articles do not say what further steps follow the seminar.

Articles.Title: APEC tourism seminar highlights AI's influence on international tourism industry - China Daily

stories.Headline: Moonshot AI launches upgraded Kimi model
stories.Summary:
Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI has launched Kimi K3.1 Pro, an upgraded version of its Kimi K3 model, with TechTimes reporting a release date of October 23. The model debuted fourth among 215 models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, scoring 55 points, which is 11 more than its predecessor. The evaluator said it would become the highest-ranked open-weight model on the index once its weights are published. Moonshot says the upgrade brings stronger coding, financial research and 3D design abilities, while deliberately limiting the model's capacity to carry out cyberattacks.

The model keeps the K3 design, with 2.8 trillion parameters, about 104 billion of them active for each token, and a one-million-token context window. It is available now through the Kimi apps, coding tools and developer platforms, and the company plans to release the full weights by November 4. To limit cyber capability, Moonshot removed cybersecurity-related data from parts of its training pipeline, including reinforcement-learning environments, while keeping general programming tasks. On its own vulnerability discovery and exploitation test, K3.1 Pro scored 81.0 percent, against 90.5 percent for a comparable version trained without the safeguards, and both figures are self-reported. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Moonshot reported 65.7 percent for K3.1 Pro, ahead of OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra at 58.2 percent and just behind Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at 66.4 percent.

Moonshot said it aims not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. TechTimes added that the company views the 9.5-point gap as keeping the model's offensive ability below that of proprietary models already available. It noted that independent researchers will only be able to check these claims once the weights can be downloaded, since Moonshot's figures are the only data until then. Artificial Analysis found the model slower and more verbose than most rivals, at 57.5 tokens per second and an estimated $2.11 per task. TechTimes also pointed to Chinese laws that can require organizations to cooperate with state intelligence work, a concern for developers sending data through the service.

The launch comes as Moonshot prepares to tap public markets. Bloomberg reported this month that the Beijing-based firm had completed a private funding round valuing it at about $50 billion and was targeting a Hong Kong debut in the first quarter of 2027. A Bloomberg Intelligence report put the gap between top Chinese and American AI models at around 3 percent, the lowest on record, and analyst Robert Lea said the pace of catching up raises questions about how long the US can keep its lead. Stanford's 2026 AI Index said the gap had effectively closed, with the best US model ahead by only 2.7 percent as of March. Tsinghua's Zhang Yaqin said Chinese models have entered the global top tier, while his colleague Tang Jie said China still needs to catch up in high-end chips and fundamental AI architecture.

Articles.Title: Moonshot AI launches upgraded Kimi model - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: Meet Tracy Pennycuick, the trailblazing Pennsylvania state senator pioneering bipartisan AI safeguards
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania state Sen. Tracy Pennycuick, a Montgomery County Republican, has worked in 2026 on legislation to protect children from harms linked to artificial intelligence. She chairs the Pennsylvania Senate's Communications and Technology Committee. She was first elected to the Pennsylvania House of Representatives in 2020 and then to the state Senate in 2022. Before politics she served 26 years in the U.S. Army, including as a combat medic and as an operations officer during Operations Desert Shield and Desert Storm, Operation Iraqi Freedom and Operation Enduring Freedom.

Pennycuick authored the SAFECHAT Act, which stands for the Safeguarding Adolescents from Exploitative Chatbots and Harmful AI Technology Act. The bill would restrict AI content that encourages suicidal ideation, self-harm or violence against others, and it would direct users to self-harm crisis resources when high-risk language is detected. She also sponsored a bill to ban AI-powered "nudification" apps in Pennsylvania and championed another bill giving law enforcement authority to prosecute people who use AI to generate unconsented deepfake sexual images of minors. She also paved the way for the passage of Kayleigh's Law, which provides lifetime no-contact protections for victims of violent crimes.

Pennycuick told the Washington Examiner that she was horrified by an incident at Lancaster Country Day School, where male students created child sexual abuse material from images of their female classmates using AI, and that the students could not be fully prosecuted because no law specifically addressed AI-generated child sexual abuse material. She said the school administration knew about it for six months before reporting it, and that the victims experienced PTSD, anxiety, eating disorders and depression. She said the girls were courageous in advocating for stronger laws and that she knew she had to be their voice. She said laws must keep pace as these tools become more common in classrooms, on smartphones and across social platforms.

The article says her legislation was arguably the inspiration for a roundtable discussion held earlier this year by Gov. Josh Shapiro about threats posed by those who exploit AI, though he did not give her credit. It says she does not seek the spotlight and that she always finds a Democrat to work with on her legislation. She said she never thought she would enter politics and is not sure she even likes politics, but she likes solving problems. She said that in the military no one knows or cares who you support politically, and that she approaches being a senator the same way.

Articles.Title: Meet Tracy Pennycuick, the trailblazing Pennsylvania state senator pioneering bipartisan AI safeguards

stories.Headline: AI-generated legal arguments under scrutiny at ADR forum
stories.Summary:
Lawyers and arbitration experts raised concerns about clients relying on AI-generated legal arguments at the Seoul ADR Festival, according to Law.asia. Wonyoung (Karyn) Yoo, a foreign attorney at Kim & Chang, spoke at the 15th Asia-Pacific ADR Conference held at the Josun Palace, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Seoul Gangnam. She said clients now arrive having already consulted AI and prepared their initial case with it. When lawyers review the documents, they often find the documents do not really support the case AI prepared. The conference is part of the ADR Festival, held at multiple places throughout Seoul.

Yoo said the challenge for legal counsel is no longer going through documents or identifying the case. The new challenge is explaining to clients that the case they created with AI does not really work. Mohamed Abdel Wahab, founding partner at Zulficar & Partners, said younger generations rely heavily on technology and AI, which may change how they perceive trust in professional relationships. He said clients today take lawyers' opinions and assessments to AI and challenge them. Myrna Barakat Friedman, an independent commercial arbitrator and mediator, said people should not use AI unless they know the subject matter of their queries.

Friedman said AI translations can be pretty good but not perfect, and users must be able to question the output to verify it. She said they must also pick up on nuances that AI misses. Joongi Kim, a professor at Yonsei University Law School, said AI can actually generate too much. He raised concerns about prompt injection, in which crafted instructions can manipulate an AI model's behaviour or output. He said that while nobody in the room would do anything unethical, there are people who will go to the dark side.

Lucas De Ferrari, a partner at White & Case, used an analogy with airline pilots to explain the role of legal counsel. He said modern pilots rely extensively on automated systems, but that does not mean their role has diminished. De Ferrari said lawyers would hold a similar role, using AI for repetitive tasks and freeing up time for arguments, judgement and expertise, the qualities clients seek from legal counsel. The Seoul ADR Festival is hosted by the Korean Commercial Arbitration Board International from 26 to 30 October 2026, and Law.asia is an official media partner of the event.

Articles.Title: AI-generated legal arguments under scrutiny at ADR forum

stories.Headline: How AI and robots are reformulating traditional Chinese medicine
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence and robotic systems are being used in China to update traditional Chinese medicine, according to China Daily. In Beijing E-Town, an intelligent TCM android named Wang Shuhe, after a medical expert of the late Eastern Han Dynasty and early Wei-Jin periods, turns the diagnostic logic of experienced physicians into accessible consultations. In Chengdu, Sichuan province, robots and AI agents are digitizing and reworking classical medical frameworks, translating subjective, qualitative diagnostics into objective, quantifiable datasets. On a tourism street in Chengdu, the writer used a VR headset to practice tai chi guided by a panda through moves set in renderings of Sichuan landmarks.

The article gives no specific dates for these developments beyond its publication on October 31, 2026. It describes the long history of TCM, saying legend credits Shennong with devising it in the Neolithic period after tasting hundreds of wild herbs, and that it was later encoded in texts tied to the semi-mythical Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor. It says the writer first arrived in China two decades ago, when discussion of TCM focused on internationalization rather than innovation, and that in the following years more enterprises and institutions committed to research and development. It also mentions research centers in Lhasa in the Xizang autonomous region, where Tibetan medicine is being updated, and in Altay in the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, where TCM has long been integrated with Tuva and Kazak medicine. The writer notes that his wife's acupuncture now uses a device that sends electrical pulses to stimulate targeted points, which she reports gives greater relief.

The article does not name any person or organization as responsible for these changes and carries no direct statements from officials or developers. It presents the shift as a continuation of TCM's habit of branching out, saying its traditional roots have never constrained it from developing in new directions. It describes the new tools as carrying forward the same curiosity attributed to Shennong and the framework for understanding balance attributed to Huangdi. The writer frames the change as machines reading patterns where healers once read the pulse, and algorithms measuring hard data where fingertips once measured qi, often finding the same rhythms.

The article presents this as part of a broader trend of investment in research and development and innovative products, with centers attached to enterprises, universities and even museums. It says such departments are proliferating in Lhasa and expanding in Altay, where unique local conditions shape therapeutic practices. It does not say what concrete results, approvals or further steps are expected. It closes by saying that despite the transformations, patients remain the same and still hope for the best possible health.

stories.Headline: AI-powered hearing aids: How they help you follow conversations in noisy places
stories.Summary:
Lim Chee Keong, a 58-year-old retired bank manager, first noticed changes in his hearing in his early 50s but dismissed them as people mumbling. The turning point came during a dinner with old friends at a noisy restaurant, when he answered a question with something completely unrelated. He booked a hearing test the following week, and an online test by 20dB Hearing found he had moderate to severe age-related hearing loss in both ears, affecting his ability to understand speech, particularly amid background noise. He was then fitted with the Phonak Audeo Eon Sphere, which was prelaunched exclusively at 20dB Hearing.

The Eon uses AI-powered technology, including Spheric Speech Clarity 3.0 and the Hypersonic chip, designed to help separate speech from background noise. It is designed to recognise changes in listening environments and adjust how sounds are processed, reducing the need for wearers to change settings manually. The Eon is 25 per cent smaller and 20 per cent lighter than the previous Sphere model, and offers around 22 hours of battery life on a single charge, even under demanding conditions such as Bluetooth streaming and noisy environments. Wearers who want more control can use the myPhonak app to personalise their settings.

Grace Wong, an audiologist at 20dB Hearing, said most people with hearing loss do not need everything louder, but extra help with certain pitches, usually the high-pitched consonants that make words clear. She said test results show what a person can hear, but conversations show what they need to hear and how they live with their hearing loss. Kausellya Subramaniam, senior audiologist at 20dB Hearing, said earlier generations already helped people hear better and the Eon takes another step towards helping the hearing aid understand the listening situation and respond accordingly. She advised patients to wear their hearing aids for at least eight hours daily during the adjustment period, and said the user is the one who can give feedback about what feels too loud, too soft or not natural.

Lim said he could hear the birds in the morning again, which he had not realised he had missed, and that the biggest difference was being able to follow conversations without guessing. He said the room suddenly sounded sharp when he first put the device on, which was a bit much for a day or two before his brain got used to it. He recently returned to a restaurant with the same group of old friends and could join in without guessing what others were saying. The article says professional fitting and ongoing support remain important in helping wearers adapt, and that 20dB Hearing's Product Lifetime of Aftercare Promise provides continued support throughout the lifespan of the device.

Articles.Title: AI-powered hearing aids: How they help you follow conversations in noisy places - The Straits Times

stories.Headline: Joe Mazzulla Reveals How AI Is Changing His Approach to Celtics Coaching
stories.Summary:
Boston Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla discussed his use of artificial intelligence with reporters on Friday, October 29, 2026, according to NESN. Mazzulla said he uses the AI tool Claude every day to help evaluate his coaching methods, organize ideas and explore different approaches to preparing his team. He said he has not used ChatGPT but is all in on Claude. He described the technology as keeping him in a constant state of searching and getting more out of him.

Mazzulla said the tool helps him organize, become more efficient and understand things. He said he uses it for conversation and riffs, such as asking what a problem looks like from a psychological perspective and what the research and data show. He views AI as another resource to challenge his thinking rather than a source of definitive answers. The fifth-year head coach has been examining the Celtics' pregame and halftime film sessions, practice routines and how players retain information.

One example involved comparing basketball, soccer and handball, three sports Mazzulla has studied extensively. He used AI to explore the similarities between them, identify shared elements of play and determine how those concepts could translate to five-on-five basketball. Mazzulla said the goal is to find more effective ways to communicate with players and maximize limited time in practices and games. He also wants the Celtics to get more out of film sessions, particularly in helping players understand and retain the game plan.

The approach reflects Mazzulla's willingness to question established routines rather than assume the team's current methods are the best options. As Boston works through the 2026-27 NBA season, the coach is looking for every available advantage. AI has become another tool in that effort, helping him explore new ideas and reconsider how the Celtics approach their preparation. Mazzulla has never led the Celtics to a lower seed than second in the East.

Articles.Title: Joe Mazzulla Reveals How AI Is Changing His Approach to Celtics Coaching

stories.Headline: Fighting wildfires with robots and artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Extreme wildfire activity has more than doubled worldwide, and fires are becoming more frequent, more intense and larger. Rising global temperatures, warmer nighttime lows and prolonged droughts are driving the trend, and it is only getting stronger. In response, federal agencies are already using drones to map fires, find hotspots and ignite controlled burns. Researchers are now testing robots for use on rough terrain and artificial intelligence in fire and smoke behavior forecasts.

The Forest Service is testing unmanned ground vehicles that could move equipment through rugged terrain. Ground robots can do tasks where people may face unnecessary hazards, such as falling trees and steep, rugged and unstable terrain. AI-enabled unmanned aerial systems, combined with improved fire-behavior modeling, better cameras and satellite data, could revolutionize wildfire detection and tracking, fire suppression efficiency and, most valuably, firefighter safety. For wildland firefighters, fatal incidents are frequently driven by aviation-related accidents, vehicle crashes and sudden medical events.

Robots and AI-enabled drones are not yet ready for routine wildfire operations. The article says there is great promise for reducing the risk exposure of firefighters while getting equipment and supplies to fire lines, as well as improving the ability to predict where fires are going. The article does not name the people responsible or include any statements from them. It also does not say what happens next beyond the testing now under way.

Articles.Title: Fighting wildfires with robots and artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: Pope Leo Comes Out Swinging Against AI Personhood
stories.Summary:
Pope Leo XIV posted a lengthy thread on X on October 30, 2026, rejecting calls to grant AI systems legal personhood. He wrote that machines are tools, not persons, and that giving them rights risks obscuring human responsibility and leaving people who suffer harm to face a faceless entity. He said AI's future is not predetermined and depends on human choices, so people have a responsibility to guide, change, and when necessary reject its applications. He added that a reliable system serving the human person is worth more than an exceptionally powerful one whose consequences cannot be foreseen or controlled.

The Pope called for AI to be disarmed and said decisions affecting human life, freedom, and the use of force must stay under effective, informed, and responsible human oversight. He said intelligent technologies must be directed toward the common good and must never become ends in themselves or serve only the interests of a privileged few. He said many ethical principles for AI are already known, and what is needed now are effective international institutions to safeguard the global common good. He called for shared standards, independent oversight, and clear accountability mechanisms so AI decisions can be examined, challenged when necessary, and met with remedies for any harm caused.

The article says lawyers, activists, and lawmakers have opposed AI legal personhood on similar grounds, arguing that rights such as free speech for AI could muddy who is responsible when things go wrong. It also says many in the AI industry insist AI systems are or may soon be sentient and some argue they should have human rights. It reports that officials from Anthropic, the maker of Claude, held talks with religious leaders this summer in which the AI representatives encouraged clergy to consider that models may be conscious. The article says those talks appear to have done little to sway the Pope, who has repeatedly raised concerns about AI without guardrails and has focused heavily on the rise of autonomous weapons.

Articles.Title: Pope Leo Comes Out Swinging Against AI Personhood

stories.Headline: LI experts offer advice on AI adoption and managing risks
stories.Summary:
A Long Island Business News panel on October 29, 2026, moderated by editor Regina Jankowski, brought together three experts to discuss how small and medium-sized businesses can adopt artificial intelligence and manage its risks. The panelists were Wencui Han, an associate professor of operations and decision analytics at Stony Brook University College of Business, Michael Del Piano, a partner in the Commercial Group at Lewis Johs Avallone Aviles, and Savio Chan, co-founder and CEO of the American AI Leadership Institute. The 60-minute discussion covered why AI represents a fundamental technological shift and how companies can use it while balancing costs, risks and responsible adoption. The panelists agreed that the time to harness AI is now.

The conversation focused on agentic AI, which moves beyond answering questions to performing tasks and automating business processes, such as checking emails, updating calendars, answering product questions and handling billing discrepancies. Han warned that connecting multiple systems too quickly can make it hard for owners to track what information and tools their AI agents can access. Chan recommended a gradual approach he described as crawl, walk, run, starting with a separate email account and noncritical tasks like booking a restaurant reservation before granting access to a primary email, financial information or business systems. Del Piano raised legal and compliance concerns, saying that entering protected health information into a free AI platform could expose companies to significant enterprise risks and HIPAA violations, and that courts in some cases have found communications with generative AI are not necessarily protected by attorney-client privilege. Han advised business owners to check their platform's privacy settings and understand whether their data may be used to train AI models.

Chan said companies should have an internal policy on AI use for all employees even before choosing the right product, and that a simple one-page document that every employee understands and signs off on can set out what AI can and cannot be used for. Del Piano agreed, saying companies need an acceptable use policy and must actually enforce it to be defensible later if a problem arises, especially with shadow AI. Han said the risk of not using AI is higher than the risk of adopting it, and Del Piano said it would be irresponsible for companies not to try to harness it to some degree because competitors will be doing so. The article is the first of two on the panel, and LIBN directed readers to register to view the webinar.

Articles.Title: LI experts offer advice on AI adoption and managing risks

stories.Headline: Weekly Rundown: Doximity launches DoseCheck; AI recommends costlier care than doctors, study finds
stories.Summary:
Doximity launched DoseCheck, a safety feature inside its Doximity Ask clinical decision support tool, on October 30, 2026. The feature is meant to catch unsafe or incorrect medication dosing recommendations generated by artificial intelligence. Instead of asking a language model to check another language model, DoseCheck uses a deterministic, rule-based layer that checks AI dosing claims against structured information such as FDA labeling and professional guidelines. The company says this raises accuracy to more than 99%, and the feature is free and has been rolled out to all Doximity Ask users on mobile and desktop.

Doximity tested nine widely used AI models with more than 8,000 dosing questions based on real physician queries. At least 2.3% of the dosing claims from these models were wrong, and 43.8% of the detected errors were serious or potentially lethal. Common sources of error included dosing newer drugs, missing patient factors such as kidney function, age, weight and medical history, and mistakes with units, decimal points or drugs with similar names. Louis-Antoine Mullie, Doximity's chief AI researcher, said AI is probabilistic while drug dosing cannot be, and that DoseCheck checks claims against a structured, authoritative database rather than asking a language model to grade its own homework.

A study published in NEJM AI found that large language models recommend more up-front testing, referrals and treatment than the physicians who saw the patients, at more than three times the cost. Researchers from the Technion, Stanford University and collaborating institutions tested 20 general-purpose and four specialized medical AI systems on records from 200 real outpatient and emergency visits. AI-suggested care cost a mean of $314 per visit, compared with $97 for care recommended by attending physicians, and suggested care was more costly in 180 of 200 cases. The authors wrote that every AI system they evaluated suggested more diagnostic tests, medications and specialist referrals than the treating physician on the same cases.

The researchers argued that much of the excess cost can be reduced through better prompting, suggesting it is partly a deployment and design problem rather than an unavoidable feature of AI. A simple cost-aware prompt cut average recommended costs from 3.2 times physician costs to 2.5 times, and a stronger "parsimonious-but-safe" prompt cut costs to 1.4 times physician costs. However, diagnostic agreement with physicians fell in 17 of the 19 systems reevaluated with different instructions. Dvir Aran of the Technion, the study's corresponding author, said getting the diagnosis right matters but so does the path taken to get there, and that efficiency needs the same attention as accuracy and safety.

Articles.Title: Weekly Rundown: Doximity launches DoseCheck; AI recommends costlier care than doctors, study finds

stories.Headline: AI & Robotics Selloff Creates Disconnect Between Valuations & Fundamentals - ETF Database
stories.Summary:
An indiscriminate selloff in AI and robotics stocks in recent months punished strong companies alongside weak ones, according to an ETF Database article by Elle Caruso Fitzgerald published on October 30, 2026. Celestica, which makes networking equipment for data centers, raised its 2027 revenue outlook to approximately $40 billion, effectively doubling expectations, yet its stock declined. Phonic reported record-high orders and sales, but its stock also fell. Zeno Mercer, head of AI and robotics research at VettaFi, said many things do not really make sense right now.

The article points to manufacturing data that it says does not match the weak market sentiment. U.S. factory construction has run at about $200 billion a year versus a historical $70 billion baseline, and PMI has expanded for nine straight months. North American robot orders rose 24.8% year over year in the third quarter of 2026 to 10,989 units valued at $723.5 million, according to the Association for Advancing Automation. That was the strongest quarter of the year, led by semiconductor, electronics, and automotive component suppliers.

Mercer is the main person quoted, and he described a genuine disconnect between prices and business momentum. He said price discovery should eventually normalize valuations upward, since robotics and AI valuations trade at a discount compared to earlier in the year. The article also describes index changes: the index behind the ROBO Global Robotics and Automation Index ETF added Global UniChip, a design partner to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, and the index behind the ROBO Global Artificial Intelligence ETF added Ambiq Micro, whose chips run at lower power than competitors. Mercer noted that many AI and robotics names have no direct tie to data centers and benefit from open-source tools and cheaper energy. VettaFi owns the site and is the index provider for both funds, for which it receives a licensing fee.

Articles.Title: AI & Robotics Selloff Creates Disconnect Between Valuations & Fundamentals - ETF Database

stories.Headline: "I'm all in on Claude" - Joe Mazzulla admits he uses AI every day to help coach the Celtics
stories.Summary:
Boston Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla said on October 30, 2026 that he uses the AI tool Claude every day for coaching. He said he loves Claude and is all in on it, and that he has not used ChatGPT. The 38-year-old made the comments in an article first published by Basketball Network. Mazzulla is the reigning Coach of the Year.

Mazzulla said he used Claude in the offseason for his personal development and for where he wanted to take the team psychologically. He said he puts last year's practice plan into the tool and asks whether it was efficient. He said the tool helps test his processes and keeps him searching. He also said everybody in the room uses it.

Mazzulla has coached the Celtics for four years, winning a record 18th championship and more than 60 games in two of those seasons. Boston never finished lower than second in the East in that stretch. In 2025-26, after the team let go of Kristaps Porzingis, Jrue Holiday and Al Horford and Jayson Tatum was out for almost the entire season, Mazzulla led Boston to the second seed. The article says the Celtics traded Jaylen Brown in the offseason and that Paul George, 36, is averaging 22.3 points over his first four appearances, while Tatum leads the team with 28.0 points per game.

The article says AI can help teams analyze data and find patterns, but it cannot fully account for a player's character, fit within a system, or a game's changing momentum. It says coaches who rely too heavily on technology risk overlooking their own instincts and the unpredictable nature of basketball. Mazzulla said he is not interested in letting AI replace the human element of coaching and sees it as another tool to improve his methods. The article says the Celtics are already showing optimistic results.

Articles.Title: "I'm all in on Claude" - Joe Mazzulla admits he uses AI every day to help coach the Celtics

stories.Headline: Responsible AI governance requires a human touch – accountability lies with corporate leadership, not the algorithm
stories.Summary:
Rakibul Hasan, a doctoral researcher at the University of Vaasa in Finland, completed a doctoral dissertation on managing artificial intelligence across national borders. The public defence of the dissertation was held on 4 September 2026. The work was published as Acta Wasaensia 591. Hasan's research sits at the crossroads of International Business and Information Systems.

The dissertation offers practical guidelines for executives and managers to safeguard the well-being of AI users. It introduces the Globally Responsive AI Organizing framework, known as GRAO, which governs AI across four interrelated dimensions: autonomy, interactivity, learning, and appearance. Hasan's research data comprises a literature review, interviews, archival material, online observations, and document analysis. The findings are meant to benefit executive leadership and middle management across startups, scale-ups, medium-sized enterprises, and multinational corporations.

Hasan said the common good and AI responsibility are at the core of his dissertation, which focuses on governance of artificial intelligence to achieve collective societal well-being. He noted that AI knows no national boundaries and current estimates suggest it already has over one billion users. He argued that AI itself cannot be trusted blindly and that responsibility rests firmly with individuals in corporate leadership positions. Instead of trustworthy AI, he said trusteeship organizing of AI makes more strategic sense.

Hasan said it is crucial to look after social well-being so that use or development of advanced technology does not create future problems while generating economic value in the market. He said business operations can align with fairness and responsibility while still generating profit for the company. The research contributes to the ongoing discourse on corporate actions aimed at advancing societal well-being. Hasan can be reached at the University of Vaasa for further information.

Articles.Title: Responsible AI governance requires a human touch – accountability lies with corporate leadership, not the algorithm

stories.Headline: Jensen Beach man sentenced to 84 years in AI child pornography, voyeurism case
stories.Summary:
Daniel Clark Warren, a 53-year-old Jensen Beach man, was sentenced on Wednesday to more than 84 years in prison on 82 counts of child pornography, in Martin County's first arrest in a case involving artificial intelligence in 2024. Circuit Judge Elizabeth Metzger sentenced him to 1,013.1 months in prison, with credit for 1,002 days already served. The judge denied the defense's request for a downward departure from the sentence. In July, before a scheduled jury trial, he changed his plea to guilty on all counts of child sexual abuse material and video voyeurism involving a minor, and the plea was amended in August.

Warren was arrested on Jan. 26, 2024, after detectives received an internet crime tip about child pornography. At least one image was of a child under the age of 5, according to the arrest report. Detective Brian Broughton said Warren takes the face of a child, removes the clothing, poses the child and engages them in sexual activity to make the images with AI. Broughton said it is scary when you look at that stuff, and the FBI warns that child sexual abuse material created with content manipulation technologies, including generative artificial intelligence, is illegal.

John Budensiek, chief deputy at the time and now sheriff, said it was Martin County's first case of AI taking a regular headshot and turning it into child porn, and he called it alarming. Broughton said the state waited several months to make the arrest because detectives were working with other jurisdictions to find out if there were other related cases. Broughton said deepfakes of celebrities and politicians have been seen for a couple of years, and he called this a new and scary level. Since then, AI has become more prominent with even better deepfakes, and the articles note later AI-generated child sexual abuse image cases in Stuart and Vero Beach.

Articles.Title: Jensen Beach man sentenced to 84 years in AI child pornography, voyeurism case

stories.Headline: German Minister Targets American Businesses With AI Tax Proposal - Americans for Tax Reform
stories.Summary:
Germany’s education and family minister, Karin Prien of the CDU, wants to impose a new tax on value created by artificial intelligence, according to Americans for Tax Reform. The proposal was reported on October 30, 2026. A tax aimed at AI providers could fall heavily on U.S. businesses, and a broader tax on AI-generated business activity would reach American companies operating in Germany. There is no concrete coalition plan yet, and no rate or scope has been defined.

The tax base is still unresolved, because Prien speaks of value creation while Digital Minister Karsten Wildberger has discussed taxing AI-related revenue. Stanford’s 2026 AI Index records $285.9 billion in U.S. private AI investment in 2025, compared with $20.9 billion across Europe. In its 2019 investigation of France’s digital services tax, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative estimated that 17 of the 27 corporate groups expected to be covered were U.S.-based. USTR concluded that the tax’s structure and operation discriminated against American digital companies.

U.S. businesses with taxable German operations already pay corporate income and municipal trade taxes, and the EU’s Digital Markets Act adds compliance requirements for designated gatekeepers including Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, and Microsoft. During USTR’s French tax investigation, Amazon testified that it had told sellers their fees would rise for sales on Amazon France. A February 2025 White House memorandum directed officials to examine foreign taxes and regulations that disproportionately burden American companies. Americans for Tax Reform said Washington has already identified discriminatory digital taxes as a trade concern.

Americans for Tax Reform argued that an AI levy would add to the tax and regulatory burden American companies already face in Europe. It said businesses may have to separate the value contributed by AI from that produced by employees, conventional software, and machinery, which could mean extra recordkeeping and disputes. The group called on American policymakers to press for fair treatment of U.S. businesses. It also urged German policymakers to rethink excessive regulation before imposing a new penalty on innovation.

Articles.Title: German Minister Targets American Businesses With AI Tax Proposal - Americans for Tax Reform

stories.Headline: The Hershey Company uses AI to reshape aspects of candy shopping
stories.Summary:
The Hershey Company said it is using artificial intelligence to help place its candy where shoppers are most likely to buy it, with Halloween approaching. Field representatives take pictures of candy displays in stores, and the AI helps identify where items sit and how that placement lines up with sales data. The company said the technology supports workers rather than replacing them. Sydney Tierney, a category leadership analyst for seasons at Hershey, said AI can locate products in the store and combine that with sales data to build insights on the best placement through different seasons.

Tierney said Hershey has three of the top five chocolate brands for Halloween, so having them in a prominent place online and in stores matters, and AI helps with that. She said AI is a tool to help human judgment, while field sales representatives are the ones who talk with store managers. The company said its use of AI is expected to expand. Eventually the technology is expected to use shelf images to determine what items are missing and whether inventory is available in the back room.

Tierney said the effort will ultimately be a time-saving tool. She said Hershey is looking at saving 10 to 15% of its representatives' time and administrative work. The company said public reaction to AI has been mixed. The report was published on Friday, October 30, 2026, and covered candy displays at a retail location in Palmyra, Lebanon County, photographed on October 29, 2026.

Articles.Title: The Hershey Company uses AI to reshape aspects of candy shopping

stories.Headline: Methodist uses AI to flag severe heart valve cases sooner
stories.Summary:
Methodist hospital in Omaha, Nebraska, said it is using an artificial intelligence platform to help identify patients with aortic stenosis, a narrowing of the heart valve that can lead to heart failure. The hospital said doctors there note the condition can become severe in just a few months. In one case, a man in his 60s went in for a test for a heart murmur and was not scheduled for an appointment for two months until the AI program caught a problem. Registered nurse Cindy Valgora, a structural heart coordinator at Methodist, said he was treated with a surgical aortic valve and was recovering before he would have been seen in the usual clinic.

Methodist uses a platform called egnite CardioCare, which does not read scans. Valgora said it takes the plain English language off reports and categorizes patients so staff can reach out to them. She said the platform sorts patients by severity and flags severe cases for the structural heart team, and staff take over from there. Dr. Jai Parekh, a structural and interventional cardiologist at Methodist Physicians Clinic, said many things get missed in the details of echocardiograms.

Methodist's new goal is to see flagged patients in one to two weeks and treat them in four to six weeks. The team said that before the program, it took eight to nine weeks from the first visit to treatment. Parekh said the aim is to give patients a better quality of life before they fall off the cliff. Valgora said she makes sure patients know how the AI is used, and that once it is explained, they understand how they got in sooner.

Methodist said the program has allowed it to see 35% more patients. Valgora said people forget how quality of life changes and improves, and that this can now be done sooner than before. Parekh said the platform supplements what staff do, never influences medical decision-making and never replaces physician judgment. Methodist said it is one of two hospitals in Nebraska taking part in an American Heart Association initiative, and that as the technology expands it could also help doctors identify patients with other types of heart valve disease.

Articles.Title: Methodist uses AI to flag severe heart valve cases sooner

stories.Headline: TCAI’s Jai Jaisimha on artificial intelligence and mental health: How should AI be used?
stories.Summary:
Jai Jaisimha, co-founder of the Transparency Coalition, spoke with Rachel Harrison, host of the podcast The Mental Health Evolution, about how artificial intelligence is affecting health care. The interview was published on October 30, 2026, in an article written by Bruce Barcott. Jaisimha discussed the factors driving this year's surge in state AI legislation and the ways AI tools are appearing in clinical settings. The article includes an excerpt of the conversation and a link to the full episode.

The coalition's mid-year report found 84 new AI laws in 27 states in the first six months of 2026. By October 15, that figure had risen to 115 new laws in 30 states. Jaisimha said constituents are speaking up more than ever about their fears, hopes and concerns about AI. He also said legislators have climbed a learning curve through years of education efforts, and even lawmakers whose bills failed in 2025 said they wanted to try again this year.

Jaisimha said a small body of legislation focuses on mental health, especially chatbots used for patient-facing therapy, and the American Psychological Association is actively involved. He said this past year was largely about general-purpose consumer chatbots, with concern that people sometimes treat a chatbot like a trusted person and that its outputs can be confusing, misdirecting or worse. He said AI is widely used for clinical note-taking and transcription, which is not patient-facing. He said future legislation will likely address health care data handling, privacy and patient opt-in, along with questions about clinician supervision, transparency and when a clinician is alerted.

Jaisimha said stakeholders may differ on review, with some preferring clinician review, others some other human-in-the-loop review and others no review at all. He said those questions will be debated alongside the limits of AI technology to ensure legislation protects everyone in the ecosystem. He said he expects more legislation on mental health chatbots next year. The article also links to the coalition's 2026 AI Legislation Report, which found 115 new laws in 30 states as Congress declined to act.

Articles.Title: TCAI’s Jai Jaisimha on artificial intelligence and mental health: How should AI be used? - Transparency Coalition

stories.Headline: Here's why an AI-generated campaign ad depicting Gov. Shapiro is allowed on the air in Pennsylvania ahead of the 2026 election
stories.Summary:
A campaign advertisement paid for by Pennsylvania treasurer and Republican gubernatorial candidate Stacey Garrity features an AI-generated version of Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro, 6abc.com reported on Friday, October 30, 2026. The commercial opens with the AI-generated Shapiro saying hello and that he has been very busy, then goes on to admit to a variety of alleged scandals and claims. The ad discloses its use of artificial intelligence about 40 seconds into the spot, saying it was created with AI thanks to big beautiful data centers. Some viewers said they quickly recognized the ad as artificially generated, and one called it something that should not be legal.

There are currently no Pennsylvania laws prohibiting the use of AI-generated content such as the ad. Pennsylvania Senator Lisa Boscola issued a memo in May announcing plans to introduce legislation that would prohibit AI deepfakes targeting candidates during election season. Delaware already has a similar law, making it illegal to distribute a deepfake of a candidate within 90 days of Election Day unless it is disclosed that the content was created using AI. Under federal broadcasting rules, stations cannot censor or reject campaign advertisements paid for or sponsored by legally qualified candidates, though stations might be able to reject the ad if a third party had submitted it.

A spokesperson for Shapiro's campaign described the ad as cheap and dishonest in a statement to Axios. Matt Beynon, a spokesperson for Garrity's campaign, said it is telling that Shapiro's only complaint with the new ad is that he was depicted using AI, and that he has never refuted a single criticism made in the ad because he knows they are all completely accurate. Lindsay Hoffman, a communications professor at the University of Delaware, said the ad's obvious use of AI may help alert viewers to the technology and its growing capabilities, and that legal frameworks often lag behind technological developments. She said people should already be skeptical when they see political ads, but that this makes it even more important.

Hoffman said she hesitates to claim AI uniquely changes the game, arguing new technologies have historically been used to influence public opinion and create confusion. She said people will find a way to manipulate any technology to change the conversation, the climate of opinion, or to cause chaos and make it difficult for people to understand what they are voting for. She also said the technology could further disengage voters who are already disconnected from the political process, possibly pushing them further away. The article does not say what happens next beyond Boscola's planned legislation and the possibility that laws will catch up to the technology at a slower pace.

Articles.Title: Here's why an AI-generated campaign ad depicting Gov. Shapiro is allowed on the air in Pennsylvania ahead of the 2026 election - 6abc Philadelphia

stories.Headline: Tech Leaders Kiss the Ring and Refuse to Call It "AI" After Trump Told Them Not to
stories.Summary:
After President Donald Trump ordered that artificial intelligence be called "Super Intelligence," or SI, technology executives complied. An analysis by CNBC found that Microsoft, SpaceX, Meta, Tesla and IBM used the term in official documents and communications during this earnings season. One SpaceX filing referred to SI 85 times. Microsoft used the phrase "Super Intelligence era" in an annual report letter. The push began last month, when Trump launched a poll on Truth Social asking supporters to choose a better name for AI.

Days later, Trump told the UN General Assembly that all US government documents would drop the term AI in favor of SI, and he made the change official with an executive order. This week he said he would be "officially BANNING" the term AI in government documents and "everything else." Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella wrote in the annual report letter that the central question in this Super Intelligence era is not just how big the opportunity becomes but how the company delivers real-world outcomes. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk has insisted on using SI in all his public appearances and posts, with occasional slip-ups, and rebranded his AI company SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI. Musk recently admitted he has "SI psychosis."

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called Super Intelligence a "more accurate" term than artificial intelligence but rejected rebranding OpenAI as OpenSI. He has generally sounded skeptical about the rebrand's usefulness. He told Politico that people are going to keep calling it AI. The article describes the tech leaders' embrace of SI as extraordinary toadying toward Trump since he returned to the Oval Office, including from those he once saw as enemies.

Articles.Title: Tech Leaders Kiss the Ring and Refuse to Call It "AI" After Trump Told Them Not to - Futurism

stories.Headline: Pflugerville Adopts New Policy Governing AI and High-Risk Tech
stories.Summary:
The Pflugerville City Council unanimously adopted a policy setting new oversight requirements for artificial intelligence, surveillance technology and municipal data. The council adopted it on October 30, 2026, according to a GovTech article by Chandler Treon. The policy covers technology purchases and vendor agreements, adding review procedures for both. Certain surveillance and biometric systems will now need City Council review and approval before they can be deployed.

Vendors face new restrictions on accessing, selling or using municipal data. Within 90 days, the city plans to set up a resident advisory commission, technology review procedures and a public transparency webpage. The article gives no other dates or figures beyond those. It also does not name any individual council member or vendor.

The City Council is responsible for adopting the policy, and it did so unanimously. The article does not include any statements from council members or other officials about the decision. It also does not say who will sit on the resident advisory commission or run the review procedures. No further comment from the city is reported.

The article does not describe what prompted the policy or what happens after the 90-day setup period. It does not say whether the commission, procedures and webpage have been created yet. It also does not say how the new vendor restrictions will be enforced. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Pflugerville Adopts New Policy Governing AI and High-Risk Tech - GovTech

stories.Headline: Center for Civic Futures awards grant to Nava Labs to help modernize state benefits technology with AI
stories.Summary:
The Center for Civic Futures awarded a grant this week to Nava Labs, the philanthropic arm of Nava PBC, to develop AI-powered tools that help states map and modernize the aging technology behind Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. The grant comes through the organization's Public Benefit Innovation Fund. The tools and service-design processes are meant to cut the time agencies spend mapping legacy systems from months to weeks. Nava plans to work with several states to test the tools and to set up an advisory group of state governments to give feedback on how the approach could be adapted elsewhere.

The project aims to help state policy, program and technology teams build a shared roadmap for modernizing benefits infrastructure, which could improve the speed and reliability of services for beneficiaries. The grant is part of a larger effort to explore how emerging technologies can help agencies with administrative challenges, as states face pressure to update IT systems for new federal changes to Medicaid eligibility checks and SNAP administration. The Center for Civic Futures recently awarded $11 million to 11 projects exploring how AI could help states address administrative burdens. A SNAP verification tool in Mississippi helped reduce the state's payment error liability by $40 million, and AI tools in New Jersey have helped deliver an estimated $19 million in benefits to more than 97,000 residents.

Genevieve Gaudet, director of Nava Labs, said people who depend on public benefits face delayed access, lost benefits and services that do not fit their needs because agencies run on systems built around decades-old constraints. Eleanor Davis, director of the Public Benefit Innovation Fund, said the civic technology field has historically focused on the applicant experience while giving less attention to the systems government employees use to process applications. She said there are many reasons that backend work is hard and that now is a critical moment to push innovation toward using AI where there has been less opportunity to improve service delivery. Nava has also been testing AI-powered tools for mainframe modernization as part of New Jersey's unemployment insurance system upgrade, and the new project will build on that work.

A 2024 report by the Urban Institute found that online-first application and recertification portals exclude many older adults who lack smartphones, high-speed internet or digital literacy. Out of roughly 13 million eligible seniors, fewer than 4 million currently receive SNAP benefits because of these barriers. In states where Medicaid and SNAP are state-administered but county-operated, workload capacity and policy interpretation can create friction across statewide technology platforms. Code for America identified several AI use cases for Medicaid service delivery earlier this year, including conversational interfaces, data quality analysis, process automation, and risk and fraud detection.

Articles.Title: Center for Civic Futures awards grant to Nava Labs to help modernize state benefits technology with AI - StateScoop

stories.Headline: OpenAI Highlights Legal Briefs Arguing AI Training Can Qualify as Fair Use
stories.Summary:
OpenAI on Friday, Oct. 30, highlighted legal briefs arguing that fair use can cover some AI training, adding third-party arguments to an unsettled U.S. copyright debate. The excerpts came from briefs filed by creators, academics, accessibility advocates and legal experts. Those filers argue that fair use can support some AI training and innovation. OpenAI's post did not announce a new court ruling. In June 2025, federal district courts accepted fair-use arguments for model training in Bartz v.

Anthropic and Kadrey v. Meta, based on the evidence in each case. The Bartz decision treated pirated books kept in a central library separately from its finding on model training. Neither decision established a nationwide rule. A May 2025 U.S. Copyright Office report said AI training can be transformative.

It also identified unlawful acquisition, model functionality, deployment and effects on markets for original works as relevant factors. The article does not name who at OpenAI is responsible for the post or what any OpenAI official said about it. It says the excerpts came from briefs filed by creators, academics, accessibility advocates and legal experts. Those filers argue that fair use can support some AI training and innovation. The article does not paraphrase any statement from those filers beyond that position.

The article says earlier district court decisions addressed fair use on the evidence in specific cases. It notes that TokenPost previously covered OpenAI's fair-use position in a summary-judgment memorandum and the Justice Department's separate filing backing that defense. The article does not say what happens next in any case. It does not say whether further filings or rulings are expected.

Articles.Title: OpenAI Highlights Legal Briefs Arguing AI Training Can Qualify as Fair Use - TOKENPOST

stories.Headline: FRE 707 and AI-Generated Evidence: Where the Proposed Rule Stands
stories.Summary:
A proposed federal rule on AI-generated evidence, known as Federal Rule of Evidence 707, was published for public comment in August 2025. The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules approved it for comment in May 2025, and the Standing Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure followed in June 2025. The comment period closed on 16 February 2026, after two public hearings and 59 written comments. The published version said machine-generated evidence offered without an expert, which would be subject to Rule 702 if a witness gave it, could be admitted only if it met Rule 702(a) to (d).

At its 7 May 2026 meeting, the Advisory Committee did not recommend final approval of the rule as published. It preferred a revised draft, known in the minutes as Version 2, titled "Evidence Produced by Artificial Intelligence and Presented at Trial Without an Expert." That draft covers "a product of artificial intelligence," writes out the four Rule 702 factors, presumes an expert is ordinarily needed, and adds a notice requirement. It also drops the exception for simple scientific instruments and takes its definition of artificial intelligence from the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020. The committee agreed that any revised rule would need a new round of public comment.

The committee's May 2026 report states that it does not recommend action on the proposed Rule 707 at this time. Its reporter, Professor Daniel Capra, told the Standing Committee in June that this was the first time in his experience that a rule published for comment had not gone forward. The Standing Committee received an information report only in June 2026, and the Judicial Conference took no action in September 2026. The Department of Justice raised continuing concerns about how the rule would work in practice, according to the minutes, and favoured considering it alongside the deepfake draft.

Rule 707 is not law and has no effective date, so it cannot take effect on 1 December 2026. Under the Rules Enabling Act, the Supreme Court must send a new rule to Congress by 1 May for it to take effect no earlier than 1 December of that year. To take effect in December 2027, the rule would have needed Judicial Conference approval in September 2026, which it did not get. The committee has said the revised version must be republished, and on the usual annual cycle a revised rule published in August 2027 could not take effect before 1 December 2029, which the article describes as its estimate rather than a date the committee has set. The committee held expert panels on AI evidence and deepfakes on 15 October 2026, and a separate draft Rule 901(c) on deepfakes is being held in reserve.

Articles.Title: FRE 707 and AI-Generated Evidence: Where the Proposed Rule Stands - Legal Desire

stories.Headline: AI Chatbot Intimacy Rule Clears House, A$109.2M [2026] - tech-insider.org
stories.Summary:
The House of Representatives passed the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026 on 28 October 2026. An amendment accepted by the government extends the bill's safety duties to AI chatbots, targeting material or conduct that simulates emotional intimacy with a child and encourages dependence on it in place of human relationships. The bill now goes to the Senate and has not received royal assent, so nothing in it binds chatbot providers yet. Early headlines suggested emotional intimacy from AI chatbots would be banned, but the wording describes a narrower duty tied to a specific design pattern and its effect on children. The bill covers social media, online games, apps and AI chatbots, with protections aimed at users under 18.

The maximum penalty for noncompliance is reported as up to A$109.2 million, with a 12-month transition period after royal assent. Under the government's description, companies would have to carry out risk assessments and set up systems to address risky service features rather than only removing harmful content after the fact. Several details remain unsettled in the reporting, including how providers would verify that a user is a minor and what standard would define encouraged dependence. Kate Chaney, the crossbench MP whose amendment the government accepted, supplied the chatbot language and said eSafety had found AI companions offer human-like, sycophantic and often sexually explicit conversations. Communications Minister Anika Wells has been the public face of the proposed rules, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has been cited discussing children treating AI agents as their best friend.

Labor describes the core duty as an overarching obligation for tech platforms to provide a safe online environment for all Australians. Academics have pressed for broader drafting, with Kieran Tranter of the University of Sydney arguing that providers should be required to test how conversations develop over time, not only filter individual messages. The next step is Senate debate, and the reporting does not say when that will happen or whether the upper house will keep the chatbot amendment as drafted. If the bill passes, providers will have a 12-month transition period to prepare, with regulators and courts expected to define the duty over time. Until then, the rules should be treated as a draft with strong political momentum rather than settled law.

Articles.Title: House Clears A$50M R&D Threshold; AI Rules Next [2026] - tech-insider.org
