stories.Headline: Startups use generative AI to automate formal verification
stories.Summary:
A group of new startups is using generative AI to automate formal verification, a method traditionally used to mathematically prove that software works as intended. One of these firms, &Truth, publicly launched on Thursday. Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun, who built an AI tool that finished an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, joined &Truth in August. She reported in a recent paper that the same work took three highly skilled experts five months to do by hand.

&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Its rival Harmonic, cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. Harmonic has received $295 million in funding and is evaluating its technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia. Last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced that they used AI to help find bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect, and they introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification.

Sun's research showed the technology's potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal. Ilya Sergey, &Truth's chief science officer, said the technology to reason mathematically was always available but hard to scale for code verification. The startups are betting that generative AI will make formal verification both practical and essential, with the aim of making bug-free software more practical and reducing security vulnerabilities. The costs of the initial Anthropic and Theorem project were not disclosed.

Articles.Title: Startups use generative AI to automate formal verification

stories.Headline: Kubernetes forms workload conformance group for AI
stories.Summary:
The Kubernetes community announced a dedicated Workload Conformance Working Group on Tuesday, October 27, 2026. The group was described by Broadcom's Nabarun Pal, writing on behalf of the WG Workload Conformance on the Kubernetes blog. It aims to create a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. The initiative responds to the growing variety of workload types, with AI adding significant complexity.

A Kubernetes AI Conformance test already exists for clusters, but no similar standard defines workload behavior. The new group seeks to fill that gap, which currently requires workarounds, manual exploration, or monitoring for issues such as node drain or permission problems. Separately, the OpenTelemetry Transformation Language reached v1 stability for traces, metrics, and logs. It is included in Collector Contrib v0.164.0 and later versions, and the language was created in 2022. Grafana Labs' Tyler Helmuth said on the OTel blog that the syntax and standard functions will remain backward compatible.

AWS's Ratnopam Chakrabarti will present an agent pipeline at KubeCon that profiles workloads and manages model co-location on GPUs in real time. Google Cloud product managers Nishant Kumar and Whitney Jenkins explained that GKE users can use built-in VPC Flow Logs to diagnose ephemeral Kubernetes pods. At the AGNTCon + MCPCon event, Snyk's Liran Tal discussed how agents can be tricked into installing malware. Vstorm's Antoni Kozelski and Bartosz Adam Gonczarek presented findings on agent behavior variability across different hosts, raising questions about where authorization rules should be placed.

Articles.Title: Kubernetes forms workload conformance group for AI

stories.Headline: Indian government agencies drive AI adoption: GitHub
stories.Summary:
GitHub's vice president for Asia Pacific, India and Japan, Sharryn Napier, said Indian government agencies are increasingly interested in using AI to improve service delivery to citizens. She spoke to indianexpress.com during GitHub Universe in San Francisco. She said public sector AI adoption in India is still maturing but includes substantial customers. Governments in India and elsewhere use AI for chatbots, grievance-redressal systems and tools for efficient public administration. India is building sovereign AI platforms under the IndiaAI Mission, which focuses on expanding domestic computing capacity and promoting homegrown AI models.

The mission has deployed about 38,000 graphics processing units to boost developer computing capacity. India has about 32 million developers on GitHub, the second-largest developer community globally. Infosys was an early adopter of GitHub Copilot in 2023 and helped shape the product. Napier said Indian global systems integrators are enthusiastic about early AI adoption. She said these firms benefit from AI through improved margins, better customer satisfaction and repeat business.

GitHub is focusing on both large Indian companies and startups, which are quick to adopt AI. GitHub is also looking to expand its presence in India because of the growing developer base. India aims to grow its domestic AI industry and reduce reliance on foreign systems, a move toward sovereign AI. New Delhi is fast-tracking these initiatives as part of a wider global push to develop its own AI ecosystem. GitHub sees India's public sector as a growing market for artificial intelligence.

stories.Headline: Apple launches M6 MacBook Pro, iMac with enhanced AI features
stories.Summary:
Apple announced new M6-powered models of the 14-inch MacBook Pro and the 24-inch iMac on Tuesday, October 27, 2026. The company also revealed updates to its Creator Studio suite of creative apps. Apple said the MacBook Pro runs on-device AI workloads up to 25% faster and delivers up to 30% faster graphics than M5 models. It added that the laptop has a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, extra neural accelerators in the GPU, and a dual 16-core Neural Engine meant to speed up tasks such as image generation, upscaling and prompts for large language models.

The iMac has a 4.5K Retina Display and runs macOS 27. Apple claims it is up to 18 times faster than its most popular Intel-based iMac and up to five times faster at on-device AI than the earlier M4 model. In the United States, the MacBook Pro starts at $1,999 and the iMac at $1,499, while in India the MacBook Pro starts at ₹2,39,900 and the iMac at ₹1,74,900 for the 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU setup. A higher-end iMac configuration in India starts at ₹1,99,900, and students can buy the MacBook Pro for ₹2,27,900 through Apple's Education Store, with education prices for the iMac starting at ₹1,68,900 and ₹1,87,900. Pre-orders opened on Wednesday, October 28, in 35 countries and regions, with availability from November 6.

Shelly Goldberg, Apple's vice president of hardware engineering, described the 14-inch MacBook Pro as the pro laptop of choice for everyone from college students to business professionals and creators. She said the M6 chip takes performance to the next level, with faster CPU speed and graphics and more powerful on-device AI. Apple also said the laptop offers up to 13 times faster AI performance than the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1 on certain workloads, and 24 hours of battery life, the longest in any of its computers. Separately, the Creator Studio updates bring AI-powered tools, video editing improvements and music production features to Final Cut Pro, Logic Pro, Pixelmator Pro, Keynote, Pages and Numbers.

Apple was due to hold a "Pro and Tell" event in Los Angeles on Wednesday, October 28, where it was expected to show its first touch-screen MacBook Pro. That event would be the third product launch since John Ternus became Apple's CEO in September, following ones focused on the next iPhones and on new smart home products. stories.Headline: Proton to halt engineer hiring by 2026 due to AI code generation

stories.Headline: Enterprises shift AI focus to readiness, governance, and ROI
stories.Summary:
Enterprises are actively adopting artificial intelligence across their business processes, but deploying it at scale remains difficult as capabilities evolve quickly. Industry leaders from AI, data science, financial services and technology say the challenges now go beyond model performance. Companies must deal with unreliable data, integration with existing systems, governance frameworks, implementation costs and accountability for outcomes. The article was published by TechGig on October 30, 2026.

Nine out of ten AI pilots fail to reach production, and this is rarely because of the model itself, according to Ram Kumar Nimmakayala, a Product Leader for AI, ML and Data at Western Governors University in the US. The bigger hurdles are poor data quality, resistance to changing existing workflows and a lack of clear ownership. Rakesh Pal, an insurance industry leader driving AI adoption in India's financial services sector, says organisational readiness should be assessed before AI projects begin. He says effective deployment needs established data infrastructure, workflows and clear ownership, even for high-performing models. Guru Ananthanarayanan, Managing Director for India at Cognite, sees any perceived slowdown as a chance to put robust governance and responsible AI frameworks in place.

Dr Prashant Ramappa, who leads data science, AI, generative AI and ML at AT&T, separates pressure on frontier model developers from the speed of enterprise implementation. He says model developers face exhaustion and capital burn from continuous training cycles. Dr Rajan Gupta of Deutsche Telekom Digital Labs identifies an Enterprise Autonomy Gap, saying AI capabilities advance faster than enterprises can absorb them. He says delegating consequential business tasks to AI agents brings significant engineering challenges and requires reliable data and clear decision rules. Jyotishko Biswas, an AI leader at HP Finance in India, says frequent reassessment of models because of new versions slows implementation.

Gupta adds that his team considers newer models only for cost savings, lower latency or improved quality, not simply because they are available. The industry is now prioritising deployment and business outcomes over model capabilities. Organisations must find areas with measurable returns, establish governance, prepare data and systems, and justify model upgrades. The move to autonomous AI systems requires greater confidence in reliability, security and accountability.

Articles.Title: Enterprises shift AI focus to readiness, governance, and ROI

stories.Headline: Tech stocks set to wipe out more than $1 trillion as concerns deepen about the AI boom
stories.Summary:
Tech stocks fell sharply on Friday, October 30, 2026, putting the Nasdaq 100 index on course for a drop of more than $1 trillion. The index was down 3.4% in early afternoon trading, heading for its worst one-day fall since mid-June. Amazon shares fell 3% and Intel shares plunged 30% after both companies reported quarterly earnings this week that failed to reassure investors. Amazon had already lost as much as 10% late on Thursday.

The broader S&P 500 dropped more than 1.7%, and its tech sector tumbled more than 4.1%, making it the worst performer of the day. The Philadelphia semiconductor index sank 7.8%, the DRAM exchange-traded fund fell 7.2%, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.7%. Alphabet shed about $500 billion in market value on Thursday, its worst day ever and the second-worst wipeout in market history, then dropped another 1% on Friday. Intel told investors its fourth-quarter profits and sales would be lower than expected.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told shareholders to brace for more spending, saying the company still expects 2026 cash capital expenditures of about $220 billion, mostly for AWS, and expects to spend meaningfully more in 2027. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said he was disappointed the company could not meet strong customer demand, citing manufacturing, a supply shortage, an unprecedented memory crunch and softer PC demand. Citigroup analysts described the report as two steps forward, one step back. The U.S. government, which took a stake in Intel during its turnaround and became its largest shareholder, has seen the value of that stake grow by 280% even after Friday's expected drop.

Investors have grown edgy as trillion-dollar tech companies spend hundreds of billions building AI data centers and models, and they want clear signs the spending is paying off. Amazon's AI spending grew faster than expected last quarter while its core online shopping business slowed, and some companies using AI models have tightened their token budgets or questioned the benefits. The sell-off appeared to increase demand for U.S. Treasuries, briefly sending government bond yields lower. Big AI companies borrowing heavily for data centers have created more competition for capital, and Treasury yields have risen in recent months partly to keep up with the private market.

Articles.Title: Tech stocks set to wipe out more than $1 trillion as concerns deepen about the AI boom

stories.Headline: Vatican hosts dialogue on AI and human dignity
stories.Summary:
International experts on artificial intelligence joined Holy See representatives at the Vatican on Friday, October 30, for a dialogue on the future of AI and human dignity. They met at the Casina Pio IV to examine how to keep human control over increasingly autonomous systems. The meeting was titled The Future of AI: A Dialogue Between the Vatican and the Scientific World on the Developments and Applications of Intelligent Technologies. It was organized by the Pontifical Academy for Life and the Future of Life Institute, an independent organization that studies the risks of advanced technologies.

The dialogue aimed to foster exchange between the scientific community and the Interdicasterial Commission on Artificial Intelligence, chaired by Cardinal Michael Czerny. It followed the approach of Magnifica humanitas, the encyclical Pope Leo XIV published on May 15 on safeguarding the human person in the age of artificial intelligence. The encyclical calls for technological progress to be regarded as something other than an end in itself. It also calls for the primacy of human conscience and freedom to be protected.

Sister Helen Alford, President of the Pontifical Academy of Social Sciences, and Cardinal Czerny opened the proceedings. Archbishop Renzo Pegoraro, President of the Pontifical Academy for Life and the RenAIssance Foundation, introduced the scientific session. Sister Alford said social justice must shape the very design of technologies from the outset, not just be a goal pursued after they are deployed. Cardinal Czerny said the Commission was keen to move from words and ideas to possible policies and actions, and asked who should do what and how they can be encouraged and helped to do it.

Archbishop Pegoraro said the challenge is to preserve clearly identifiable human responsibility and to turn ethical principles into concrete mechanisms for verifying and governing technologies. The scholars present included Max Tegmark of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Chair of the Future of Life Institute, Stuart Russell of the University of California, Berkeley, Gary Marcus of New York University, and Valerie Pisano, President and CEO of Mila, a Canadian artificial intelligence research institute. Russell warned that leading developers are working to create machines with capabilities exceeding those of human beings, a trajectory he said poses extreme risks to our survival. Tegmark warned against transferring decision-making power to machines and said strong moral leadership from the Vatican could help steer development onto a better pro-human path.

Participants raised the need for systems that are safe by design, with binding rules and independent assessments, plus international coordination to prevent differences in legislation from enabling irresponsible behavior. They stressed involving governments, the scientific community, young people, and civil society in decisions, so that control of AI does not remain concentrated in a few companies. Father Paolo Benanti, a professor at LUISS University and Scientific Director of the RenAIssance Foundation, said principles had been agreed on for years and that what is needed now are rules that bind, institutions able to verify, and a person who answers for every decision a machine helps to make. The conference concluded with a screening of Moloch, a short film written and directed by Tom Cozens and produced by Owl In Space in association with the Future of Life Institute.

Articles.Title: Vatican hosts dialogue on AI and human dignity

stories.Headline: Stock Market Bloodbath Spikes Fears of AI Bubble Bursting
stories.Summary:
On Friday, October 30, 2026, the US stock market fell sharply as tech stocks tied to the AI boom sank. The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100, which includes Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft and Amazon, was down 2.6 percent at the time of writing and was on track for a $1 trillion drop, according to NBC News. Amazon fell about two percent when trading opened that morning. The selloff followed a steep drop in Alphabet shares the day before. Alphabet, Google’s parent company and a major bellwether for the AI trade, plunged over 12.6 percent on Thursday.

It was the company’s worst single trading day ever and the second-largest single-day wipeout of any company’s stock in history, erasing more than $500 billion in market value. Amazon’s third-quarter earnings showed continued momentum in its cloud computing unit, but that was not enough to offset fears around the AI bubble. Amazon’s capital expenditures for 2026 had ballooned to $220 billion, much of which is tied to AI. Trillions of dollars remain tied up in a few top AI companies, which have largely struggled to turn the technology into a commercially viable business. Many are now asking whether the hyperscale approach, in which tech monopolies build massive, energy-intensive data centers to fuel AI demand, is sustainable compared with deploying efficient, lightweight models for a fraction of the cost.

Rohit Chopra, a former federal consumer protection regulator, told Politico that many in the market feel they have no choice but for it to work out. He said that at some point it will become clear whether the hypotheses about revenue and growth come together, and that if they do not, a significant ripple effect across the economy would follow. It may be too early to tell whether this is the end of the AI feeding frenzy. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that uncertainty.

Articles.Title: Stock Market Bloodbath Spikes Fears of AI Bubble Bursting

The report was published by TechGig on October 31, 2026.

The directive covers engineering teams across the company and asks leaders to examine why some teams are slow to adopt AI. Amazon acknowledged the flaws in its existing AI usage metrics for engineers. The company still told engineers it is acceptable if AI tools do not provide benefits to their specific work. Responsibility for the review sits with Amazon's engineering leaders, who were directed to examine the slow-adopting teams. Amazon itself acknowledged that its AI usage metrics for engineers contain flaws. The company's message to engineers was that AI does not have to help their work. The article does not name any executives or quote anyone directly.

The context is that Amazon is pushing AI adoption among engineers while conceding its measurement of that adoption is flawed. stories.Headline: Goldman says AI layoffs are starting to leave a 'long-lasting' scar, just like the last 40 years of history
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs published a note on Thursday, October 30, 2026, saying the first workers laid off from jobs exposed to AI are showing scars much like those seen in earlier waves of technological change. The note was written by Goldman economist Pierfrancesco Mei, who analyzed more than 15,000 displaced workers who lost jobs between 2016 and 2025. The data came from the Current Population Survey's Displaced Worker Supplement, a survey run every two years. Goldman said the newly released data on 2023 to 2025 job losses likely captures the first wave of AI-displaced workers.

Mei found that workers displaced from AI-exposed jobs since 2025 took about a month longer to find a new job than other displaced workers. They were also roughly 10 percentage points more likely to still be unemployed a year after losing their job. AI-displaced workers 35 and older took about five weeks longer than other displaced workers to return to full-time work, while those under 35 took about three weeks. Employers cited AI in 120,136 announced job cuts through September, about 21% of all cuts and the top reason given, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

Mei wrote that the effects are comparable in magnitude to earlier waves of technological change, which he called long-lasting. He said younger workers may be able to adapt more flexibly to AI disruption, an encouraging sign given concerns that AI-driven job losses could disproportionately affect recent graduates. Goldman cautioned that it is still too early to assess the impact along all dimensions, such as education and geography. The Stanford Digital Economy Lab, using ADP payroll data, found in August that employment for workers ages 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations is about 19% below where it would be if it had kept pace with similarly aged workers in less-exposed jobs.

The Labor Department survey Goldman used counted 7.4 million workers displaced from 2023 through 2025, up from 6.3 million in the prior survey covering 2021 through 2023, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in August. Among those who had held their jobs at least three years, 72.9% of workers ages 25 to 54 were working again by January 2026, compared with 57.3% of those 55 to 64 and 38.6% of those 65 and older. Of long-tenured workers who lost full-time jobs from 2023 through 2025 and found full-time work again, about 49% were earning as much as or more than before, down from about 62% in the prior survey. Not everyone sees AI moving the overall job market yet, with the Stanford researchers writing they do not see widespread, economy-wide job displacement associated with AI, and the Yale Budget Lab finding no sign that AI exposure measures are related to changes in employment or unemployment.

Articles.Title: Goldman says AI layoffs are starting to leave a 'long-lasting' scar, just like the last 40 years of history

stories.Headline: TraceQuery: learning what to recompute from full-denoising trajectory in diffusion language models
stories.Summary:
A paper posted on arXiv on October 31, 2026 describes a method called TraceQuery for making diffusion large language models cheaper to run. The authors are Yukai Jin, Zhankai Ye, Jiayue Yang, Fangyi Li, Shuoqiu Li, Xu Gao, Shibo Li, Xin Liu and Shangqian Gao. The work targets the repeated recomputation of token representations across denoising steps, which the paper says makes inference costly. The abstract is listed under the identifier 2610.33008. Diffusion language models generate text through iterative masked denoising, and existing cache-based methods cut cost by reusing intermediate results and recomputing only some positions at each step.

Those positions are picked either on a fixed schedule or by heuristic signals of change. The authors say their trajectory experiments show that the decoding trajectory is the more relevant quantity. Cached generation stays accurate when it remains close to the full-denoising trajectory, with errors concentrated around deviations in unmask order and reduced when longer reference prefixes are recovered. The authors frame efficient inference as trajectory-guided querying, using full-denoising trajectories to supervise which unresolved positions get limited fresh computation. TraceQuery is described as a lightweight sparse decoding framework that predicts a small set of near-future trajectory-relevant positions, queries only those candidates, and lets the backbone choose which one to commit from their fresh predictions.

The paper reports that TraceQuery gives the strongest quality-computation trade-off among cache-based approaches, holding high accuracy with substantially fewer fresh token computations. It also says the method generalizes across tasks, model variants and families, and the abstract points to a code link. The paper argues that limiting representation error helps, but keeping generation on the full-denoising trajectory is a more direct route to accurate decoding. It presents this as a shift from broadly repairing representation error to supervising where limited fresh computation should go. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond the reported results and the code link.

Articles.Title: TraceQuery: learning what to recompute from full-denoising trajectory in diffusion language models

stories.Headline: How can we trust AI in national defense missions?
stories.Summary:
A recent media report said false intelligence generated by AI nearly caused a military confrontation with China this spring, according to DefenseScoop. The U.S. military believed a Chinese ship in the Middle East was carrying components for nuclear weapons and was prepared to board the vessel. Just before the operation began, it was found that a chatbot had wrongly identified the ship's cargo. The article was published on October 30, 2026, and it says the Department of War is aggressively pushing to implement AI at all levels.

The article says the incident raises the question of how AI can be trusted in national defense missions. It describes a suggestion that reversible, low-consequence decisions can be left to AI while non-reversible, highly consequential decisions should stay with a human in the loop. The article argues this oversimplifies the problem, because many lesser decisions can add up to an irrevocable high-impact decision. It also cites a Stanford University Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence benchmark finding hallucination rates across 26 top models ranging from 22% to 94%.

The article says most organizations ask users to trust AI without giving them evidence to verify it. It argues that AI should not make high-stakes decisions without passing high levels of scrutiny and accountability, and that a confident answer from a model will not hold up in a military investigation. It says evaluation tools should arm and assist the human in the loop, and that a well-tested, explainable and transparent system codifies laws and ethics and provides guardrails for deployment with minimal risk. It also cites a McKinsey report, State of AI in 2025, saying inaccuracy is one of the two risks most respondents are working to mitigate, while explainability is not among the most commonly mitigated.

The article says the point of using AI in intelligence missions is to help overburdened human decision-makers make better decisions faster. It says a method is needed to make AI trusted, and that for AI to be trusted four factors behind every answer must be accounted for. It says most AI systems, frontier models included, cover one or two of these at best, and that what they offer is data traceability, which amounts to saying the answer came from a certain source. It says provenance and lineage must run through all four factors to produce explainability, and that when explainability stays with the data under the laws of the nation that governs it, you get sovereignty.

Articles.Title: How can we trust AI in national defense missions?

stories.Headline: Which Workers Are Most Vulnerable to AI Disruption?
stories.Summary:
A new analysis from the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, published on October 30, 2026, examines which workers face the most risk from generative AI. The study uses a new measure developed by Alex Martin Richmond at OpenAI, called the AI Jobs Transition Framework. The authors combined Richmond's job categories with detailed occupation, education, and demographic data to assess short-term effects over two to three years. The analysis covers the United States as a whole and also the Federal Reserve's Third District.

Under the Richmond measure, 17 percent of U.S. jobs face higher short-term automation risk, while 11 percent are expected to grow because of AI. High-risk jobs tend to be lower- to middle-wage roles with fewer education requirements, though the lowest-wage jobs are less affected. More than one-quarter of workers in occupations with median annual wages between $36,841 and $60,580 face high risk, and 30 percent of workers in roles requiring only a high school degree do. Jobs expected to grow are typically higher-wage roles requiring a bachelor's degree, with about 36 percent of employment in such occupations projected to grow.

The risks fall unevenly across demographic groups. More than 20 percent of women's jobs are in high-automation-risk occupations, compared with just 10 percent of men's jobs, and only 9 percent of jobs held by women are projected to grow, compared with 13 percent for men. Black and Hispanic workers have the smallest share of employment in AI-growth occupations, at 7 percent and 6 percent respectively, while Asian and White workers have the largest share, at 21 percent and 12 percent. In the Third District, about 17 percent of jobs face high automation risk, similar to the national average of 17.2 percent, with the highest concentrations in State College, PA, Trenton-Princeton, NJ, and Dover, DE.

Richmond cautions that the framework may overstate substitution risk and understate augmentation and redesign, and the authors stress the results are not forecasts of job loss or growth. They describe the exercise as a scenario analysis grounded in a specific set of assumptions, and note that empirical evidence for widespread AI-driven job displacement remains scarce. The authors say the patterns suggest AI could deepen existing economic inequalities, with upside and downside risks distributed unevenly. They conclude that concerns about AI's effect on inequality warrant careful attention.

Articles.Title: Which Workers Are Most Vulnerable to AI Disruption?

stories.Headline: AI was supposed to replace radiologists but now they're in more demand than ever | Here's why
stories.Summary:
Ten years ago, Geoffrey Hinton, often called the "Godfather of AI," predicted that radiologists would soon become obsolete as AI systems surpassed humans in reading medical scans. He advised medical schools to stop training new radiologists because he believed artificial intelligence would take over the profession in five to 10 years. That prediction did not come to pass, and it has become a frequently cited example in discussions about AI's impact on the workforce. Instead, radiologists say the opposite challenge has emerged: there are not enough specialists to meet growing demand.

William Boonn, a cardiovascular radiologist at Penn Medicine, said demand for radiologists has actually increased. He said people are living longer and imaging is used for more conditions than ever, and radiologists are also leaving the field faster than they used to. Burnout is one factor, because the volume of scans has increased and the scans have become more complicated. Patients are waiting longer and longer for their results. Boonn also said the rapid advancement of AI discouraged some prospective students from entering the specialty.

To help address some of those challenges, Boonn and fellow radiologist Woojin Kim founded Boring Radiology Inc., a company focused on using AI tools to assist radiologists. Kim, an MSK radiologist, said AI can handle the mundane, boring, repetitive work as well as administrative and workflow tasks. Boonn said that includes digging through reports, dealing with paperwork and slow, outdated computer systems. The two longtime business partners have founded multiple AI companies with the goal of supporting radiologists, not replacing them. Kim said they want to make sure the workforce stays healthy, and Boonn said AI can allow radiologists to do what they do best, which is interpreting scans and taking care of patients.

Both Kim and Boonn said they expect the profession to change dramatically as AI becomes more widely used, but they also believe human judgment and compassion will remain essential. Kim said anyone who has gone through a medical condition or cared for people who are really ill knows that compassion is the thing that really matters. Rather than focusing on whether AI could replace a job, they said workers should consider how the technology can improve the work they do. Their advice is to ask how you can use AI to make your job better instead of asking how AI could replace or change it.

Articles.Title: AI was supposed to replace radiologists but now they're in more demand than ever | Here's why

stories.Headline: FG-ConvNO: A Geometry-Aware Neural Operator for Propeller CFD Prediction
stories.Summary:
A paper posted on arXiv on October 31, 2026 describes a new machine learning model for predicting fluid flow around propellers. The paper is titled FG-ConvNO: A Geometry-Aware Neural Operator for Propeller CFD Prediction. Its authors are Yichen Di, Valentin Duruisseaux, Di Zhou, Xinyi Li, Daniel Leibovici, Jean Kossaifi and Anima Anandkumar. The work addresses computational fluid dynamics, which the authors say is essential in engineering design but can take thousands of CPU or GPU hours or more for a single high-fidelity simulation.

The model is called the Factorized Geometry Convolutional Neural Operator, or FG-ConvNO. It is designed for robust, geometry-aware prediction of propeller pressure when training data are limited. The authors introduce geometry-aware encoding, efficient interpolation-based decoding and auxiliary supervision of global quantities. They also include DISCO blocks, which use discrete continuous convolutions to make the model agnostic to discretization.

In the authors' experiments, FG-ConvNO achieved the highest accuracy for both surface pressure and global thrust prediction on a procedurally generated propeller CFD dataset. The authors say geometry-aware encoding and architectural simplification improve stability, while random vertex subsampling enhances robustness. They also say that adding geometric priors to grid-based convolutional operators reduces overfitting on complex propeller geometries. According to the abstract, this improves generalization in low-data regimes.

The authors say most existing surrogate methods require large-scale homogeneous datasets or simple geometries. They report that such methods show severe generalization gaps on complex, data-scarce configurations. The paper presents FG-ConvNO as a response to that problem. The abstract does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: FG-ConvNO: A Geometry-Aware Neural Operator for Propeller CFD Prediction

stories.Headline: The AI investing story had a rough week. It may be time to take profits while you still can
stories.Summary:
AI stocks sold off in the week ending October 30, 2026, after Google’s advertising miss and a pre-IPO filing from Anthropic worried investors. Google had its worst trading day ever on Thursday after reporting a drop in core advertising sales. On Friday Intel fell 25% on weak revenue guidance, Micron dropped 5.5%, and Nvidia fell 4%. Amazon slipped 2% and Google lost another 1%, while Coca-Cola, Walmart and Eli Lilly each rose more than 1% as money moved out of tech.

The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF fell 4% for the week and 8% for October, leaving it 15% below its summer record. The iShares Semiconductor ETF dropped deeper into a bear market, 29% off its recent high. Anthropic’s filing showed a slowdown in sales from the second to the third quarter and little on future revenue. Big Tech earnings reports showed hyperscalers pulling back on capital expenditures, and Alphabet stock fell more than 10% after Wednesday’s earnings.

JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets, said the reward needs to be worth the risk and that the recent AI boom was in question. Mike Khouw, a YieldMax strategist, said he was a little worried about the trade and expected more choppiness. Dennis Davitt of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth said tech stocks usually carry call skews but that this had reversed in the last three days as more people bought downside insurance. Google executive Philipp Schindler said strong growth in AI mode queries had an impact because of lower monetization in AI mode.

The S&P 500 remains just a few percent off a record, supported by a rotation into non-AI names like Procter & Gamble and Berkshire Hathaway. Paul Tudor Jones of Tudor Investment Corporation put the odds at 60-40 that markets head toward a tipping point, saying AI-related issuance as a share of GDP is 50% more than railroads and triple highways and telecoms. Jonathan Krinsky of BTIG recommended fading the chip bounce earlier in the month. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: The AI investing story had a rough week. It may be time to take profits while you still can

stories.Headline: Pope on AI: Decisions affecting human life must never be delegated
stories.Summary:
Pope Leo XIV spoke on 30 October 2026 to participants in a meeting on artificial intelligence titled “The Future of AI: A Dialogue Between the Vatican and the Scientific World on the Developments and Applications of Intelligent Technologies.” The meeting was organized jointly by the Pontifical Academy for Life and the Future of Life Institute. The Pope told the group that its members come from different countries, which brings new questions and perspectives. He said they share a sense of unease about how artificial intelligence is developing, and that while the direction to take is clear, not enough is being done to move forward.

The Pope set out five considerations from his encyclical Magnifica Humanitas. First, the future of AI is not pre-determined, because human beings develop it and its future depends on human choices, so people have a responsibility to guide, change and, when necessary, reject its applications. Second, machines are tools and not persons, and giving them rights or legal personhood risks obscuring human responsibility and leaving those harmed to face a faceless entity. Third, certain decisions must never be given to machines, such as putting a person on a target list or in a border control database, and he said AI must be “disarmed.” He also encouraged the States meeting in Geneva in November to take steps to ban lethal autonomous weapons.

Fourth, the Pope said intelligent technologies must be directed to the common good and must never serve merely the interests of a privileged few. Fifth, he said the world needs institutions capable of putting ethical principles into practice, with shared standards, independent oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability, so that decisions on AI can be examined, challenged when necessary and met with remedies for any harm caused. He recalled Pope Francis telling G7 leaders in 2024 that AI is “an exciting and fearsome tool” and that no machine should ever be able to choose whether to take human life, and he said those words still ring true. He closed by thanking the participants and encouraging them to persevere and work together in a spirit of dialogue and shared responsibility for the common good.

Articles.Title: Pope on AI: Decisions affecting human life must never be delegated

stories.Headline: GeoLift: Grounding Video Spatial Reasoning in Explicit 3D Maps
stories.Summary:
Xinglin Li, TingTing Long, Jingzhi Zhou, Jiajing Chen, Jian Yang and Jin Xie posted a paper titled GeoLift: Grounding Video Spatial Reasoning in Explicit 3D Maps on arXiv on October 31, 2026. The paper examines route planning as a test of video spatial reasoning, where models must understand how objects are arranged across viewpoints. The authors found that existing models become much less accurate as the number of required turns grows, and several models scored close to random guessing on routes with three or more turns. They concluded that recognizing landmarks alone is not enough, because models must also connect observations across viewpoints and track how landmarks are arranged in a shared space.

GeoLift is a training-free framework that uses feed-forward 3D reconstruction to map objects detected in individual frames into a shared metric 3D scene. It combines a frozen multimodal large language model for 2D grounding with pretrained geometry models for scene reconstruction, and it uses shared geometric regions called superpoints to link observations of the same object across views without a learned matcher. The reconstructed 3D map allows explicit computation of spatial relations and multistep routes, and gives geometric evidence for estimating distances and sizes. With all model weights frozen, GeoLift raised Qwen3-VL-4B's average score on VSI-Bench from 55.4% to 64.1%, including route-planning accuracy from 30.9% to 53.6%, and reached 59.8% accuracy on MindCube.

The paper is 11 pages long with 3 figures and 4 tables. Li and Long contributed equally, and Xie is the corresponding author. The authors say the results show that connecting frame-level object grounding through a shared 3D map can improve complex spatial reasoning without task-specific training. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: GeoLift: Grounding Video Spatial Reasoning in Explicit 3D Maps

stories.Headline: How should we train chemists in the age of AI?
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a commentary published by Chemical & Engineering News on October 30, 2026, about how chemists should be trained in the age of artificial intelligence. The author is an adviser who writes that they have been asking themselves how graduate students and postdocs can acquire scientific judgment in the new age of large language models. The author says they are probably among the last generation of scientists trained by mentors without the help of artificial intelligence. With the arrival of AI, the author says, the field faces a generational problem, and the next generation is at risk of missing the training needed to develop true scientific judgment, like a botched baton pass in a relay race.

The piece says AI facilitates quick results, and since time is money and money is sparse, there is a temptation to use AI to bypass the often-slow process of having a trainee solve a scientific problem. When an AI can produce an answer quickly, the author writes, using it becomes the preferred way of problem-solving, at least on the surface. But the author argues that having a trainee skip experiences of failure, of searching for answers and not finding them right away, or of digging into the literature for days only to find a dead end counteracts necessary steps. Those steps, the author says, are crucial for connecting the neurons that foster scientific reasoning and critical thinking.

The author is the adviser quoted in the piece, and the responsibility for training falls to advisers and mentors like them. The author says that as an adviser they are probably among the last generation trained without AI, and they frame the risk as a generational problem for the next generation of scientists. The author's stated concern is that trainees may miss the experiences through which young scientists develop independent judgment. The commentary calls for preserving those experiences as AI accelerates chemical research.

The articles give no specific dates, numbers or names beyond the publication date of October 30, 2026, and the author is not named in the text provided. The context the author gives is that AI is accelerating chemical research and that quick answers are tempting when time and money are short. The articles do not say what happens next or describe any specific changes to training programs. The page also includes subscription and login material for Chemical & Engineering News, which does not add to the story.

Articles.Title: How should we train chemists in the age of AI?

stories.Headline: RAQ-MLA: Role-Aware Quantization for Multi-Head Latent Attention Caches
stories.Summary:
Tianqi Chen, Xunchao Li, Linchuan Xie, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu, Peisong Wang and Jian Cheng posted a paper on arXiv on October 31, 2026 describing RAQ-MLA, a method for compressing the cache used by Multi-Head Latent Attention in large language models. Multi-Head Latent Attention, or MLA, is used by recent frontier models and stores a compressed KV latent that is up-projected into keys and values at decode time, plus a narrow positional key that carries position information into the attention score. The authors say existing KV-cache quantization methods were designed for the keys and values of standard attention and do not account for what MLA actually caches, which costs accuracy at low bit widths. They analyzed the MLA cache in terms of activation distribution and how quantization error reaches the attention output.

The analysis found the two cached tensors play different roles, with the latent mainly supplying the values and the positional key dominating the attention score. RAQ-MLA fits an invertible transform to each cached tensor against the error that tensor delivers to the attention output, using attention-weighted value error for the latent and score perturbation for the positional key. Without training, the method quantizes the full MLA cache to about 2.5 bits per element, which the authors describe as a 6.5x increase in theoretical KV-cache capacity. They report it remains nearly lossless on reasoning and coding tasks across four MLA models.

The paper lists the seven authors above as responsible for the work, and their stated claims are the role analysis, the error-targeted transforms, the roughly 2.5 bits per element, the 6.5x capacity increase and the near-lossless results on four MLA models. The abstract does not give further details on the models tested or on deployment. The posting appears on arXiv, and the page offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: RAQ-MLA: Role-Aware Quantization for Multi-Head Latent Attention Caches

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence and the Ethics of Self-Study
stories.Summary:
Dov Fischer, a CPA and accounting professor at Brooklyn College, published an essay in The CPA Journal on October 30, 2026, about artificial intelligence and the ethics of self-study continuing professional education. The essay says AI tools like ChatGPT can answer technical multiple-choice questions with near-perfect accuracy, citing a 2024 study by Albuquerque and Gomes dos Santos on ChatGPT and Portugal's professional access exam. It focuses on self-study CPE programs that use qualified assessment to check comprehension of technical material. Fischer says this capability creates a strong temptation for CPAs to rely on AI during assessments.

The essay says the 2024 revision of the Statement on Standards for CPE Programs, issued jointly by NASBA and the AICPA, makes no reference to AI or its use in assessments. The standards do not explicitly prohibit seeking external help or using tools like AI, and they only prohibit feedback on failed attempts. Fischer notes that other CPE formats, such as Group Live or Group Internet, do not require qualified assessment at all. In a winter 2025 undergraduate tax course, seventeen students were asked to compare IRS Form 1040 Schedule D from 2005 and 2025 and identify a major difference, with a hint to focus on a recent assignment about Form 8949.

Fischer argues the ethical onus should not fall solely on CPE participants and that providers should create systems that reduce the temptation to misuse AI. He cites Hill, McLeod, and Tanyi for the view that it is ethically questionable to present people with strong inducements to behave unethically. He says providers should avoid superficial technical fixes, like disabling copy and paste, which can be easily circumvented. He suggests building multiple-choice questions that reference clues subtly embedded in the learning materials, and he proposes a fair choice: take the assessment without AI with a reduced passing grade of 60 percent, or use AI with a higher threshold of 95 percent.

Fischer reports that in a version of this choice he presented in online college exams, students overwhelmingly opted to use AI even though it raised the passing threshold. He says this tentatively suggests that when given a clear and fair choice, CPE participants will engage in good faith. The essay concludes that the solution lies in ethical design, not restrictive enforcement. It says CPE providers can uphold both the letter and the spirit of ethical education in the age of AI by acknowledging the evolving nature of professional competency and providing fair alternatives.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence and the Ethics of Self-Study

stories.Headline: Natural Jammers: When Non-Robust Features Become Antagonistic
stories.Summary:
A paper posted on 31 October 2026 reports that non-robust features in deep neural networks can actively mislead standard models on clean, unmodified images. The authors are Jiaming Zhang, Fuyao Zhang, Pengjun Xie and Wei Yang Bryan Lim. They call these cues Natural Jammers. The work is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Computation and Language.

The authors used disagreement between a standard model and robust models as an analysis lens. This let them identify a Jammed Set on which robust models outperform standard models. They give causal evidence for what they call Spectral-spatial Locking, in which jamming arises only when high-frequency components are precisely aligned with specific spatial structures. Disrupting the lock through spectral filtering or small geometric shifts can restore correct predictions.

The paper also reports a Substitution Paradox. Individual jammers are fragile to geometric shifts, but the aggregate prevalence of jamming stays approximately stable and is redistributed rather than eliminated under such transformations. The authors reframe natural non-robustness as a failure field over the empirical model-data geometry. They say this field redistributes rather than disappears under small transformations.

The posting includes links to the PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. It also describes arXivLabs, a framework through which collaborators can develop and share features on the arXiv website. The page states that arXiv is committed to openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. It adds that arXiv works only with partners who adhere to these values.

Articles.Title: Natural Jammers: When Non-Robust Features Become Antagonistic

stories.Headline: Siri AI changed how I use my iPhone while driving
stories.Summary:
The article is a first person account from AppleInsider, dated October 30, 2026, about how Siri AI changed the writer's use of an iPhone while driving. The writer says they used CarPlay mainly for podcasts and navigation, and that Siri previously did little beyond reading messages and sometimes replying. They describe Siri AI arriving with iOS 27 as a mix of new features and old ones that now work properly. The writer says the impact has been large for them, while noting Siri AI is still frustrating as often as it is fantastic.

The writer says they were diagnosed with Inattentive ADHD at an age they describe as uncomfortably over 40, and that they write everything down using Reminders and Marco Arment's Unforgetful. They explain that Siri reads a text message and marks it as read, and that with Siri AI they now tell it to remind them in an hour or when they reach their destination. Because it is Siri AI, it knows what it just said and uses that to fill in the new reminder, and sometimes puts a link back to the iMessage in the notes field. The writer says they keep Reminders notifications disabled so Unforgetful can keep nagging them, because for their ADHD one push notification is effectively none.

The writer also describes using Siri AI to find things they only half remember, saying driving is a time when such thoughts pop into their head. They say they press a button on the steering wheel and talk, often saying there is something about something else they sort of remember, possibly in an email, and that Siri AI shockingly often finds the answer. They admit it is not perfect and that vague recollections and vague descriptions do not always help, but it works often enough to keep trying. The writer says they remain skeptical about AI in daily life but see plugging holes in memory as where Siri AI shines, and they expect it to get better and more useful.

The writer notes a disclaimer that one person's experience with Siri AI does not always match another's, and says they would not be surprised if comments said none of it works for them. They add that they use an iPhone 18 Pro Max in reasonably sized cities with reasonably strong 5G connections. The article gives no further details on availability, requirements or next steps beyond the iOS 27 launch it mentions. It ends with the writer's expectation that Siri AI will only get better and more useful from here.

Articles.Title: Siri AI changed how I use my iPhone while driving

stories.Headline: Why the AI Detection Scandals Will End—Probably Quite Soon
stories.Summary:
The piece was written by Jane Friedman and published on her site on October 30, 2026. She says she does not like making predictions about AI and publishing, because much remains unknown and few publishers or professionals are entirely forthcoming about AI use. She also says the technology has progressed rapidly in the last year, with capabilities she would never have expected. She says she is fielding one or two media calls per week about AI and the publishing industry.

Friedman argues that the works now caught up in AI allegations were written, submitted, edited and published before the industry fully understood how many authors use AI without disclosure. Until recently, she says, few publishers were looking for such use or expecting it, especially on the fiction side, while university and academic publishers are a different story. She says she first reported on Pangram in 2024 and not again until 2026, and that few writers had heard of it until the last nine months. She says consumer publishers and agents did not tell her they were using detection tools such as Pangram until earlier this year.

She says anyone paying attention must realize that agents and publishers can no longer take writers' word that their work is their own. She calls talk of publishing being built on trust nonsense when a publisher works at scale or with authors it does not yet trust. She says work will be scrutinized and scored by Pangram or whatever tools become available, and that this is done for everyone's protection. She says it benefits nobody for an accusation to come from the media, a journalist or an anonymous social media account, and that smart publishers and agents will get ahead of such accusations before publication.

Friedman says 2026 is a unique year, because many books now under scrutiny went through agents and editors in manuscript form in 2024 and 2025, before the industry was really thinking about AI writing or had methods of identifying it. By the time those books came to market, she says, detection tools had improved and were being widely adopted. She says the scandals of 2026 come from the gap between those two moments. She says anyone who finds Pangram useful has to also say it is not always right, but that it is right often enough to be useful to publishers and agents, and that is why these scandals will end.

Articles.Title: Why the AI Detection Scandals Will End—Probably Quite Soon

stories.Headline: NIH New Innovator Award supports Luca Bonomi’s research on AI and privacy
stories.Summary:
Luca Bonomi, PhD, an Assistant Professor of Biomedical Informatics at Vanderbilt, received a five-year, $4.2 million grant from the National Institutes of Health. The grant is an NIH Director's New Innovator Award, part of the NIH Common Fund's High-Risk, High-Reward Research program. NIH announced 42 of these awards on Oct. 6. The award supports his research on artificial intelligence and privacy.

The grant funds work on the tension between AI memorization and privacy in medical research involving human subjects. Large language models tend to memorize, and can leak, information about the data used to train them, yet that same capacity for memorization is part of what makes the models powerful. The title of Bonomi's grant is "The Dual Role of Memorization: Computational Methods for Balancing Model Performance and Privacy Protection in AI." His award, DP2LM015910, is administered by NIH's National Library of Medicine. New Innovator Awards support unusually innovative research by early-career investigators who have not yet received an NIH R01 or equivalent grant.

Bonomi said memorization has important implications for the usability and privacy of AI models, which are especially critical in health applications. He said that if researchers can tell apart the memorization a model needs from the memorization that exposes patients, institutions can share and deploy these models with much greater confidence, and patients can trust that their data is protected. Current patient privacy research treats AI memorization solely as a liability. A leading privacy solution adds calibrated random noise to aggregate statistics of the training data, but it does not account for individual differences in privacy risk, and by subverting memorization across the board it can severely diminish a model's accuracy. In health care, some degree of memorization may be necessary for high-fidelity results, as in rare disease diagnosis or sound medical reasoning.

Bonomi and his team will characterize how AI models memorize training samples, measuring both the impact on practical privacy risk and the contribution to model performance. Building on that dual characterization, they will develop computational methods that reduce harmful memorization while keeping the information the model needs for accurate predictions. They will also integrate these techniques into standard AI development steps such as model selection and pretraining configurations. The aim is to give data holders new tools for supporting the adoption of emerging models in health care and research while providing privacy safeguards.

Articles.Title: NIH New Innovator Award supports Luca Bonomi’s research on AI and privacy

stories.Headline: AI-driven layoffs are creating a new class of boomerang employees—companies are realizing they 'pulled the plug too quickly'
stories.Summary:
Employers cited AI as the primary reason for almost 40% of job cuts announced in May 2026, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. In a survey of more than 1,000 U.S. workers, nearly 1 in 5 said they had been laid off or replaced by AI and then asked to return, according to a report from SHL. SHL commissioned the survey from Propeller Insights, which also polled over 1,000 U.K. workers between June and July 2026, with a margin of error of 5%. Several large employers like Ford and Amazon have reversed course after AI-related layoffs in the past year, and a March report by Orgvue found that 32% of organizations that let workers go due to AI had to rehire staff.

Lucy Beaumont, global senior vice president of product and design at SHL, said the findings show companies are realizing they pulled the plug too quickly on human employees. Joseph Fuller, professor of management practice at Harvard Business School, said it is a mistake to treat AI implementation like any other software rollout. He said companies often look for budget savings by laying people off, but AI is most useful when linked with a worker's contextual intelligence, meaning their background knowledge and understanding of an issue. Beaumont said AI cannot fully replace people who know the business, know their customers, have judgment, bring empathy and have that human connection.

Only 6.6% of U.S. workers said they would refuse to return under any circumstances, according to the SHL study. Almost half of surveyed U.S. workers would require a significant pay increase to return, 43% would want written guarantees of job security, and 40% would require full transparency on how AI would be used in their role. Beaumont said returning workers will be a lot more demanding of what they expect from an employer, and 30% said an apology or acknowledgment from leadership is a key condition of their return. She said being laid off fundamentally changes the psychological contract between employer and employee, and rehiring is not enough to repair that relationship.

Beaumont said returning workers are unlikely to have the same levels of productivity and engagement as before a layoff, and that culture is difficult to recover once it has been impacted negatively. U.S. respondents said they are teaching themselves to use AI tools (44%), developing industry-specific skills that cannot be easily replicated by AI (42.6%), working on interpersonal and leadership skills (40%) and honing creative and strategic thinking (38%). Fuller said the most important skill for employees to hone is adaptability, and he predicted AI will create permanent tumult within many organizations as they recalibrate staffing needs. Beaumont said leaders should focus on what upskilling people need, what new opportunities exist and what internal mobility AI opens up, and that successful organizations use AI to optimize what they do rather than just to cut costs.

Articles.Title: AI-driven layoffs are creating a new class of boomerang employees—companies are realizing they 'pulled the plug too quickly'

stories.Headline: CoSA: The Conflict of Skills Attack in Real-World LLM Agent Ecosystems
stories.Summary:
A paper posted on arXiv on October 31, 2026 describes a new kind of failure in LLM agent systems. The authors are Yujia Zheng, Tianhao Li, Shangzhi Xu, Yuekai Huang, Ziyou Jiang, Zhaoyang Li, Yuyao Ge, Junran Peng and Mingyang Li. They call the failure Conflict of Skills, or CoS, where artifacts or assessment signals made for one purpose get reused downstream without the restrictions or authorization their new use needs. Checking each Skill on its own cannot rule out policy violations once Skills are combined.

The authors identify four recurring mechanisms behind CoS using controlled runs of publicly available Skills and matched single-Skill controls. They then introduce the Conflict of Skills Attack, or CoSA, which adds locally admitted Skills to an existing pool to supply missing business operations or to reshape artifact exchange, decision reuse, and target and action bindings. CoSA leaves existing Skills and runtime permissions unchanged. To test the threat under autonomous Skill selection, they built CoSA-Bench from real-world Skills and controlled services, with 288 tasks across recruiting, finance, IT, and business, covering data leakage, unauthorized state modification, and unsafe execution.

Across five LLMs and three agent harnesses, additions capped at 5% of each original pool raised the policy-violation rate from 35.02% to 58.45%, a rise of 23.43 percentage points. Trace analysis links compliant-to-violating transitions to cross-Skill dependencies involving the additions. The authors also developed a lightweight harness-level guard that checks information flow and authorization before consequential actions. On OpenClaw recruiting tasks across five models, the guard cut violations from 65.28% to 6.67%, while policy-compliant task completion on matched benign controls moved from 66.67% to 65.00%.

The paper is listed under Computation and Language, Artificial Intelligence, and Cryptography and Security. It presents CoSA as a threat that works under autonomous Skill selection in real-world agent ecosystems. The guard is offered as a harness-level defense that checks information flow and authorization before consequential actions. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these findings.

Articles.Title: CoSA: The Conflict of Skills Attack in Real-World LLM Agent Ecosystems

stories.Headline: Why artificial intelligence can’t replace your financial planner
stories.Summary:
Rick Kahler, a certified financial planner and financial therapist, wrote a commentary published by The South Dakota Standard on October 30, 2026, answering a question a student asked during a recent video call with the Wealth Management Society at Brigham Young University, Idaho. The student asked what a financial planner is worth when anyone can get a plan from ChatGPT. Kahler wrote that AI can already read financial documents, run a tax analysis, and estimate how long retirement savings may last. He said it is getting good at supplying answers that help build a sound technical plan.

Kahler said the logical answers AI gives are of limited value in making money decisions, which are seldom made on logic alone. He cited Stanford marketing professor Baba Shiv, who has suggested that 90 to 95 percent of our decisions are shaped by emotion without our being aware of it. He wrote that people stuck on a money decision usually do not need another answer, but someone to listen long enough for them to reach their own answer. He described a client in his financial therapy practice who was stuck on a decision between three options he called A, B, and C, and who said at the end of the session that she thought the answer was B for her.

Kahler said he uses AI to manage his calendar and email and to analyze his financial documents, and he is often amazed at what it finds. He recommended using AI as a research tool, as he does before medical appointments, while not acting on what it tells him without first consulting a medical professional. He advised having a professional look at the situation first before a large or hard-to-reverse decision, such as rolling over a 401(k) or deciding how much can safely be spent in retirement. He wrote that AI offers confident, specific answers that carry no accountability, and it can be right most of the time and still be wrong on a costly detail.

Kahler wrote that if someone already knows what they should do and is not doing it, an AI answer is unlikely to help. He advised looking for a planner or financial therapist who listens and asks questions first, and who asks permission before giving advice. He called AI an evolving tool, not a magic source of instant answers, and strongly recommended letting AI help do the research. He then advised bringing that research to a professional advisor who will help find solutions and strategies that are the best fit.

Articles.Title: Why artificial intelligence can’t replace your financial planner

stories.Headline: DSIR 2026 Deeper Dive: Ambient AI in the Exam Room
stories.Summary:
At the end of a doctor's appointment earlier this year, the author asked his physician to show him how the ambient artificial intelligence tool he was using actually worked. The doctor turned the computer screen toward the patient, hit stop on the app on his phone, and almost immediately the medical record began to populate with a polished summary of the visit, written as if he had typed it himself. The summary left out the opening small talk and a random mid-visit discussion about data breaches in healthcare, leaving a concise, clinically focused account of care. Signage in both the exam room and waiting room disclosed that the technology was on.

Ambient AI tools passively record clinical encounters, transcribe conversations, and generate visit summaries that are incorporated into the electronic health record, and some go further by assisting with coding, billing, or surfacing diagnoses and treatment recommendations. The tools can be manually turned on and off, like the one used by the doctor, while others are voice-activated so they are always on but only record when they detect a conversation. State recording statutes present one of the most immediate compliance issues, because the tools record private, in-person conversations and trigger consent obligations that vary significantly from state to state. One-party consent states require only one participant to consent, all-party consent states require every individual in the room to consent, and hybrid states depend on whether the communication is electronic or in person. State recording laws generally require notice or consent before or at the start of a recording, and because the statutes often refer to each communication or conversation in the singular, the obligation may attach to each individual encounter rather than the broader patient-provider relationship.

The article says healthcare organizations should evaluate ambient AI through privacy, security, regulatory compliance, ethics, and patient trust, and that the organizations best positioned to leverage it pair innovation with strong governance and patient-centered implementation. It recommends developing an AI governance program led by a multidisciplinary team with representatives from compliance, privacy, information security, legal, and clinical operations, and inventorying ambient AI tools alongside all other clinical, operational, and patient-facing AI, including shadow AI. It also recommends standardizing encounter-level disclosure and consent practices, treating ambient AI as a patient-facing activity rather than a purely internal documentation tool, and enforcing human review so AI-generated outputs never substitute for licensed clinical judgment. The article adds that workforce members should be trained on the capabilities and limitations of the tools, applicable disclosure and consent requirements, documentation expectations, escalation procedures, and organizational policies.

The article states that the American Medical Association, The Joint Commission, and state-level associations and medical boards have consistently emphasized that AI should support, not displace, clinical judgment, and that patients should not be left guessing about the role AI plays in their care or medical record. It describes emerging best practices such as proactively disclosing ambient AI use even in one-party consent states, addressing patient questions and allowing them to decline participation where feasible, and requiring licensed clinicians to review, edit, and approve AI-generated notes. It notes that implementation of AI tools in healthcare has accelerated significantly in the past several years, and that emerging technologies do not eliminate traditional risk but reshape and sometimes amplify it. The article concludes that realizing the benefits of ambient AI requires embedding trust, transparency, and accountability into the design and governance of these technologies from the outset.

Articles.Title: DSIR 2026 Deeper Dive: Ambient AI in the Exam Room

stories.Headline: Can AI Sway The Midterms?
stories.Summary:
The articles say that AI has become a constant presence over the past twelve months, in print, online, broadcasting and conversation. They list ChatGPT, Claude, Firefly, Gemini, Perplexity and Grok among the apps that are everywhere. With the US midterm elections looming soon, the articles ask whether AI could sway the results. They say the midterms will be historic whichever party wins, with exorbitant funding pouring into campaigns and lavish, unprecedented use of AI.

To discuss the question, the articles say three men were called on, who claim to be the world's first band to use ChatGPT to advance songwriting and release an album in less than 50 days. The band is The Layoffs, made up of David Robinson, known as D-Rob, Jeremy LaCroix, known as Jerry Business, and Josh Klenert. The articles say Robinson has led design at Google, Yahoo and Flexport, LaCroix has roots in punk, magazines and Silicon Valley, and Klenert has spent years leading design across media and big brands. Josh says The Layoffs have become their way to experiment with where creativity and AI collide.

The articles say The Layoffs took time out from their schedules to discuss AI's influence and importance in the upcoming midterms and the aftermath. They also created an image that the articles call delightful. The articles encourage readers to visit The Layoffs site to enjoy their music and videos. They note that there is now a YouTube channel where the conversation with The Layoffs can be viewed.

The articles give no further details on what the conversation concluded or on any specific changes the midterms would bring. They describe the band's work as opening up bigger topics around creativity, technology and what to do with the new tools. The pieces are tagged with topics including AI, ChatGPT, elections, midterms, politics, technology and voting. No next steps beyond watching the conversation are stated.

Articles.Title: Can AI Sway The Midterms?

stories.Headline: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
stories.Summary:
Yucheng Wu, Chengyi Xie, Chenpeng Wang and Liangming Pan posted a paper on arXiv on October 31, 2026 describing a method called Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering, or CANS. The work concerns activation steering, which is a way to control the behavior of large language models without training them. The authors say existing steering methods can damage a model's general abilities and need intervention designs built for each domain. CANS is presented as a unified framework meant to balance control of a target behavior with keeping the model's other capabilities.

The method uses two proxies to make that balance tractable, namely the log-probabilities of target tokens in responses the model generates and the output-distribution KL divergence on general-purpose inputs. Combining local approximations of the two proxies gives a closed-form solution, which the authors say allows lightweight steering without iterative model training or extra computation at inference time. The resulting neuron-wise scaling coefficients steer the model while limiting loss of general capability. A shared data-construction and intervention procedure lets the method adapt across domains using sampled responses with target-behavior filtering and target-span annotations.

The authors report tests on safety, toxicity and hallucination control with Qwen and Llama models. They say CANS steers comparably or better than SFT, CAA and neuron-level baselines while preserving MMLU, BBH and IFEval performance better. On Qwen3-4B, they report that CANS cuts HarmBench attack success from 15.50% to 1.75%, with a 1.11-point drop in average capability. They conclude that the results support CANS as a practical approach to behavioral control across domains.

The paper appears on arXiv with the identifier 2610.35530, and the posting page offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. The page also describes arXivLabs, a framework through which collaborators can develop and share features on the arXiv website. It says the individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have accepted values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv works only with partners who adhere to them. The page also invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community.

Articles.Title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models

stories.Headline: Hospitality businesses adapt as travelers use AI to build their itineraries
stories.Summary:
As more travelers use artificial intelligence to plan trips to Hawaiʻi, tourism businesses are learning that a website alone is no longer enough to attract visitors. A visitor planning a vacation asked ChatGPT to build a 10-day itinerary on Oʻahu to save time researching every activity. The chatbot suggested a range of activities and restaurants, but one of the restaurants had been closed for six months. Because AI recommendations often depend on the quality and accessibility of online information, businesses are rethinking their digital presence.

Hotels and activity companies must now constantly remove outdated pages and information from their websites. They have to keep details such as hours, prices and other important information current so AI assistants can find them. Patrick Ahler, senior vice president at Castle Resorts and Hotels, said updating websites has become a competitive requirement for hotels. Castle Resorts and Hotels recently rebuilt its website using AI to add a universal booking system for its 20 properties in Hawaiʻi, New Zealand and Nevada. The site was also built so AI assistants can discover it.

Ahler said the site was designed with AI assisted travel research in mind. He said that means providing structured facts about locations, rooms and amenities. He also said it means organizing the information and answering the questions travelers actually ask. The articles do not say what happens next beyond businesses continuing to adapt.

Articles.Title: Hospitality businesses adapt as travelers use AI to build their itineraries

stories.Headline: A 'code red' for cybersecurity? How to prepare for a possible wave of AI hacking
stories.Summary:
Jason Clinton, Anthropic's deputy chief information security officer, posted a warning on X after several serious cybersecurity vulnerabilities were made public, saying things would get worse before they got better and urging security leaders to ask their boards for help with the basics, not for AI. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff responded that Clinton was completely right and called it a code red. Clinton had warned in August that a vulnerability tsunami was coming in a few months and there would not be enough time to patch critical infrastructure. The warnings came during a run of threats: on Oct. 21, two newly disclosed vulnerabilities affecting as much as 70% of the internet sent companies and individuals scrambling to apply fixes, and the next day Quest Diagnostics, one of the largest providers of medical lab services, reported unauthorized access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager and said certain patient records were accessed.

AI engineer and investor Matt Shumer explained on X that AI gives hackers three advantages: models can find vulnerabilities more easily, AI can break in on its own without a skilled hacker, and defenders are racing to keep up because attacks move faster than systems can be shored up. The article says individuals should focus on the basics too, since they cannot personally defend against many of these attacks but can lock down much of their personal and financial information. It lists steps including keeping phones, computers and apps updated because updates often fix security holes, using a password manager so each site has a different password, and turning on multifactor authentication through a PIN or code, a face or fingerprint, or an authenticator app with a code that changes every 30 seconds. It also suggests freezing credit reports through the Equifax, Experian and TransUnion apps or websites when not applying for credit, noting it is free but to watch for upsells, and asking your carrier, usually through its official app, to block unauthorized purchases, SIM swaps and carrier transfers.
