Further steps include getting an IRS Identity Protection PIN, a six-digit number that prevents someone else from filing a tax return using your information and collecting your refund, which the IRS says is easiest to get by logging into your online account. The article says you can freeze or lock a retirement account to prevent outbound electronic money transfers, which Fidelity calls a money transfer lock. It advises being skeptical of any text, email or phone call you do not recognize, assuming it is an attempt to get your personal information, not clicking or responding to anything you are not sure is genuine, and calling or visiting the source directly, since pressure or urgency likely means a scam and banks and government agencies do not operate that way. It also suggests setting a family safe word that you do not share with anyone else, because AI has made it easy to clone voices and create fake images, and asking for the safe word if a family member asks for help or information they do not normally need. The article says that while you cannot prevent every hack, taking some preventative measures now greatly improves your odds of staying safe.

Articles.Title: A 'code red' for cybersecurity? How to prepare for a possible wave of AI hacking - ABC News

stories.Headline: TrustJev: Separating Policy Authority from Untrusted Evidence in LLM-Based Decisions
stories.Summary:
Zhiwei Xu, Xuyang Liu, Xiaolin Peng, Weixian Deng, Jiabao Gao, Zirui Li, Tian Qiu, Boya Zhou, Wei Jiao, Hai Wan and Xibin Zhao posted a paper on arXiv on 31 October 2026 describing a framework called TrustJev. The paper says decision models let software pick from predefined actions using natural language inputs. It says the external evidence that supplies facts for these decisions may also contain instructions that try to override the application's policy. The authors propose TrustJev, which combines protected policy scoring with bounded evidence corrections.

A single Transformer backbone computes policy scores and a correction budget from trusted policy and candidates, then bounds evidence corrections by that budget. Paired supervision encourages stable predictions when instruction insertions keep the task facts, and changed preferences when edits change the correct answer. Authority supervision lets evidence count when the policy alone cannot determine the decision. The authors tested a 0.6B implementation against 14 baselines on three datasets covering authentication, instruction hierarchy and executable authorization rules.

The paper reports that TrustJev achieves the highest mean Balance, the harmonic mean of accuracy on non-attack and attack inputs, beating the strongest baseline on each by 0.57 to 1.05 percentage points. In the authorization benchmark it correctly answers all 32 attacks per source in a fixed pool for 95.77% of sources, against 80.98% for the strongest comparator. The authors say TrustJev keeps comparable inference memory and median latency, with extra overhead mainly during training. The paper does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: TrustJev: Separating Policy Authority from Untrusted Evidence in LLM-Based Decisions

stories.Headline: TrustLife: A Trust-Aware Artificial Intelligence Lifecycle Management Framework for Secure Embodied Robots with Multi-Cloud Deployment Optimization
stories.Summary:
A paper published on 31 October 2026 describes TrustLife, a framework for managing the whole lifecycle of artificial intelligence in embodied robots, which are robots that act in the physical world. The authors say existing machine learning operations frameworks focus mainly on training and deployment efficiency and overlook trustworthiness, safety validation and adaptive deployment across different cloud platforms. TrustLife combines dynamic quality assessment, adaptive automated machine learning, a trust verification engine, a multi-cloud deployment optimizer, runtime monitoring and adaptive retraining in one closed-loop architecture. The work covers the AI lifecycle from data governance to online model evolution.

The framework aims to jointly optimize model trustworthiness, deployment latency, computing resource allocation, operating cost and runtime reliability across heterogeneous cloud platforms. In experiments on embodied robotics benchmarks and mixed multi-cloud environments, TrustLife reached a deployment success rate of 97.2%, a runtime reliability of 96.7% and an average inference latency of 129 ms. The authors say it consistently outperformed state-of-the-art AI lifecycle management frameworks. They conclude that it improves trustworthy AI lifecycle management along with deployment efficiency, operational stability and cloud resource use for secure embodied robotic systems.

The paper is published in Fundamental Scientific Reports in Multidisciplinary Areas, volume 2, issue 3, and is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. The article does not name its authors in the text provided. It cites earlier work on trustworthy AI, trust in automated machine learning, MLOps and cloud robotics, including studies by Li and colleagues in 2023, Toreini and colleagues in 2020, Bayram and Ahmed in 2025, Helmer and colleagues in 2024, Kehoe and colleagues in 2015 and Billeter and colleagues in 2024. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: TrustLife: A Trust-Aware Artificial Intelligence Lifecycle Management Framework for Secure Embodied Robots with Multi-Cloud Deployment Optimization

stories.Headline: AI Is Destroying Academic Publishing
stories.Summary:
Anna Wexler, an assistant professor of medical ethics and health policy at the University of Pennsylvania and an associate editor at a bioethics journal, wrote in The Atlantic on October 30, 2026, that AI is affecting every part of academic publishing. She said weak articles once stood out at a glance because of bad writing and poor citations, and she would reject them without peer review. Now such papers arrive with fluent prose, plausible arguments and citations that pass initial AI checks, and the problems only show on a closer look. She gave the example of sentences that look like real arguments but rarely make sense, and citations that lean on open-access or highly cited work because popular AI models cannot easily reach paywalled articles.

The article says reviewers are using AI too. Wexler described a review from a senior scholar that read like an unedited paste from an AI model and criticized authors for not citing a text they had cited. One review of her own co-authored paper came in a ChatGPT-style header and bullet format and asked for 22 major and 14 minor edits. She said journals are being flooded, with some reporting submissions doubling or tripling since ChatGPT was released a few years ago, and submissions across the Elsevier portfolio were about twice as high in 2025 as in 2024. One journal doubled its unpaid volunteer editors to cope, and a study of 7.3 million articles published from 2020 to 2025 found that by 2025 more than half showed evidence of AI assistance, up from 12 percent in 2023.

Wexler said editors, including her, are minimally compensated or unpaid and lack the time to review the growing number of submissions critically. As a result, even as editors reject more papers outright, they send more AI-assisted papers out for review, passing the work to two or three other overworked scholars who are themselves getting more requests. She described a cycle in which AI-assisted papers reach busy editors, go to rushed reviewers who sometimes use AI to write the review, and come back revised by authors using AI. She said the problems are most likely in the humanities and social sciences because conceptual argumentation is easier to mimic than experimental results, though AI can generate much of an article even in the hard sciences.

She said the journal article has long been the currency of academic social capital, and that currencies collapse when people can no longer trust them. She said even a handful of top-tier journals cannot survive in a system where tens of thousands of other outlets cannot tell serious scholarship from work that only looks like it. She described assigning a recent article to her trainees that looked fine on a skim but showed AI hallmarks on close reading, and noted that one of its authors had been on a conference panel with her on the challenges of AI in academic publishing. She said that if she can no longer tell her postdocs and graduate students that rigorous scholarship has a value a journal can recognize, she is not sure what future she is preparing them for.

Articles.Title: AI Is Destroying Academic Publishing

stories.Headline: Patrick Stewart was thinking about AI ethics years before ChatGPT launched
stories.Summary:
Patrick Stewart died yesterday after a short battle with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. He was best known for playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek: The Next Generation, which ran for seven seasons from 1987 to 1994. In the 1989 episode “The Measure of a Man,” his character made a legal argument that the android Data should not be treated as Starfleet property but as a sentient being with the rights of all sentient beings. Stewart also gave an interview to Smithsonian magazine in 2014 about artificial intelligence and whether future AI beings should have the same rights as humans.

At the time of that interview, Stewart was in his tenth year as Chancellor of the University of Huddersfield in the United Kingdom, a position he held from 2004 to 2015 before continuing as its Emeritus Chancellor. The university was known for its engineering and applied research programs and today runs an Institute for Applied Artificial Intelligence. In his answer, Stewart recalled that Whoopi Goldberg had said during a script conference that the episode was really about slavery. He said that if we create independent life but keep it under our control, that can be called a form of slavery, and he hoped moral questions would be addressed as enthusiastically as technical ones.

Stewart told Smithsonian that he was fascinated by the technology and happy that his university was at the forefront of that kind of research. He said he was excited by it but that, just as questions had to be asked about personal liberty and the nature of privacy as social networking and reality television became more successful and money-making, we now have to look at what the nature of privacy is and what one can expect as a right. The article says today’s AI is still far from truly sentient and nothing like the benevolent android Data. It says today’s moral questions about AI revolve around its impact on jobs, social cohesion, mental health, privacy, and its use in warfare.

Articles.Title: Patrick Stewart was thinking about AI ethics years before ChatGPT launched

stories.Headline: DoorDash said it’s only received ‘several hundred’ orders from AI agents
stories.Summary:
DoorDash said on its third-quarter earnings call that it has received only "several hundred" orders from third-party AI agents such as Muse, Instinct and Fo. The company said in its 2025 report that it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily. CEO Tony Xu said users still mostly place orders through DoorDash's own app. The call took place on October 30, 2026.

Xu said agent-based ordering is still a very dynamic area. He said you never want to fight gravity, but you also don't want to be delusional, and he noted that only several hundred orders in total have come from some of these third-party agents. He said DoorDash wants to learn more about agentic use cases and build a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that there could later be an opportunity to advertise within these agents.

DoorDash has its own agents, including a text-to-order agent launched in September, a CLI agent introduced in July, and a chatbot called Ask DoorDash launched in June that lets users order through prompts and photos. The company also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering. The article says the agent-based ordering space is still evolving, with websites deciding whether to allow such agents access. Amazon has been blocking personal agents, while Walmart has welcomed them to win business from competitors.

Articles.Title: DoorDash said it’s only received ‘several hundred’ orders from AI agents

stories.Headline: Webinar: Beyond the Composition of Matter – AI and the Biosimilar Patent Landscape
stories.Summary:
A webinar will discuss how artificial intelligence is used to analyze patent landscapes for biologics and biosimilars. The event is hosted by IPWatchdog and is scheduled for Thursday, November 19, at 12 PM ET. It follows introductory remarks from Gene Quinn, the founder and CEO of IPWatchdog. Edmund Koundakjian of Mintz and Sunny Malhotra of Novo Nordisk will give outside-counsel and in-house perspectives. Josephine Garban and Candice Kwark, both of Patlytics, will co-moderate.

The session will cover how a commercial biologic can be protected by patents on formulations, dosing regimens, methods of treatment, manufacturing and purification processes, delivery systems, and other product attributes. Because of this, expiration of the foundational composition-of-matter patent rarely determines when protection effectively ends or when biosimilar competition can begin. The panelists will discuss using AI to identify and map patent families, organize claims, compare scope, track legal status, and monitor a global portfolio. They will also address distinguishing patents that may materially affect a product or proposed biosimilar from results that are merely technically related. The discussion will cover adapting analysis to objectives such as lifecycle management, loss-of-exclusivity planning, freedom to operate, biosimilar entry, licensing, and dispute preparation.

The panelists will examine where AI can reduce manual effort and where legal, scientific, and technical judgment remains indispensable. They will also evaluate how data quality, verification, and human review affect the reliability of AI-assisted conclusions. The articles state that faster analysis is not necessarily more reliable analysis, and that incomplete data, inconsistent family relationships, jurisdictional differences, and poorly framed questions can produce results that appear comprehensive while overlooking patents or claims that materially affect strategy. Attendees are expected to leave with a practical framework for evaluating AI-assisted biologics patent analysis and incorporating verified results into life sciences IP strategy. The articles do not say what happens after the webinar.

Articles.Title: Webinar: Beyond the Composition of Matter – AI and the Biosimilar Patent Landscape

stories.Headline: Tech giants need legacy businesses to keep growing as they pour trillions into the AI buildout
stories.Summary:
The tech megacaps are placing a multitrillion-dollar bet that their infrastructure spending will produce years of profitable growth, according to CNBC. In this earnings season, Meta joined Alphabet and Amazon in reporting negative free cash flow, leaving Microsoft as the only hyperscaler still positive. Meta posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, Amazon's outflows swelled to $42.4 billion and Alphabet's reached $9.07 billion. Microsoft's cash generation fell 27% to $18.63 billion, its second straight quarterly decline, and the company said it will turn to the bond market as it ramps up AI infrastructure spending.

Amazon said growth slowed in both its retail and ad business, with online sales up 2% year over year, down from 10% a year earlier and short of analysts' estimates. The midpoint of Amazon's revenue guidance came in below the $244.5 billion analysts expected, a disappointing figure for the quarter that includes the holiday shopping season. Amazon expects capital expenditures this year to reach $220 billion, and analysts project that number will top $280 billion next year, according to FactSet. Meta says capex will reach as high as $145 billion this year, and analysts see it passing $210 billion in 2027, and Meta announced on Monday that it plans to raise a total of $95 billion in stock to support its AI investments.

Alphabet's core search business saw a third straight quarter of slowing growth and missed analysts' projections, and YouTube-related advertising revenue also came in light. Evercore analyst Mark Mahaney told CNBC that Google's strong cloud revenue was good news but its decelerating digital advertising business was the overwhelming bad news. Forrester analyst Tracy Woo said in an email that Alphabet's massive capex investment has been tolerated for now but the company is walking a fine line, and she said the concern is less the current earnings miss and more the possibility that future AI spending grows faster than the cash generation of the franchises expected to support it. Christopher Ballard, a managing director at Check Capital Management, said Alphabet's negative free cash flow of $9 billion is tiny relative to its overall business, which had operating income above $40 billion for the quarter, and he said the company is borrowing from the for-now to invest in the future in a responsible manner.

Investors sent Meta shares down 7% after its report last week even though the company beat on revenue, and Alphabet suffered its steepest drop ever on Thursday while Amazon slid in extended trading after its report. Rising interest rates are making it costlier for companies to raise debt, putting pressure on cash-burning neoclouds that have become critical to the global buildout. Although the hyperscalers didn't provide specific capex projections for next year, they all implied their data center spending spree will continue to grow, even if it means reporting some uncomfortable metrics. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on Thursday's earnings call that it might be more convenient if the acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and the capex could be spread over that time, but that is not the world we live in and not the opportunity.

Articles.Title: Tech giants need legacy businesses to keep growing as they pour trillions into the AI buildout

stories.Headline: A decade of machine learning for materials development
stories.Summary:
Over the past decade, machine learning for materials has grown from predicting properties to generative design and experimental discovery, according to a Nature Reviews Materials article by Wang Xiaonan of Tsinghua University. The article cites work including crystal graph convolutional neural networks published in Physical Review Letters in 2018 and E(3)-equivariant graph neural networks published in Nature Communications in 2022. It also points to scaling deep learning for materials discovery in Nature in 2023 and a generative model for inorganic materials design in Nature in 2025. An autonomous laboratory for accelerated synthesis of inorganic materials appeared in Nature in 2023, and SurFF, a foundation model for surface exposure and morphology across intermetallic crystals, appeared in Nature Computational Science in 2025.

The article says the next challenge is to understand how materials evolve and function across scales under real operating conditions. It says that understanding must then be translated into reliable materials development. The cited work also includes a dual-engine artificial intelligence framework for sustainable aviation fuel component synthesis in the Journal of the American Chemical Society in 2026. PolyRL, a reinforcement learning method for polymer generation aimed at multi-objective polymer discovery, appeared in Digital Discovery in 2026.

Automated self-optimization, intensification and scale-up of photocatalysis in flow was published in Science in 2024. Wang is affiliated with the Beijing Key Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence for Advanced Chemical Engineering Materials and the State Key Laboratory of Chemical Engineering and Low-Carbon Technology in the Department of Chemical Engineering at Tsinghua University in Beijing, China. The article states that the author declares no competing interests. The references also include autonomous chemical research with large language models, published in Nature in 2023.

The article presents a figure on machine learning for materials development across data, experiments and scales. The article does not say what happens next beyond describing the next challenge of understanding materials across scales under real operating conditions and turning that into reliable development. It offers no timeline, funding details or specific next steps. It directs readers to related subjects and to the Nature Briefing newsletter for more stories.

Articles.Title: A decade of machine learning for materials development

stories.Headline: SafeComm-Agent: A Security-Aware Communication and Inference Optimization Framework for Multi-Agent Embodied Intelligence Systems
stories.Summary:
A study published on October 31, 2026, in Fundamental Scientific Reports in Multidisciplinary Areas proposes SafeComm-Agent, a framework for multi-agent embodied intelligence systems. These systems combine vision, language, and sensor-based perception to support collaborative navigation, manipulation, and autonomous decision-making in dynamic environments. The authors say frequent inter-agent communication, redundant large-model inference, and multimodal adversarial attacks can raise computational overhead and compromise physical task safety at the same time. The framework is designed to coordinate multimodal attack detection, agent communication, and adaptive reasoning computation together.

The framework first combines Vision Transformers, Vision-Language Models, cross-modal consistency analysis, and uncertainty estimation to spot anomalous observations and derive agent-level security risks. It then uses a Graph Neural Network to build a dynamic security-aware communication graph, while Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning decides when to communicate, which agents to contact, and what information to send. Risk-aware message compression and adaptive Test-Time Compute regulate communication and inference budgets, and Monte Carlo Tree Search adds verification for high-risk states. In Habitat-based simulated environments with controlled multimodal adversarial perturbations, SafeComm-Agent reached a task success rate of 94.6% and an attack detection F1-score of 93.2%. Compared with full-communication MARL it cut inference cost by 26%, and it reduced total computational cost by 39% compared with full-communication and full-computation execution.

The article does not name individual authors or give specific quotes from them. Responsibility for the work is presented at the level of the study itself, which reports the design and the experimental results. The authors state that the results demonstrate effective joint optimization of security, communication, and adaptive inference. The article does not describe any statements beyond this framing of the findings.

The context is the growing use of multi-agent embodied systems that integrate vision, language, and sensor perception for tasks such as collaborative navigation and manipulation. The article cites prior work including Habitat, Habitat 2.0, RT-2, and surveys of LLM-based multi-agent systems, along with research on learned multi-agent communication and adversarial vulnerabilities in vision-language-action models. The experiments were run only in simulated Habitat environments with controlled perturbations, and the article does not say what happens next. It gives no timeline for real-world testing, deployment, or follow-up studies.

Articles.Title: SafeComm-Agent: A Security-Aware Communication and Inference Optimization Framework for Multi-Agent Embodied Intelligence Systems

stories.Headline: Wall Street Is in Denial: AI Financing Problems Are Already Here, Barclays Strategist Warns
stories.Summary:
Barclays strategist Alexander Altmann warned on a Bloomberg Odd Lots podcast released Thursday that Wall Street is in denial about AI financing problems. He said investors remain extremely bullish even as warning signs build. He pointed to Cipher Digital, which proposed $850 million in convertible notes on Oct. 13 alongside a debt-for-shares exchange, and whose shares fell nearly 13% on dilution concerns. He said the anxiety spread to CoreWeave, an AI cloud provider that borrows heavily to build data centers.

CoreWeave's bond yields climbed toward 15% in mid-October, up from 9.675% when issued. Altmann said spreads on data-center bonds, including financing tied to Meta Platforms, had been widening for months. He said there is evidently a financing problem within neoclouds, meaning specialized AI cloud providers. Only about 60% of respondents to a preliminary Barclays investor survey expected financing problems, and Altmann argued the figure should have been 100%.

Altmann said AI companies are competing for financing in an already crowded debt market. Barclays expects $1.1 trillion in net corporate bond issuance this year, even as interest rates remain elevated. He said AI is not issuing debt in a vacuum, and he agreed that lenders are becoming more selective. He said a major hyperscaler cutting planned capital spending could finally shake investors' confidence, though he suggested that might not happen until next year.

Altmann noted that subprime financing trouble appeared 12 to 24 months before the 2008 financial crisis reached major banks, and he sees a potential parallel in AI, though he stressed he was not making a direct comparison. On Polymarket, traders put the odds of an AI industry downturn at 9% by Dec. 31, rising to 23% by June 30. That contract requires three major distress events within 90 days, a far more severe outcome than the financing problems Altmann describes. For CoreWeave and its peers, financing pressure has arrived before their biggest customers have even begun cutting spending.

Articles.Title: Wall Street Is in Denial: AI Financing Problems Are Already Here, Barclays Strategist Warns

stories.Headline: Democrats see AI hate as winning issue heading into 2028
stories.Summary:
Democrats weighing 2028 presidential bids have increased their criticism of artificial intelligence in recent months, according to an analysis shared exclusively with Axios. The research from Upswing, conducted for the nonprofit Reset Tech, looked at nearly 30,000 X posts from 38 accounts tied to 21 potential contenders and 3,868 press releases from 16 officeholders between Jan. 1 and Oct. 15. Among those 21 Democrats, tech mentions on X nearly quadrupled and press release mentions nearly tripled since the start of the year. The contenders named include Gavin Newsom, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Kamala Harris, Pete Buttigieg and Jon Ossoff.

Tech is now the second-most common topic in those releases, trailing only jobs and the economy, with the most mentions around data centers and phone bans in schools. New York is so far the only state to pass a data center moratorium, though bans have been proposed in both Democratic- and Republican-majority states. House Democrats drafted a resolution opposing government bailouts for AI companies if the so-called bubble bursts, and there are various legislative proposals including model transparency measures and kill switches. A September YouGov poll found most Americans across the political spectrum take the risks of AI causing harm seriously.

Rishi Bharwani, U.S. director of Reset Tech, told Axios that Democrats are taking a meaningful advantage on AI after the topic was initially seen as a jump ball for both parties. He said AI regulation has gone from the back burner to a top issue over the last six months. He added that while the economy is still what matters most to voters, AI is increasingly part of the financial conversation as it dominates markets and the macroeconomic backdrop. The analysis says Democrats are turning AI anxiety into a political rallying cry ahead of 2028, while Republicans remain divided over how to respond.

Articles.Title: Democrats see AI hate as winning issue heading into 2028

stories.Headline: Cognizant commits to US workforce expansion amid AI training push
stories.Summary:
Cognizant, a New Jersey-based IT consulting and services firm, said during its Q3 2026 earnings call on Wednesday that it plans to expand its U.S. workforce and prioritize AI upskilling. The call followed a U.S. Department of Labor decision to suspend Cognizant's access to the Permanent Labor Certification Program, known as PERM. The company was one of a handful of large channel firms the Labor Department and Vice President JD Vance sanctioned for outsourcing IT labor earlier in October. In September, before the Trump administration's actions, Cognizant had pledged to hire 1,500 U.S. college graduates and grow its bench of certified AI engineers and operations specialists to 15,000.

Cognizant grew revenues nearly 5% year over year to $5.7 billion in the three-month period ended Sept. 30. CFO Jatin Dulal said the company has approximately 32,000 employees in the U.S. and has invested significantly to scale its local talent base over the last several years. He said Cognizant does not expect the PERM suspension to have a material impact on its talent strategy or operations. In October the company partnered with Google Cloud to launch the Gemini Frontier Capability Group, an AI-focused business unit to be staffed with more than 18,000 Frontier Certified Engineers, a designation Cognizant created earlier this year for AI-enablement technicians.

CEO and Director Ravi Kumar S said the company is evolving its workforce and building frontier roles around the capabilities needed to design, deploy and operate AI-native solutions. He said these roles combine engineering, AI fluency and business expertise with greater accountability for client outcomes. Kumar said major technology transitions have historically required capacity to deploy new technology at scale, and that Cognizant is building that capacity across its talent, engineering platforms and partner ecosystem with frontier AI companies, hyperscalers and enterprise technology providers. He added that more than 45,000 associates have earned nearly 100,000 AI platform certifications, with another 65,000-plus in progress.

Cognizant grew its Microsoft practice through last year's acquisition of Azure services provider 3Cloud, which brought in 1,000-plus Azure engineers and more than 1,500 Microsoft certifications. In April the company acquired managed service provider Astreya, a move Kumar said bolsters its workspace and data center service capabilities. Kumar said the trillions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure build-out creates opportunities across data center operations, networks, AI environments and digital workplace services, and that the Astreya acquisition strengthens its ability to serve that market. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these plans.

Articles.Title: Cognizant commits to US workforce expansion amid AI training push

stories.Headline: If the AI Bubble Scare Gets Worse, This Is the Chip Stock I'd Still Hold
stories.Summary:
A Motley Fool article published on October 30, 2026, by Rick Orford argued that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing is a chip stock worth holding even if fears of an artificial intelligence bubble grow. The piece appeared as markets fell, with the Nasdaq down 3.42%, the S&P 500 down 2.15%, and the VIX up 27.12%. Nvidia fell 5.22%, AMD fell 12.02%, and Intel fell 30.71% that day. The article framed TSM as a way to gain AI exposure without betting on a single chip designer.

TSM runs the world's largest third-party foundry business, making chips designed by customers for AI, smartphones, and other electronics. It began volume production on its 2-nanometer process node in the fourth quarter of 2025, and volume production for its N2P and A16 nodes was ramping up in the second half of 2026. Its longer-term roadmap includes the A14 node, expected to enter volume production in 2028. Of 19 analysts covering the stock, 16 rated it a strong buy, two a buy, and one a hold, with an average price target suggesting 23% upside over the next year. The stock's price-to-earnings ratio was over 27.

The article said TSM would not be immune to an AI downturn, since data center customers and other chip users could cut spending or delay orders. It also cited geopolitical risk because TSM's manufacturing base is concentrated in Taiwan, where a conflict with China could disrupt production. Orford disclosed that he had no position in any of the stocks mentioned, while The Motley Fool reported positions in and recommendations of Advanced Micro Devices, Nvidia, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing. The article described TSM's manufacturing expertise and place in the AI supply chain as giving it a compelling long-term bull case.

The piece said steady advances in manufacturing matter because AI developers demand chips that deliver more compute without letting power consumption and operating costs spiral. It argued that TSM does not need every AI application to succeed, only enough customers to keep investing in advanced chips. It also noted that demand for compute is spreading across GPUs, CPUs, and custom ASICs, and that TSM manufactures all of those types. The article concluded that TSM may be one of the strongest ways to invest in AI even if bubble fears intensify.

Articles.Title: If the AI Bubble Scare Gets Worse, This Is the Chip Stock I'd Still Hold

stories.Headline: AI-guided discovery of self-assembled monolayers combining synthetic accessibility and interfacial stability for perovskite solar cells
stories.Summary:
Researchers used an artificial intelligence-guided framework to design self-assembled monolayers for perovskite solar cells, as reported in Nature Synthesis on 31 October 2026. The framework combined graph neural network-based retrosynthetic predictions with high-throughput screening based on density functional theory and expert chemical knowledge. It started from over 90,000 structures built from 308 fragments and narrowed them down to 300 candidates. These candidates were ranked using a composite score of eight descriptors, which went beyond intrinsic electronic properties to include synthesizability, hole reorganization energy and structural features such as heteroatom content and aromaticity. The top candidate, named AI-1, is readily synthesizable and incorporates favourable heteroatom functionalities.

It achieves optimal energetic alignment and forms robust S, Pb coordination bonds at the buried interface, which suppresses non-radiative recombination and enhances interfacial stability. Devices incorporating AI-1 reached a power-conversion efficiency of 27.2% and retained more than 95% of their initial efficiency after 2,000 hours of maximum-power-point tracking at 65 °C. Mechanistic studies show that the multifunctional methylthio side chain is vital, because it reinforces interfacial bonding and balances passivation with chemical robustness. The authors say the work shows that artificial intelligence-guided design can systematically deliver self-assembled monolayers that unite high efficiency with long-term operational stability. They add that the findings provide general principles for interface engineering. The paper states that source data are provided with it, and that other data are available in the paper or its Supplementary Information.

It also states that the code for functional group extraction, molecular generation, high-throughput theoretical calculations, molecular screening and ranking, and data analysis is available on GitHub. The work addresses a large challenge in perovskite photovoltaics, which is navigating the vast chemical space to find self-assembled monolayers that combine synthesizability, interfacial compatibility and long-term device stability. The article situates the results among related studies on self-assembled monolayers for perovskite solar cells and modules. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the published findings and the released data and code.

Articles.Title: AI-guided discovery of self-assembled monolayers combining synthetic accessibility and interfacial stability for perovskite solar cells

stories.Headline: Sam Altman Absolutely Hates the Idea of People Running Their Own AI Models at Home, Argues They Shouldn't Own Computers
stories.Summary:
Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, said on the Cheeky Pint podcast that people running their own AI models at home does not make sense. He argued that memory supply problems come from individuals wanting to run models locally instead of leaving chips for large data centers. He said it is terrible from a global allocation perspective for everybody to have part of the world's limited supply of dynamic RAM in their own computer. He added that the cloud, run by large companies like OpenAI, is the answer because it offers maximum utilization in a constrained environment.

The comments came as shares of US chipmaker Intel fell almost 30 percent on a Friday, the worst stock collapse in 52 years. Analysts said the wipeout could be due to a major slowdown in the PC market. The article says the AI boom has made components, especially memory and storage, nearly unaffordable. It also says there is a massive circuit board shortage, and PC makers say they are already fully booked through the end of 2030.

Altman said many people assume open-source models will let them run AI on their own computers and that data centers will not be needed. He rejected that view and said the cloud is a far better use of available hardware. He said that given the world will be limited in silicon capacity, everyone has a shared interest. The article says his comments drew anger from the PC gaming community, with Reddit users calling him self-centered and saying he cannot understand why people want to own their own computers.

The article says the AI industry is struggling to commercialize its offerings while expenses balloon at alarming rates, which terrifies investors. It says running local inference undermines reliance on expensive cloud services from companies like OpenAI. It also says frontier AI labs are trying to secure AI chips as supplies run low. The article does not say what happens next beyond noting that tech enthusiasts are likely to disagree with Altman.

Articles.Title: Sam Altman Absolutely Hates the Idea of People Running Their Own AI Models at Home, Argues They Shouldn't Own Computers

stories.Headline: Exclusive: Dark Matter acquires House Numbers’ agentic AI platform
stories.Summary:
Dark Matter Technologies has acquired the artificial intelligence platform and related intellectual property of House Numbers, a venture capital-backed AI company. The deal was announced on Friday, October 30, 2026. It brings House Numbers' AI agent platform and the team behind it into Dark Matter's home lending technology business. Financial terms were not disclosed.

House Numbers was founded in 2021 and developed AI agents that monitor loan files for changes, work through loan conditions, make recommendations, and communicate with borrowers and lenders by email, text and voice. The platform has been in production for two years and has processed loans for more than 100 lenders, according to Dark Matter. House Numbers co-founder and CEO Jeff Levinsohn joins Dark Matter as chief AI officer. Co-founders Arthur Granado and Benjamin Hoffman join as vice president of engineering and vice president of AI adoption and enablement, respectively.

Dark Matter CEO Vikas Rao said the two companies first discussed a partnership before he proposed an acquisition. He said the deal allows Dark Matter to integrate the technology deeply into its products rather than offer it as a separate service. Rao said the House Numbers team will work across Dark Matter's products, and the company plans to run the acquired technology within its Amazon Web Services infrastructure with controls for security and regulatory requirements. He said the technology is not about eliminating humans, and that AI agents perform tasks instantaneously but humans review the work.

Dark Matter plans to integrate the technology into its loan origination system, its built-in point-of-sale platform and its broader product lineup, which includes Aiva Intelligence and the Elevate loan servicing platform. House Numbers has 19 agentic AI use cases in production, with additional applications in development, Rao said. Dark Matter expects customers to begin seeing new capabilities within weeks, with additional releases planned over the following months. Rao estimated the total cost of producing a loan remains around $12,000, with roughly $6,000 attributed to operational expenses, and said shaving $1,000 off that $6,000 would be game changing. Rao also said Dark Matter hopes to pursue more deals in 2027, and that its parent company, Constellation Software, encourages portfolio companies to consider complementary acquisitions.

Articles.Title: Exclusive: Dark Matter acquires House Numbers’ agentic AI platform

stories.Headline: From Scientific Task Automation to the Continuous Evolution of Theory: The Ancestor–Mother–Child Machine Architecture for the Fifth Paradigm of Theoretical Research
stories.Summary:
A paper posted on Zenodo on October 31, 2026, proposes a machine architecture for theoretical research. It comes from the School of Management at Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan, China. The paper describes an ancestor-mother-child machine architecture. It aims to address how individual research findings enter long-term theoretical accumulation and change the starting points and methods of later research, an organizational problem the paper says must be addressed when artificial intelligence takes part in theoretical research.

In the architecture, the ancestor machine provides general research methods and maintains shared rules. The mother machine translates these into domain theories and research procedures, then generates child machines around specific questions. Child machines inherit relevant knowledge and methods to propose and test candidate explanations. After the mother machine reviews their findings, approved changes enter domain theories and research procedures, and issues concerning shared premises go to the ancestor machine for review. Revised knowledge and methods inform the next round of generation, so each round builds on existing understanding and changes the basis of subsequent work.

The paper says the architecture is intended to support a theoretical organism that can absorb new evidence and continuously generate and revise explanations. It presents an illustrative reconstruction of research on memory retention under artificial hibernation to explain this process of generation and feedback. The paper describes the architecture as an organizational framework for the fifth paradigm of theoretical research through human-machine collaboration. The work is published under a Creative Commons Attribution license, which allows re-distribution and re-use as long as the creator is credited.

Articles.Title: From Scientific Task Automation to the Continuous Evolution of Theory: The Ancestor–Mother–Child Machine Architecture for the Fifth Paradigm of Theoretical Research

stories.Headline: Chinese Hackers Use AI-Powered ARTEX to Target Over 200 Organizations Worldwide
stories.Summary:
Chinese state-sponsored hackers used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX in attacks on high-value targets, according to a CrowdStrike analysis reported on October 30, 2026. CrowdStrike attributed the activity to a China-based targeted intrusion adversary it tracks as Vapor Panda, previously known as VexatiousTemper. The group was first identified in February 2021 and overlaps with a threat cluster Trend Micro calls Earth Estries. Starting October 17, 2026, Vapor Panda used the tool against more than 200 distinct organizations worldwide.

The targets included foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, semiconductor, defense, and think tank organizations in the U.S., and telecommunications providers in multiple regions. The list also covered 19 U.S.-based organizations in the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and financial sectors. Post-exploitation activity was confirmed at nine organizations, where the attacker deployed BLOODALCHEMY, a derivative of ShadowPad, followed by credential spraying, network scanning, and reconnaissance. Vapor Panda also conducted password-spraying and credential-scanning against at least 12 additional organizations, including U.S.-based think tanks and government entities in Europe.

CrowdStrike said agentic tooling like ARTEX lets a small team pursue a wider target set at speed than manual operations would support. The operation used ARTEX with DeepSeek and an unknown subscription-based commercial large language model, with planner and worker agents coordinating toward a common goal. A human operator stayed in the loop, directing agents to write web shells, extract domain administrator passwords, and enumerate endpoint sensor coverage. CrowdStrike said that in a single intrusion the planning agents consumed on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens.

CrowdStrike said the agents pursued multiple attack paths in parallel across web applications, cloud services, container environments, Active Directory, and mail and VPN infrastructure, and shifted to alternatives when a path failed. The disclosure coincided with four previously undocumented China-linked groups: Hollow Panda, Overcast Panda, Titan Panda, and Veiled Panda. Overcast Panda was linked to close access intrusions using a proprietary FlowCloud backdoor deployed via direct physical access when targets traveled to China. Titan Panda exploited a hard-coded IIS machine key vulnerability in Intapp Time Server, with attacks first detected in April 2026.

Articles.Title: Chinese Hackers Use AI-Powered ARTEX to Target Over 200 Organizations Worldwide

stories.Headline: U.S., China Are In AI Infrastructure Booms. But They're Running Different Races.
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence buildout is often described as a race between the U.S. and China. But the two largest economies are competing in a complex marathon where the finish line is unclear. The U.S. appears to have taken an early lead, powered by large companies including Nvidia, Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta Platforms. The article was published by Investors.com on October 30, 2026.

The article says the U.S. lead comes from those big technology firms. It does not give specific figures for spending, computing capacity or growth on either side. It frames the competition as a marathon rather than a sprint, with no clear endpoint. No other dates, numbers or named officials appear in the article.

The article does not name anyone responsible for the buildout or quote anyone about it. It does not say what the competition requires or what changes it brings. It only describes the U.S. as holding an early lead through its major companies. It gives no statements from officials or executives.

The article offers little context beyond the comparison between the two countries. It does not say what happens next or what steps either side might take. It does not describe China's position in detail or name Chinese companies involved. More to follow.

Articles.Title: U.S., China Are In AI Infrastructure Booms. But They're Running Different Races.

stories.Headline: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz warns that the AI boom is 'a great opportunity to go deceive people'
stories.Summary:
Tyler Shultz, a former Theranos employee and a key whistleblower, spoke to The San Francisco Standard about the AI boom, in an interview reported on October 30, 2026. Shultz’s first job out of college was at Theranos, where he helped expose dangerously inaccurate blood testing devices that reached Walgreens stores and gave faulty results to real patients. Theranos reached a peak valuation of around $10 billion even though its technology never actually worked, and the company used its own machines for only a fraction of tests while outsourcing others to third-party equipment. His grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State and Secretary of the Treasury George Shultz, was a notable investor and board member.

Shultz said the only reason people are talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now is that she wants them to be talking about her. He argued that the days of having a thirty-minute coffee with someone and sending them $100,000 should be over, and that Holmes took that model and scaled it to $100 million. He said Holmes raised what he called the biggest angel round of funding of all time, and that even at smaller levels investors need to recognize they are giving tremendous power to whoever receives that money. Theranos funding often came from individual investors like the DeVos and Walton families rather than venture firms, and the company did not share scientific information or evidence that its machines worked with potential investors, citing trade secrets.

Shultz said a huge danger with AI is that it is really hard to do due diligence on it, and really hard to tell the difference between something truly unique and new versus a ChatGPT wrapper. He said that if you want to deceive people, this is a great opportunity to go deceive people. He also said he has a feeling of unease about what might come next, that Holmes is certainly preparing and beginning her second act, and that he does not know exactly where it will go. The documentary “You Can See Everything,” directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, follows Holmes’s final weeks before prison and has become one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time.

The film shows Holmes and her partner, hotel heir Billy Evans, working on Haemanthus, a diagnostics company they call “Theranos 2.0,” which has reportedly raised about $20 million in funding. Holmes is serving a prison sentence of over 11 years, and the article says her case is closed. The film intentionally refuses to characterize Holmes as a master manipulator or a victim, instead highlighting her knack for making people pity her even when they know her crimes. The article says the film glosses over Theranos’s more heinous crimes, such as giving dangerously faulty medical information to real patients and its targeted harassment of Shultz when he tried to sound the alarm about his former employer.

Articles.Title: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz warns that the AI boom is 'a great opportunity to go deceive people'

stories.Headline: Wikimedia Foundation Tries to Save Itself From Oblivion by Brokering AI Copyright Deal
stories.Summary:
The Wikimedia Foundation submitted an amicus brief on Thursday to the court overseeing the New York Times lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft. The Times filed that lawsuit in December 2023, alleging the companies illegally used millions of its copyrighted articles to train AI chatbots that now compete with the publication. OpenAI and Microsoft have argued that scraping the Times content and other web material to train ChatGPT and Copilot is fair use under U.S. copyright law. The brief runs roughly 5,800 words and was filed by the nonprofit that runs Wikipedia and a dozen other free knowledge sites.

The brief argues that both sides in the lawsuit take overbroad positions that are impractical as AI use grows. It proposes a middle path, with AI developers allowed to train models on freely available online content but not allowed to reproduce that content however they please. It says pretraining, the early phase where models learn from large troves of data, should be fair game, while outputs such as retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, should concern the court. It contends that a chatbot copying and reproducing expressive sources in responses to user queries should not count as fair use.

Stephen LaPorte, general counsel for the Wikimedia Foundation, said in a statement that a ruling not applying fair use principles carefully could threaten the sustainability of free knowledge and stifle open source technologies. He said the court needs to understand that Wikipedia is created through a collaborative process that requires a strong foundation of open and accessible human knowledge. The brief itself says it would be contrary to copyright law's purposes to block LLM capabilities, such as monitoring sites for illegally posted personal information and assisting human contributors with edits, by labeling LLM development as categorically not fair use. The nonprofit also wrote in a blog post earlier this year, marking Wikipedia's 25th anniversary, that Wikipedia remains one of the highest-quality datasets for training large language models.

Earlier this year the foundation announced partnerships with Amazon, Meta, Mistral, Perplexity and Microsoft, through which the companies would pay to use Wikipedia content to train new models. The article says a blanket ruling for the AI companies could spell the end of the collaborative, license-based publishing model on which Wikipedia operates. It says a final verdict in the Times lawsuit will likely take a while, along with other cases publishers have filed against AI companies. It adds that AI models are notoriously opaque, making it hard to determine what happens between training data going in and new outputs coming out, and that the legal battle over AI and copyright could take even longer than the one over social media.

Articles.Title: Wikimedia Foundation Tries to Save Itself From Oblivion by Brokering AI Copyright Deal

stories.Headline: AI agents won’t pay the way you do
stories.Summary:
Brian Dammeir, head of payments and financial management at Plaid, said AI agents may choose payment methods differently from human shoppers. He spoke in an Oct. 19 interview at the Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas. Plaid is a San Francisco-based financial data aggregator that transfers consumer account information between banks and fintechs. Dammeir said bots are not bothered by checkout flows, account creation forms, password setup or poor user interfaces. An agent will focus on the payment parameters the consumer has provided, such as maximizing discounts or card-issuer rewards, Dammeir said.

It will then pick the method it sees as matching those guidelines. As a result, banks, card issuers, merchants and card networks will likely see shifts from how people pay today. He said bank payments could be adopted more broadly and the mix of payment methods could change, depending on the consumer experience. Dammeir said agents will talk to agents and make decisions for all parties, and whoever builds technology for those agents to make the best decision will do better. He said it is too early to tell whether that ends up being the card world, the bank-payment world or other methods.

He said the consumer drives behavior, and most consumers will not know the details underneath but will understand the value they get. He said agents can work through the question more effectively than consumers have been able to, and the agent can be an expert while the consumer does not have to be. Dammeir said most agents today generally have one or two wallets available and that it is early days. He expects the picture a year from now to look very different, with a lot more options, including paying by bank in certain contexts.

Articles.Title: AI agents won’t pay the way you do

stories.Headline: Salesforce agrees to acquire Rune, which raised ~$30M to make AI military logistics software, as it expands its year-old Missionforce defense business (Chris Metinko/Axios)
stories.Summary:
Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire Rune Technologies, a developer of military software and hardware for logistics and sustainment. The announcement was reported by Chris Metinko of Axios, 22 hours before the article's timestamp of October 30, 2026. Rune had raised about $30 million to build AI military logistics software. Salesforce announced its national security-focused Missionforce offering a year ago, and the article says it looks to be heavily eyeing government and defense.

The deal brings Rune into Salesforce's defense business, which is about a year old. Rune's work covers both software and hardware for logistics and sustainment. The article gives no purchase price and no other financial terms for the agreement. It also does not say when the acquisition is expected to close.

The article does not name any executive or spokesperson for Salesforce or Rune, and it carries no direct statements from either company. Responsibility for the deal sits with Salesforce, which signed the definitive agreement, and with Rune as the company being acquired. The stated rationale is Salesforce's push into government and defense through Missionforce. No further comment from the companies is included.

The context is Salesforce's expansion beyond its core customer relationship management business into national security work. Missionforce was announced a year before the deal, and the article describes the company as heavily eyeing government and defense. The articles do not say what happens next, such as regulatory review or a closing date. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Salesforce agrees to acquire Rune, which raised ~$30M to make AI military logistics software, as it expands its year-old Missionforce defense business (Chris Metinko/Axios)

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence and Multi-Omics in Cardiovascular Diseases: A New Era of Precision Medicine
stories.Summary:
A review article on artificial intelligence and multi-omics in cardiovascular diseases was published ahead of print in Cardiac Research on October 29, 2026. The authors are Zhipeng Zhang, Qiaoxi Yang, Yukuan Liu, Xiaoyu Shi, Ruibo Hou and Xudong Xing. The article carries the DOI 10.1097/re9.0000000000000038 and is published by Wolters Kluwer Health, LLC. on behalf of Higher Education Press. The work is a review, not a study, and it examines opportunities and limitations in this field.

The article says cardiovascular diseases arise through interactions across genetic, molecular, cellular, anatomical and physiological scales. It says these dimensions are often studied in isolation. It argues that combining multi-omics with medical imaging, electrocardiography, electronic health records and wearable measurements can give a fuller view of cardiovascular disease than any single modality. It says artificial intelligence provides a computational framework for analyzing these heterogeneous data and for linking molecular alterations to disease phenotypes, clinical trajectories and therapeutic opportunities.

The authors say progress is limited by sparse and incompletely matched datasets, cross-modal misalignment, limited interpretability, poor generalizability, and unresolved privacy and governance challenges. They say overcoming these barriers is essential to make AI-enabled multimodal integration a robust foundation for more mechanistically informed and precise cardiovascular medicine. The article states that the authors are the ones responsible for the review and its conclusions. The copyright notice names the Author(s) 2026.

The article is a review of the opportunities and limitations of AI-enabled multimodal integration in cardiovascular research and clinical translation. It does not report new experiments, results or a timeline for future work. It presents the barriers as open problems that must be addressed before this integration can serve as a foundation for precision cardiovascular medicine. The full text is available through the journal, and the article is published ahead of print.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence and Multi-Omics in Cardiovascular Diseases: A New Era of Precision Medicine

stories.Headline: Google hit with criminal probe over unapproved AI data center deforestation
stories.Summary:
A criminal investigation has been launched into environmental damage caused by Google's Finnish subsidiary, Tuike Finland Oy. Police in Finland opened the probe after receiving five complaints about the Muhos data center project, according to an official police statement published on October 30, 2026. The company is accused of suspected breaches of environmental law and environmental damage. Lesser criminal offenses related to ambiguities and shortcomings in drainage and water management are also being investigated.

The case involves 816 acres of forest near Muhos that were cleared without authorization and turned into an expanse of mud. Google is also said to have cleared 500 acres of forest near Otanmäki as it pushed ahead with data center development. The article reports that the facilities threaten 40% higher electricity bills, and that wolves have moved into Finnish villages after their habitats were destroyed. Finland's Licensing and Supervision Authority, known as LVV, backs the police investigation.

Google representatives have previously publicly apologized for the unauthorized forest clearings near Muhos. A Google representative said the company would cooperate with the police investigation and continue to focus on maintaining compliance at its sites, according to Reuters. The article notes that the scale of any punishment and proposed remedies will probably be of most concern to the tech giant's executives. It also says that since the apology, there seems little doubt the company is guilty of some wrongdoing.

Google sees Finland as an attractive location for data center development because of its cool climate, affordable power, and government endorsement of AI projects. The company has also benefited from being able to develop in low population density areas and from a populace with a low propensity to protest. The article says Google is now testing the Finnish public with its trampling of the environment. It adds that the wolves, pollution, and potentially higher electricity bills were not helping Google's case even before the criminal investigation.

Articles.Title: Google hit with criminal probe over unapproved AI data center deforestation

stories.Headline: Is AI Safe Enough To Develop Nuclear Power? Wyoming Is About To Find Out
stories.Summary:
TerraPower founder Bill Gates said during an Oct. 15 tour of the Natrium nuclear reactor project in Kemmerer that the company is using artificial intelligence to check its plans and designs, including paperwork such as Nuclear Regulatory Commission permits. The same approach is being used in state research: with a $906,382 grant from the U.S. Department of Energy, researchers at the University of Wyoming and the Idaho National Laboratory are developing AI-enabled models to predict more reliably how heat moves through nuclear fuel. Jackson Harter, a computational scientist at INL, spent the last four years building the reference models the NRC uses to evaluate the sodium-cooled reactor project. Laura de Sousa Oliveira, an associate professor of chemistry at the University of Wyoming, is leading the project that pairs AI with INL software to map heat movement through fuel.

Harter said INL is the primary adopter of AI to accelerate workflows in the United States and that no other lab comes close. He said AI helps his team draft regulatory and safety documents in a fraction of the time it would take from scratch, leaving more time to develop and test safety measures, but that human scientists remain in charge. He described AI as a tool that can get you between 70 and 90% of the way there, adding that the expert must examine the output and is ultimately responsible. De Sousa Oliveira said the large language model will not invent new physics or methods and will be limited to established procedures and trusted software, managing the workflow rather than guessing at answers or making decisions on its own. She said that if used judiciously, as with any other tool, it should allow better performance and better safety margins, and she said her group tests its AI tools against calculations for which the answers are already known.

Samantha Fowler, a Natrona County resident who researches statewide nuclear development on her own time, presented a research binder on nuclear development to the Campbell County commissioners on Sept. 16 and urged officials to demand transparency and hold federal regulators like the NRC accountable to basic safety standards. She told Cowboy State Daily she worries speed will win out over strict human oversight, that mistakes in nuclear development can have serious consequences, and that using automated shortcuts risks blurring the line between human accountability and machine efficiency. She said that once people start relying on AI for smaller things, nothing stops that from expanding, which she called her Pandora's box concern, and that efficiency should never come before public safety or accountability. Harter said people are often afraid of things they cannot see, and that while disasters such as Chernobyl in Ukraine and Fukushima in Japan stick in people's minds, the data shows nuclear is the safest form of energy when measured by deaths per megawatt hour. He said he was once a skeptic of nuclear power himself before becoming an engineer and is now confident in the safety of modern plants like Natrium.

Articles.Title: Is AI Safe Enough To Develop Nuclear Power? Wyoming Is About To Find Out - Cowboy State Daily

stories.Headline: Philippines, New Zealand explore AI to improve power services
stories.Summary:
The Philippines and New Zealand are exploring how artificial intelligence can improve electricity regulation, monitor power outages, and simplify customer services. Energy officials, regulators, and technology executives from both countries discussed possible AI applications at an event on Oct. 8 at the Manila residence of New Zealand Ambassador Catherine McIntosh. The reception was organized with the technology firm Gentrack and New Zealand Trade and Enterprise. It brought together representatives from the Department of Energy, the Energy Regulatory Commission, and New Zealand's technology sector.

The Energy Regulatory Commission outlined efforts to move beyond basic digitalization toward a system using data analytics and intelligent technologies. Among the initiatives under development is ASK ERiC, an AI-enabled chatbot to help consumers navigate ERC information, regulatory procedures, and public services. The commission is also exploring AI-assisted compliance monitoring, including agentic AI that could track compliance submissions, identify missing requirements, and flag potential violations for review. It is likewise considering regulatory analytics to identify patterns in outages, including frequency, duration, geographic distribution, and unusual trends. As of September 2026, the ERC had 28 information systems supporting its processes, up from 25 operational systems reported by August after the May launch of the ERCify digital platform.

ERC Director III Heiddi Venecia R. Barrozo outlined these efforts. The commission said adopting AI must not compromise accountability, accuracy, explainability, or information security, and that AI-generated findings would still require verification and human oversight before use in regulatory decisions. Gentrack solution architect Hyun Woo Kim said every country has its own unique problem and unique way to solve it, stressing that AI tools must be designed specifically for the energy sector. He cited S&P Global research published March 31, 2026, showing that 64% of surveyed energy and utility organizations were investing more than 10% of their total IT budgets in AI, while only 43% of AI projects were considered on track to generate a return on investment within 12 months. The study also found that 7% of surveyed organizations were allocating more than 30% of their IT budgets to AI.

Kim described three stages of AI adoption in utility operations: systems that assist human customer service representatives, customer-facing self-service platforms, and autonomous AI agents handling customer interactions and defined workflows within safeguards. Gentrack demonstrated applications involving bill explanations, account inquiries, workflow automation, and compliance support, along with low-code and no-code technologies. New Zealand Trade and Enterprise representatives reaffirmed their commitment to cooperation with the Philippines in innovation, sustainability, and economic growth. The articles say the benefits will depend on the accuracy of the systems, protection of consumer data, and whether utilities and regulators can translate investments into measurable improvements in service quality and affordability.

Articles.Title: Philippines, New Zealand explore AI to improve power services - Daily Guardian

stories.Headline: San Mateo Union High District weighs AI use in classrooms
stories.Summary:
The San Mateo Union High School District is working through questions about when, where and how artificial intelligence should be used in classrooms. Students, parents and educators broadly agree that AI should support critical thinking and learning rather than replace it. Staff will spend the school year developing guardrails to keep that distinction. District leaders said the goal is to prepare students to use AI tools while still becoming thoughtful, ethical, creative and capable human beings.

A progress update on the committee's work came at a meeting on Oct. 22. Julia Kemp, who works in curriculum and instruction, said the district is moving beyond the debate over whether AI should be used at all. Since a study session on the topic in May, the district has developed AI literacy modules to give students a baseline understanding of the technology's purpose and value. Work also began on drafting a syllabus template for teachers and on how the technology should be used.

Kemp said the technology is evolving rapidly, which requires districts interested in innovation to review and calibrate policies as needed. She said the district can be nimbler than usual and pointed to the shift online during COVID as evidence it can thoughtfully integrate AI in a way that centers students and humans. Superintendent Randall Booker raised concerns about students who lack access to technology, the internet or education about AI at home, asking how far behind they would be. Trustee Robert Griffin said the problem will not be solved this year, next year or probably in five years.

When students should have modules on AI use will also have to be determined, possibly during orientation days at the start of school years or during school periods. Kemp said it will be particularly important to ensure teachers are comfortable enough with the tool to integrate it in the classroom. The steering committee is set to meet three more times during the remainder of the 2026-27 school year. Any future policy decisions will be informed by the committee's work.

Articles.Title: San Mateo Union High District weighs AI use in classrooms - San Mateo Daily Journal

stories.Headline: Florida Takes Unlikely Lead Role in State Push to Regulate AI
stories.Summary:
Florida has become an aggressive regulator of artificial intelligence and major technology platforms, using litigation, child protection requirements and proposed safeguards to challenge the federal government's preference for lighter oversight. The state is an unlikely leader in that effort, since its conservative Republican governor and legislature might ordinarily be associated with limiting government intervention in business. Gov. Ron DeSantis and Attorney General James Uthmeier have cast technology oversight as a defense of children, consumer privacy and human agency. Their campaign highlights a widening state-federal divide over who should set the rules for the digital economy.

Florida opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI in April after reviewing communications between ChatGPT and the suspected gunman in the fatal 2025 shooting at Florida State University. In June, the state filed what is described as the first state civil lawsuit against OpenAI and Chief Executive Sam Altman, alleging the company knowingly released an unsafe product that facilitates self-harm and violence, and those allegations remain claims rather than findings of liability. Uthmeier sought a temporary injunction in September that would bar OpenAI from developing new models without stringent safety safeguards, extending the state's intervention beyond compensation to restrictions on future product development. A 2024 Florida law prohibits social media accounts for children younger than 14 and requires parental consent for certain older minors, and an initial preliminary injunction on free speech grounds was later reversed in the state's favor. Florida also joined New Mexico in rejecting a proposed $18 billion Meta child safety settlement.

Uthmeier has proposed additional requirements for age determination and parental consent when minors download applications, and he said parents deserve real control and that companies must design for safety, not addiction. OpenAI has said it supports working with states on pragmatic policies while maintaining that its platform is not responsible for users' criminal acts. House Speaker Daniel Perez blocked DeSantis' proposed AI Bill of Rights after it passed the Senate, aligning with the Trump administration's opposition to what it sees as burdensome state requirements. A December presidential executive order directed the administration to work with Congress toward a minimally burdensome national standard, reflecting federal concerns about conflicting state rules.

Florida's technology debate also focuses on data centers, with disputes over approval authority, possible moratoriums and demands on electricity and water supplies. For companies, Florida illustrates how state enforcement can create significant operational exposure even when federal policy favors deregulation. Yet its legislative divisions also show that an aggressive attorney general and governor cannot automatically translate their priorities into comprehensive law. The resulting landscape combines active litigation, contested legislation and continuing uncertainty over the boundaries of state authority.

Articles.Title: Florida Takes Unlikely Lead Role in State Push to Regulate AI - PYMNTS.com

stories.Headline: Experts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights case
stories.Summary:
Australia's attorney general's department acknowledged on Friday that it was "extremely alive" to concerns raised in a parliamentary committee hearing, where Nationals senator Ross Cadell asked about the constitutional implications of allowing AI companies to scrape copyrighted material. The hearing followed warnings from Coalition senators and the recording industry that weakening copyright law could breach section 51 of the constitution, which allows the commonwealth to make laws about the acquisition of property on just terms. The debate centres on proposals reportedly sought by AI companies, including an "opt-out" model suggested by Anthropic that would let it scrape content unless a rights holder deployed digital protections signalling an objection. No legislative proposal has been aired.

Anne Twomey, professor emerita of law at the University of Sydney, said granting AI companies a new right to use copyrighted material while diminishing the rights of copyright holders could "potentially" trigger constitutional issues, depending on how legislation was drafted. She said the high court had recognised a number of exceptions to section 51 and that one would want to be quite confident before enacting such legislation. Cadell said an opt-out model raised a real question of whether the government was acquiring the intellectual property rights of others, and he warned it could open the federal government to liability for what he called the biggest compensation rights case in history. A spokesperson for attorney general Michelle Rowland said the government was committed to supporting creatives and pledged that any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation.

Shadow attorney general Michaelia Cash said the government should not sell out Australian creators and rights holders in the rush to entice AI investment, and said the constitutional question of property rights and their acquisition on just terms was a live issue the Coalition would examine depending on what the government put forward. Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association, claimed any proposal to allow scraping was clearly an acquisition of property and appeared to be a clear path to a constitutional challenge. Chris Maund, chief executive of Mushroom Records, said current copyright law was working and that AI companies should use existing licensing arrangements, noting companies such as Spotify were already making AI-related deals. He said an AI company could train in Australia to circumvent copyright laws applying outside the country, and that international creative industries were watching closely.

Prime minister Anthony Albanese has promised the strongest possible protection and warned it would be theft if creatives were not paid for their work, while some AI companies have rejected licensing agreements under existing law, saying it was too difficult. Officials did not directly answer when Cadell asked about international implications and liability for compensation to foreign rights holders. Cadell said that while there was lots of talk about the benefits of AI, taking these rights away would have known consequences, and that he did not want to hurt people for a may. The articles do not say when the government will make its announcement on AI.

Articles.Title: Experts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights case - The Guardian

stories.Headline: DEP To Hold Dec. 3 Meeting/Hearing On Air Permit For Installation Of Emergency Generators At Aligned AI PA Data Center In Shippingport Boro, Beaver County - PA Environment Digest Blog
stories.Summary:
The Department of Environmental Protection published notice in the October 31 PA Bulletin announcing a December 3 public meeting and hearing on an Aligned AI PA data center Air Quality Plan Approval for the installation of emergency generators in Shippingport Borough, Beaver County. The Plan Approval, numbered PA-04-00953A, would authorize construction and temporary operation of air contamination sources and air cleaning devices associated with the proposed data center. The notice on page 7093 of the PA Bulletin has a complete list of the air pollution sources covered by the permit and their potential to pollute. The meeting and hearing will be held at the Chippingport Community Building, 163 SR-3016, Shippingport, PA from 6:00 to 8:00 p.m.

Persons wishing to present testimony at the public conference and hearing should register with Emily Green in the Department's Office of Environmental Justice at 412-442-4042 or via email to emgreen@pa.gov. Persons unable to attend the conference and hearing may submit a written statement and exhibits within ten days after the public conference and hearing.
