Michael Bailey, a professor at Georgia Tech, said self-replicating models are real and will be seen, but whether they take the exact form Anthropic describes is an open question. Bailey said the framing is somewhat of a misnomer because the models do things like sharding, which is not full propagation like a worm or virus.

Bailey said what Mirai showed is that botnets could be composed of everyday devices like cable routers and IP-enabled cameras, which were thought useless to an adversary but are actually quite effective. He said adaptability itself is not new, since Mirai already worked across heterogeneous devices, but each new architecture required human work. He suggested more capable AI models will redistribute who does the work of creating botnets and change the economics between attackers and defenders. Canal said the companies are likely worried about other AI companies being reckless, and that they know those companies have the same incentives to deliver models fast for market share.

Anthropic suggests ISPs notify customers of an infection and then limit their internet access to a short list of safe websites, a strategy deployed during Mirai. It also suggests regulation, pointing to the UK, where easily guessable default passwords on IoT devices are now banned under the PSTI Act. Bailey argues the appropriate response looks a lot more like what has been done in systems security for a very long time, and that even misbehaving agents will have a hard time against hardened devices. Canal said it would be difficult to add safeguards to an open-weight model to prevent it acting as a worm, and that nothing robust exists so far.

Articles.Title: What Happens When AI Starts Self-Replicating?

stories.Headline: ITC takes down unknown number of websites following Wiz Research AI-assisted discovery of global cybersecurity vulnerability
stories.Summary:
On Oct. 21, the cybersecurity firm Wiz Research used OpenAI’s advanced AI models to find vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used to build 70% of websites globally, according to the Associated Press. That same day, Dartmouth’s Information, Technology and Consulting office issued a “major incident” report on its webpage for “websites and systems service disruption.” On Oct. 22, the office temporarily took down some Dartmouth websites. The PHP Foundation, the language’s nonprofit developers, released a patch for the vulnerabilities on Oct. 21.

ITC wrote in its Oct. 21 incident report that a widespread security vulnerability had been identified affecting websites and software worldwide, including systems at Dartmouth. The office said it was applying security fixes as quickly as possible to minimize disruption, and that some Dartmouth websites might be unavailable while patches were applied. An ITC spokesperson did not respond to requests for comment on whether any Dartmouth websites were affected by the PHP vulnerabilities, but wrote in an email that the College’s web services were “not affected” by an internet user’s Oct. 20 discovery of compromised Transport Layer Security certificates, which was not directly related to the PHP issue. The incident was still listed as “Identified” on ITC’s live status webpage as of publication, and a College spokesperson did not respond to requests for comment.

Computer science graduate student Benjamin Kallus, who won more than $30,000 in bug bounties for finding and patching vulnerabilities in Google products between 2023 and 2025, said a properly weaponized memory corruption bug can give control of the computer running the vulnerable software, and that such bugs have been exploited against websites running unpatched versions of PHP. He said any College website coded with PHP could be vulnerable, but Dartmouth’s infrastructure is protected by being internal-facing, requiring a Dartmouth login, so he was not very worried about an outside break-in for now. Computer science lecturer Vasanta Kommineni said using a VPN such as Dartmouth’s GlobalProtect to limit access to institutional websites is a typical precautionary step. Kallus added that maintenance of open-source infrastructure like PHP is a perennial problem because it relies on volunteers, and that big companies rely on this infrastructure without contributing back.

Articles.Title: ITC takes down unknown number of websites following Wiz Research AI-assisted discovery of global cybersecurity vulnerability

stories.Headline: AI, DevOps and the Cost of Hosting: From Idea to Production for $0
stories.Summary:
Over about five weeks of intermittent work, roughly three days of full work with the AI coding agent Claude, a developer rebuilt a photo-collage app from an Angular 8 project that would not build into a distributed system running in production. Claude upgraded the front end to Angular 22 and fixed the build on Node 24, set up RabbitMQ with Docker Compose, added real-time notifications over SignalR, fixed a crash loop caused by an unreadable iPhone photo, and redesigned the system so any server can process any job. It also added a dead-letter queue, confirmed publishing, idempotent workers, recovery of stuck jobs and automatic clean-up, wrote 41 automated tests, and scrubbed leaked passwords and personal photos from the Git history. The app was deployed to Oracle Cloud's Always Free tier on a small instance with 1 CPU and about 6 GB of RAM, after the developer opened ports 80 and 443 in Oracle's network firewall.

Load testing on the live server produced 538 collages with zero failed jobs, and the server handled 64 people creating collages at the same moment. Its ceiling was about 62 collages a minute, one per second, and beyond that users queue. With 4 people creating at once, 95% of collages arrived within about five seconds, while at 64 each person waited about a minute. The test showed the disk runs out first, not the CPU, because each collage stores about 5 MB, mostly the PNG output, so at full speed the disk would fill in under two hours. Switching to JPEG and shortening retention fixes that, and three more free CPUs are available when traffic grows.

The developer wrote that the software problems took minutes while the hardware and network problems took longer, and that when code becomes cheap to produce the bottleneck moves, which for him meant hardware. He described Oracle's free tier as a play for loyalty rather than charity, since Oracle wants successful projects to stay and grow into its paid services, and it can reclaim free instances that sit idle. He said he expects hosting and data centres to become a very profitable business as more people turn ideas into working software. For now, he wrote, Claude handles the coding, QA and DevOps while Oracle's free server keeps an idea online long enough to find out whether it deserves to grow.

Articles.Title: AI, DevOps and the Cost of Hosting: From Idea to Production for $0

stories.Headline: Foxconn hopes to own 50% of the global AI server market within a couple years
stories.Summary:
Foxconn, the Taiwanese electronics group also known as Hon Hai Technology Group, hopes to take 50% of the global AI server market within a couple of years, Chairman Young Liu told CNBC in an interview with Christine Tan. Liu said the company's share could reach around 45% next year, up from about 40% now. He said he thinks Foxconn can grow up to 50%. The company is best known for assembling Apple's iPhones but has increasingly turned to AI infrastructure as a growth driver.

Liu said AI infrastructure should make up 60% to 65% of Foxconn's revenue in the next three to five years, not counting edge AI devices. He said production capacity is fully booked for at least the next year and a half. Demand so far has come largely from AI model developers and cloud service providers, while governments and enterprises have not yet fully embraced the technology. He described AI demand as quite strong.

Foxconn plans to move further up the supply chain in the United States to serve that market better and respond faster to rising demand. Liu said higher U.S. manufacturing costs mean the company will start with higher-margin products such as AI server racks and data center equipment, and greater scale there could eventually lower costs. He stressed careful spending, saying overinvestment will kill the company. He said Foxconn could spend more than its planned $3 billion to $5 billion a year on AI depending on how far it expands vertical integration, and that weaker demand from one customer could be offset by growth elsewhere, though an industry-wide slowdown would be a much bigger challenge.

Articles.Title: Foxconn hopes to own 50% of the global AI server market within a couple years

stories.Headline: Axios C-Suite: The 6 dimensions of AI leadership
stories.Summary:
Jim VandeHei wrote in the Axios C-Suite newsletter, published on October 31, 2026, that AI is not a choice but an urgent enabler of revenue, growth and cost. He said he had heard from two companies deeply involved in AI tutoring of CEOs that at best 15% of CEOs are AI-savvy, and that most board chairs know even less about the technology. He argued that leaders of AI-enabled companies need six new layers of AI leadership and expertise. He said he would outline the six layers in that newsletter and use future editions to help readers master each one.

The six layers he listed are: understand AI, use and explain it, govern it, implement and measure it, restructure teams and companies to exploit it, and make sure companies and products show up inside it. On governance, he wrote that 71% of directors named AI as the top skill their boards need to strengthen, and 82% said information on AI's link to risk and business performance was fair, poor or unavailable. He said the technology changes weekly and that implementation is a living, never-ending project. He described the coming companies as human/agent hybrids operating at a speed never seen before, and said he is three years into this work and tinkers with structure constantly.

On responsibility, he said the CEO cannot outsource understanding AI, and that it will soon be a vital part of every decision. He said he hired a personal AI savant to work with him outside the company's formal structure, and that leadership on using AI must come from the CEO, at least broadly, because staff are desperate for reassurance that it will be unleashed smartly and safely. He said the CEO decides who owns AI and what is off-limits, while specifics fall to the CTO or CIO. He said boards are largely flying blind on AI, and that CEOs need to flatten their organizations fast and rethink the CIO, CTO and CPO roles to find one person responsible for proprietary data, the tech and security stack, and AI enablement companywide.

He said most CEOs are clueless about showing up inside AI, and that all companies need to restructure content, marketing and messaging to surface inside large language models and agents. He noted that the CEO of Profound, which he called the leading company monitoring this dynamic, recently gave C-Suite readers tips on fixing this fast. He said consultancies including Accenture, Teneo, Thoughtworks and FSG are helping CEOs with some pieces, but that everyone needs a holistic solution. He invited CEOs and their teams to ask to join the newsletter for deeper coverage of the six dimensions in the weeks ahead.

Articles.Title: Axios C-Suite: The 6 dimensions of AI leadership

stories.Headline: Israeli AI founders bring Jigso team to Placer.ai in push beyond traditional analytics
stories.Summary:
Or Shani and Tomer Naveh, co-founders of the Israeli artificial intelligence startup Jigso, are joining the U.S. location analytics company Placer.ai along with a team of AI and machine learning specialists. The two founders have spent 16 years developing AI and machine learning products. They will work with Placer.ai's existing teams on technology designed to identify patterns, detect unusual activity and generate business recommendations from location data. Placer.ai provides information about foot traffic and activity at physical locations, including stores, shopping centers, hotels and commercial properties.

Placer.ai's platform is used by more than 5,000 organizations, including Fortune 500 companies, to assess consumer behavior, compare locations and track changes in market activity. The company wants to move beyond conventional analytics, where customers examine data and draw their own conclusions, toward systems that automatically identify developments that may require attention. These could include unexpected changes in visitor numbers, shifts in consumer patterns or other indicators relevant to business decisions. Shani and Naveh previously co-founded Albert.ai, an early AI platform for automating digital advertising decisions, which went public and was later sold. They then established Jigso, which built an AI platform that connected to enterprise systems and analyzed business information to identify anomalies, surface insights and support automated actions.

Noam Ben-Zvi, CEO and co-founder of Placer.ai, said the company's ambition was never to be just an analytics platform. He said Placer.ai had already invested in AI development and that the incoming team would work alongside its existing specialists. Shani said Placer.ai's data resources were a central factor in the decision to join, adding that great AI needs great, unique data. The announcement did not specify how many Jigso employees are joining Placer.ai or disclose any financial arrangements. It also did not detail which new products or features the team will be responsible for developing.

The move comes as businesses increasingly experiment with AI systems that can do more than respond to questions or produce reports. Placer.ai is pursuing a similar approach using its proprietary location data, though it has not provided a timetable for introducing new capabilities resulting from the team's arrival. For Placer.ai, the immediate significance is the addition of an experienced Israeli AI team to an existing development operation. Whether that translates into substantial changes for customers will depend on how effectively the company integrates the new expertise and turns its ambitions for automated analysis into working products.

Articles.Title: Israeli AI founders bring Jigso team to Placer.ai in push beyond traditional analytics

stories.Headline: The Nasdaq 100 Briefly Fell Into a Correction as the AI Trade Cracks
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq 100 briefly fell into correction territory on Friday, October 30, 2026, then climbed back above the line before the close. It dropped 3.46% to close at 28,384.85, after an intraday low of 28,093.24. That low was 10.0% below the October 6 record close of 31,224.47, so the index crossed the 10% line during the session. It closed 9.1% below the record, meaning it never finished a day in correction.

The selling started in chip stocks. Intel fell 28.6% after guiding fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, below the $16.5 billion it had just reported. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 7.2%, its worst day since June 23, and lost 15.4% for October. Invesco QQQ Trust closed at $690.49, down 3.47%, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% to 25,437.00, its lowest close since July 31.

Joe Tigay, a portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said the AI trade was moving out of the hopes and dreams phase and into what he called the show me phase. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said the company still expected 2026 cash capital expenditures of approximately $220 billion. On Intel's call, management said data center demand exceeds supply, but guided fourth-quarter gross margin to 38%, compared with 44.1% in the third quarter, and warned of a PC slowdown linked to memory prices. Apple slipped 1.23% but at $5.03 trillion became the most valuable company, ahead of NVIDIA, which fell 4.2% to $204.64 and was worth $4.94 trillion.

This was the third time in 2026 that the index fell more than 10% below a record, after March 27 and July 29, and both earlier times it later set new records. The VIX hit 23.93 during the session but closed at 19.41, up 12.91%. The next tests come quickly: Apple is expected to report after the close on November 2, though it has not confirmed the date, the midterm elections follow on November 3, the October jobs report comes out on November 6, and NVIDIA reports in mid-November. The key level to watch is a Nasdaq-100 close below the October 30 intraday low of 28,093.24, which would put the index in correction on a closing basis.

Articles.Title: The Nasdaq 100 Briefly Fell Into a Correction as the AI Trade Cracks

stories.Headline: Google stock's historically bad day raises fears of AI bubble popping
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, the parent company of Google, lost more than $500 billion in market value on October 30, 2026, according to NBC News. The drop was described as a historically bad day for the stock and raised fears that the AI bubble may be about to pop. NBC News correspondent Allie Canal reported on big tech's spending and how AI is affecting the job market. The report was published on October 30, 2026, at 03:23.

The coverage tied the loss to concerns about spending on artificial intelligence across big tech. The Financial Times published a related article on October 28, 2026, with a headline saying the AI bubble had already popped in China. That article's text was not available because it sat behind a subscription page. The subscription offers shown on the page included a standard digital plan at $299 for the first year and a trial at $1 for four weeks, after which the price was $75 per month.

NBC News reported the market value loss and the fears about the AI bubble, and it presented Canal's reporting on big tech spending and AI's impact on jobs. The Financial Times article's author and specific claims were not visible in the available text. The FT page did not include any named person commenting on the loss. No one was quoted directly in the material that could be read.

The NBC report framed the drop as a sign of worry about whether AI investment has grown into a bubble. The FT headline suggested the bubble had already burst in China, though the article's details could not be read. The available articles did not say what would happen next for Alphabet's stock or for AI spending. They also did not give any further dates or figures beyond the $500 billion loss and the FT subscription prices.

Articles.Title: Google stock's historically bad day raises fears of AI bubble popping

stories.Headline: Prediction: This Under-the-Radar AI Stock Could Have a Big 2030 Ahead
stories.Summary:
Marvell Technology's Data Center segment brought in $2.1715 billion last quarter, up 46%, and now makes up 79% of total revenue, according to a 24/7 Wall St. article published on October 31, 2026. The article says AI-related bookings remain exceptionally robust, according to CEO Matt Murphy. The shares are up 194.58% year to date but sit below their peak. At $249.92, the stock is 24.2% below its 52-week high of $329.73.

The article says reaching $500 by 2030 would require a gain of 100.1%. It says that path depends on three things: the custom business more than doubling year over year in fiscal 2028, non-GAAP operating margin reaching the top of its 38% to 40% target range, and Google programs ramping in fiscal 2029. Management guided Q3 non-GAAP gross margin to 57.5% to 58.5%, below Q2's 58.9%, and raised its fiscal 2027 operating expense outlook to approximately $2.55 billion. The article also notes that a small group of hyperscalers drive most of the revenue and that the Google warrant could dilute shareholders by up to 7%.

Wall Street gives the stock 40 Buy-or-better ratings with zero Sells and a consensus target of $341.44, implying about 36.6% upside, the article says. It lists 8 Strong Buy recommendations, 32 Buy ratings and 6 Holds. Murphy said there is a lot of upside bias in the numbers in fiscal 29 and beyond in custom, and he called the full potential of the hyperscaler agreement game-changing. The article's own model has a base case of $284.80, or 17.23% upside, within a one-year range of $218.43 to $352.54, and its 2030 bull case reaches $509.10 by October of that year.

The article says the biggest risk is hyperscalers cutting capital spending or bringing more chip design in-house. It says a sharp slowdown in AI infrastructure spending would disrupt the plan. At today's price, the article says, Marvell trades at 41x forward earnings, which it calls reasonable for a company guiding to roughly $12 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue. It says the stock has run from $70.62 to $329.73 over the past 52 weeks and has returned 1943.93% over 10 years.

Articles.Title: Prediction: This Under-the-Radar AI Stock Could Have a Big 2030 Ahead

stories.Headline: Chinese hackers used DeepSeek and other AI tools in sweeping global cyberattacks, report finds
stories.Summary:
Chinese state-linked hackers used artificial intelligence, including the DeepSeek model, to attack more than 200 organizations worldwide in just 11 days, according to the cybersecurity company CrowdStrike. The campaign hit governments and businesses around the world. NBC News reported the findings on Oct. 29, 2026. The report says the campaign shows how AI lets hackers work at a scale that once took far more human effort.

The figure of more than 200 organizations covers the 11-day span of the campaign. The tools named include DeepSeek, a popular AI model, along with other AI tools. CrowdStrike is the cybersecurity company that published the findings. The targets were governments and businesses worldwide, and the report describes the campaign as sweeping.

CrowdStrike is responsible for the report, and its findings say AI is changing how hackers operate. According to the report, AI now allows attacks on a scale that previously required far more human effort. The article attributes the findings to the company and does not name individual officials or give direct quotes. The hackers are described as state-linked, meaning they are tied to the Chinese state.

The report places the campaign in the wider context of AI being used to make cyberattacks faster and larger. It does not say what response, if any, followed the attacks. No next steps are given for the targeted organizations or for the governments involved. The article gives no further details beyond the findings it describes.

Articles.Title: Chinese hackers used DeepSeek and other AI tools in sweeping global cyberattacks, report finds

stories.Headline: US forces in Europe are bracing for 'Ukraine's worst day.' AI could help them fight an overwhelming flood of missiles and drones.
stories.Summary:
US forces in Europe are preparing for large-scale combat and the kind of heavy missile and drone attacks Ukraine has faced. US officials believe future battlefields could produce so much data from sensors and networks that human operators would be overwhelmed. Army soldiers are looking to software, including artificial intelligence, to help process that data and keep up with the speed and scale of the threats. At the Association of the United States Army convention in Washington, DC, last month, service leaders and soldiers spoke about using AI to help troops make decisions. Brig.

Gen. Steven Carpenter, head of Multi-Domain Command Europe, said earlier this year that US forces in Europe needed to be ready to process more than 1,500 potential targets a day while defending against as many as 1,200 incoming missiles and drones. He said that volume of targets and threats could overwhelm human analysts, and that AI could help them keep up. In a conflict, soldiers could use AI to analyze battlefield data and targets based on a commander's objectives and other parameters. The system could then assess available military capabilities and recommend responses, from conventional weapons strikes to electronic warfare or cyber operations.

Carpenter said the estimates reflect what officials think Ukraine's worst day is. Carpenter said it is important to use super intelligence for things humans are not necessarily good at, namely speed and scale, but that humans should not be taken completely out of the loop. He said the human is making the decision and the final call, looking at everything needed to prosecute a valid target within the Law of Armed Conflict. He said the intent is not to replace analysts but to unburden them so they can focus on really tough targets, such as a dual-use facility or other potential targets that need more analysis. Earlier this year, a joint US Army and NATO exercise in Europe saw troops use a homegrown AI system to consume and sort data, and Army officials said they aimed to test it on a larger scale at a future exercise.

The Army is also incorporating AI into its Next Generation Command and Control, its new warfighting system. NGC2 uses AI and machine learning to give commanders and soldiers real-time data on targeting, capabilities, ammunition levels, maintenance needs, intelligence feeds, and simulated enemy attacks. AI and autonomy are being integrated quickly across uncrewed systems, command and control processes, and other technologies. Russia's war against Ukraine has involved frequent, heavy drone and missile bombardments, with complex strike packages of ballistic and cruise missiles and one-way attack drones, more of which are equipped with jet engines that make them faster and harder to kill.

Articles.Title: US forces in Europe are bracing for 'Ukraine's worst day.' AI could help them fight an overwhelming flood of missiles and drones.

stories.Headline: European shares ease as AI-driven tech selloff deepens
stories.Summary:
European shares fell on Friday, October 30, 2026, as technology stocks came under pressure from renewed worries about rising AI investment costs. The pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 0.29% to 647.23 points by 0929 GMT. The technology sector index led the declines, falling 2%. The drop came after earnings from Amazon and Intel brought back concerns about heavy AI-related spending and the returns it can generate. The STOXX 600 was still set to post both weekly and monthly gains, and it was on track for its best month since June.

Sector heavyweight ASML fell 5%, while STMicroelectronics, BESI and Infineon fell between 3.3% and 4.8%. Chip stocks Soitec and Aixtron fell 5.7% and 3.6% respectively. French consumer prices rose more than expected in October, recording the highest inflation rate since December 2023. Michael Hewson, chief analyst at MCH Market Insights, said the market was trying to wrestle with the equation of a huge amount of capital spending relative to the timeline of a return on investment. He said that at the moment, they do not have an answer to that.

Political unrest in France also weighed on sentiment this month, as the country faces pressure from rising living costs and elevated government debt, driving French bond yields to multi-year highs. Robust earnings from companies such as ASML, Shell and Airbus reinforced confidence in the health of European corporates. LSEG I/B/E/S data showed European blue-chips were heading for their second-best quarterly earnings in four years. Universal Music Group jumped 11.2% after posting a pick-up in subscription streaming revenue in the third quarter. Investors also awaited third-quarter euro zone gross domestic product figures later in the day.

Articles.Title: European shares ease as AI-driven tech selloff deepens

stories.Headline: Closing the Industrial Knowledge Gap with Consumer-Grade Enterprise AI
stories.Summary:
In 2020, the U.S. Census Bureau reported that nearly one-fourth of manufacturing workers were aged 55 or older. The U.S. Department of Energy has identified the loss of undocumented operational knowledge as a risk to productivity and operational continuity as experienced workers retire. The Aviation Technician Education Council's 2026 report cites an Oliver Wyman projection of a North American shortage of about 9,100 certificated mechanics that year. NIST estimated $119.1 billion in preventable losses for U.S. manufacturers, including $18.1 billion from downtime. Vaibhav Kumar, Global Chief Technology Officer at IFS, discussed these issues with Eysan Yazici on the Emerj AI in Business Podcast.

Kumar said cumbersome enterprise software is a barrier to capturing and retrieving knowledge, because entering data is a point of friction for experienced workers. He said consumer-grade interfaces make it easier for workers to record what they know and make existing records usable for newer employees, creating a cycle in which easier contribution adds more knowledge and useful answers give people a reason to keep contributing. He described how conversational experiences like those in Claude or ChatGPT can be layered over enterprise business data. He gave the example of a CFO whose question currently passes through a VP, a manager and an analyst before returning without an answer, and said a conversational layer lets the CFO ask directly and get an answer within a minute. He said a presentation that once took three days now takes about 15 minutes to generate from a detailed prompt plus 30 to 40 minutes of refinement, and that the human still defines the intent and owns the output.

Kumar said the human always drives the agent, and that background automation is something users opt into and can choose when to be brought back in the loop. He said AI depends on existing systems holding relevant operational data, but pushed back on the idea that data must be 100 percent clean first, since large language models can recognize duplicate records and help cleanse data. He described data as having gravity and recommended starting with the systems holding the most meaningful data. He also warned that some vendors repackage existing integration interfaces as Model Context Protocol servers and sell them as AI capability, and said the real test is whether a product delivers a generalizable, consumer-grade AI experience. He identified AI literacy across the workforce as a priority, noting that public discussion leads many people to conclude the technology is not capable.

Articles.Title: Closing the Industrial Knowledge Gap with Consumer-Grade Enterprise AI

stories.Headline: What Real AI Adoption Looks Like
stories.Summary:
Brian Kennedy is Director of Innovation, Real Estate, at BCLP and has 20 years of experience across legal practice and innovation. He now leads innovation across the firm’s global Real Estate practice, focusing on moving AI from exploration to structured adoption at scale. He is one of many expert speakers appearing at Legal Innovators UK, which runs on November 4 and 5, 2026, at The Minster Building near the Tower of London. He will join a session called “The Reality of Realignment.” Free tickets are available for those working inside law firms and within corporate legal teams.

Kennedy said innovation means finding new and better ways of delivering legal services that add value for the firm and its clients, by bringing together the right people, processes and technology. He said innovation teams are now expected to advise on upskilling, resourcing and the firm’s value proposition, and that change management and culture matter even more as AI touches lawyers’ work more fundamentally. On measurement, he said the metric has to match the mission, with time savings and profitability for internal efficiency, client experience for client-facing solutions, and qualitative measures such as lawyer satisfaction for everyday productivity tools. He said traditional ROI models may not fit generative AI, comparing an overall ROI figure to asking the ROI of having a computer, and that the real test is whether an initiative moves the firm closer to its strategic objectives.

On culture, Kennedy said the technology is only half the story and that the common mistake is treating innovation as a technology rollout when it is really a change management exercise. He said lawyers need the willingness to step back and reimagine workflows so they become AI-native, and that innovation has to be a shared responsibility rather than something handed to the innovation team or delegated to juniors. On training, he said formal training is the layer most exposed to the pace of change, because a tool may have moved on by the time a programme is built around it. He said formal training should be the foundation, supplemented by faster informal channels such as lawyers sharing what they learned that week, quick show-and-tells and wins shared in team meetings, feeding back into a continuous learning loop.

Kennedy argued that access to AI platforms and proficiency in using them will both become table stakes, and that real competitive advantage will come from differentiation. He said that if firms rely on the same off-the-shelf capabilities as everyone else, clients have less reason not to insource the work using the same tools, but tailoring AI output to a firm’s judgment, tone and voice and proprietary know-how makes its use of AI a genuine point of differentiation. He described AI’s reach across legal workflows as trying to eat an elephant, which can only be done one piece at a time, and said advantage comes from deciding which piece to tackle first and tying those choices to commercial strategy. Looking five years ahead, he said a genuinely technology-enabled firm will not look like today’s firm with better tools bolted on, and that the aspects of practice that change most will be those calling on judgement, empathy and the ability to persuade.

At the session, Kennedy hopes people leave with a clear understanding that the next phase is not about more pilots or proof of concepts but about driving genuine structural change, reimagining workflows and the wider process rather than adding a tool on top of how things were done before. He said the clearest sign of real progress is when AI becomes the primary delivery mechanism for a particular task or activity rather than an available option sitting alongside the old way of working, at which point the workflow itself looks fundamentally different. He said he expects the panel to bring its own examples of where that is already happening and that he is looking forward to hearing where others have got to. The interview was conducted by Emma Nguyen, Marketing Executive at Cosmonauts, with graphics by Charles Kabunga, Design Lead at Cosmonauts.

Articles.Title: What Real AI Adoption Looks Like

stories.Headline: Jacksonville State University to Host AI Forward Summit Connecting Education and Industry in February
stories.Summary:
Jacksonville State University will host a two-day summit on artificial intelligence in education and the workforce. The event, called AI Forward: From Classroom to Career, is scheduled for February 11-12, 2027, at Merrill Hall on the university's campus in Jacksonville, Alabama. It will bring together K-12 educators, higher education professionals, students and industry leaders. The summit aims to examine how artificial intelligence is changing teaching, learning and workplace practices and to offer chances for schools and businesses to work together.

The summit will focus on three areas: K-12 education, higher education and student success, and business and industry. Planned activities include keynote presentations, breakout sessions, panel discussions, an AI Exhibitor Expo, an AI Showcase poster session and networking. Anthony Robbins, a Jax State alumnus and former vice president at NVIDIA, will be the featured keynote speaker and will discuss AI's influence on education, industry and workforce development. Representatives from Coca-Cola UNITED, Honda, AmFirst Credit Union and other industry organizations are expected at featured sessions.

The university is accepting presentation proposals, with a deadline of November 9, 2026. Proposals can be for 30-minute presentations, 10-minute presentations or the AI Showcase poster session, and will be judged on relevance, clarity, practical application, audience value and alignment with the summit's goals. Selected presenters are expected to be notified in early December and will receive complimentary registration. President Dr. Don C. Killingsworth Jr. said AI is already reshaping classrooms and workplaces and that higher education has an important role in helping students use these tools thoughtfully and responsibly.

Registration is free but advance registration is required, with early registration through January 9, 2027, and final registration closing January 27. The first day, Thursday, February 11, will include the expo, opening keynote, breakout sessions, cross-sector discussions and the AI Showcase. Programming continues Friday, February 12, with more breakout sessions and presentations, and optional post-conference workshops are available Friday afternoon. The event is open to K-12 teachers and administrators, college faculty and staff, students, business professionals, workforce development organizations and community partners, and more information is available at www.jsu.edu/aiforward.

Articles.Title: Jacksonville State University to Host AI Forward Summit Connecting Education and Industry in February

stories.Headline: Asian tech stocks slump as AI rout deepens on disappointing U.S. earnings
stories.Summary:
Asian technology stocks fell sharply on Friday, extending recent declines as worries over the slowing artificial intelligence trade were amplified by weak earnings from major U.S. companies. Chipmaking stocks were the worst hit, with TSMC, the region's most valuable company, falling 1.8% in Taiwan trade. Server and electronics assembler Hon Hai Precision Industry, better known as Foxconn, fell 3%. South Korea's Samsung Electronics fell 5.9%, extending losses after its third-quarter earnings missed some lofty expectations on Thursday, while rival SK Hynix fell 8.3%.

Japanese chip stocks also fell sharply, with Tokyo Electron losing over 5% and Murata Mfg sliding 11% ahead of their September quarter earnings. Advantest slid 5.8%, reversing strong gains from the prior session after the NVIDIA supplier clocked strong quarterly earnings. Tech conglomerate SoftBank Group, which is heavily exposed to AI, dropped nearly 7%. Japanese stocks were also spooked by a hawkish Bank of Japan, which left interest rates steady but said inflation had reached its 2% target, opening the door to more interest rate hikes.

The BOJ also signaled a sharp increase in sales of its exchange-traded fund holdings, a move that presents direct pressure on Japanese equities. Losses in chip shares came tracking an over 20% wipeout in Intel on Thursday evening, after the U.S. chipmaker's fourth-quarter guidance largely underwhelmed. While Intel benefited from increasing demand for data center processors, its PC business faced mounting headwinds from soaring component costs and weakening consumer demand, a trend that has impacted electronics manufacturers across the board. Doubts over the long-term prospects of AI also surged after top spender Amazon missed top and bottom-line estimates for the September quarter, while its cash flow position fell further into negative territory.

This came following a similarly disappointing print from Google owner Alphabet earlier this week, which raised more questions over just how much returns the billions of dollars poured into AI infrastructure will generate. Tech companies are racing to better monetize AI, amid few signs so far that the nascent tech will be profitable in the long term. This notion battered tech valuations in recent weeks, as investors widely rotated out of high-flying tech stocks and into more defensive sectors. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these recent moves and the rotation into defensive sectors.

Articles.Title: Asian tech stocks slump as AI rout deepens on disappointing U.S. earnings

stories.Headline: High-level panel discussion on artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
A high-level panel discussion on artificial intelligence took place at Villa Europa in Rome. The European Union hosted the event as part of the Festival della Diplomazia 2026. The panel included Lucilla Sioli, head of the EU's AI Office, and Brian Burch, the US Ambassador to the Holy See. Jozef Barlaš, secretary of the Holy See's Dicastery for promoting integral human development, and Kenn Crossley, CIO of the UN's World Food Programme, also took part. Students of global governance and international relations studying in Rome joined the discussion.

The debate centred on the potential of AI and the need for human-centric regulation. The EU's AI Act is described as the first continent-wide regulatory framework for the development, deployment and use of safe, ethical and trustworthy AI. The EU is also a signatory of the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on AI, the first legally binding international treaty on AI. The convention has been signed by 20 countries so far, including the US, Japan, Canada, Iceland, Norway, Switzerland, Ukraine, San Marino and Uruguay. Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas inspired the exchanges in Rome.

The event was hosted by the Delegation of the European Union to the Holy See, the Sovereign Order of Malta, the UN Organisations in Rome and the Republic of San Marino. The discussion was described as lively and covered the challenges of international cooperation on artificial intelligence. The panel examined AI's growing impact on diplomacy, humanitarian action and multilateral cooperation. The articles do not say what, if anything, follows from the discussion.

Articles.Title: High-level panel discussion on artificial intelligence – Villa Europa

stories.Headline: China maps state-led push to deploy AI across shipping
stories.Summary:
China’s transport ministry published a 22-point guide for deploying artificial intelligence across shipping, ports and maritime safety earlier this week, addressed to China Cosco Shipping, China Merchants Group and China Communications Construction Group, as well as provincial transport authorities. The guide is part of Beijing’s push to turn its national “AI Plus” strategy into practical industry applications. The ministry said water transport relies on labour-intensive, repetitive and hazardous work, which creates an inherent need for deep AI adoption. It said it aims to develop solutions that can be replicated and scaled up across the sector.

A ministry spokesperson said China’s water transport sector was undergoing a revolution, citing 60 automated container and dry bulk terminals already in operation. The guide proposes AI tools for predicting equipment failures, detecting unusual vessel movements and coordinating emergency responses, and it says drones and unmanned surface and underwater vessels could assist search-and-rescue operations. For international shipping, it calls for a system to flag unusual vessel movements along key routes and at major ports, and Lloyd’s List understands related projects are in early planning, including tools to forecast port congestion. The guide also covers commercial uses such as designing routes, selecting port calls, deploying vessels, managing schedules and cargo flows, forecasting container demand, repositioning empty boxes and monitoring spending. Decarbonisation is the third pillar, with AI tools to navigate carbon regulations, compare fleet-deployment strategies, calculate emissions, estimate compliance costs and develop plans for cutting emissions.

The guide sets no binding deadlines or investment targets, leaving provincial authorities, state-owned groups and other bodies to set their own priorities, and it encourages them to seek government and dedicated funding. It also acknowledges risks from putting AI deeper into shipboard systems, and the ministry called for security testing against manipulated inputs and poisoned data. Tianchen Xu, a Beijing-based economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said it is unclear how much support the government would commit at the moment. He said the more financial incentives provided, the quicker the adoption, and that good AI projects would go into commercial use while others risk becoming box-ticking exercises.

Articles.Title: China maps state-led push to deploy AI across shipping

stories.Headline: Chinese archaeologists prepare for hi-tech excavations with AI and deep-sea robots
stories.Summary:
Chinese archaeologists are preparing to use AI and deep-sea robots in future excavations under a new five-year plan, the South China Morning Post reported on 31 October 2026. The 15th five-year work plan for archaeology sets out a hi-tech turn for the field. Scientists will be tasked with deploying big data technology and underwater drones to unearth centuries of lost history. The plan also aims to trace Chinese history, decipher the origins of East Asian humans and expand the country's cultural soft power.

Under the plan, scientists will develop technologies including remote sensing, ancient DNA analysis, underwater archaeology robots and AI models for virtual restoration of excavated artefacts. They will also expand international partnerships to conduct fieldwork across Asia. Joint research will be launched in the Austronesian-speaking regions, the Himalayan area and along the Silk Road and Maritime Silk Road. The article gives no further dates or figures beyond the 31 October 2026 publication date and the 15th five-year plan.

The article does not name individual officials or scientists and carries no direct comments from those responsible. It attributes the details to the 15th five-year work plan for archaeology. The scientists will be tasked with deploying the big data technology and underwater drones, according to the report. No specific person is quoted saying anything about the plan.

The context given is that the plan aims to trace Chinese history, decipher the origins of East Asian humans and expand the country's cultural soft power. The article does not say what happens next beyond the work set out in the plan. It does not give a timeline for the technologies or the international fieldwork. It does not say who will oversee or fund the work.

Articles.Title: Chinese archaeologists prepare for hi-tech excavations with AI and deep-sea robots

stories.Headline: AI Tools Could Speed Housing Development & Permitting
stories.Summary:
Valerie White, who leads national housing strategic initiatives at the Local Initiatives Support Corporation, wrote a column published by HousingWire on October 30, 2026, about how artificial intelligence could speed up housing development and permitting. She said the housing industry has grown less productive since the 1970s, just when the country needs it to do more. She described experiments in which planners use AI to collect and analyze large amounts of data, while people still make the final decisions. She also pointed to early results from AI tools in Seattle, Honolulu and Los Angeles County.

The column gives specific numbers. In Seattle, a pilot AI screening tool catches missing or incomplete information in construction permit applications before reviewers see them, and it could cut intake review time by roughly half and reduce correction cycles by about 35%. In Honolulu, residential projects using an AI-powered tool called CivCheck reached a permit decision in an average of 32.5 days in early 2026, down from 73 days, while average corrections fell from 23.5 to 7.7. One company says its microfactory process can cut construction costs by a third and deliver homes three times faster than traditional construction. In Los Angeles County, people enrolled in the Homelessness Prevention Unit, which uses a predictive model built with the California Policy Lab, were 71% less likely to enter a homeless shelter or have contact with outreach teams.

White said AI will not build a single home on its own and should not be trusted to decide where money goes or who gets housed, because people must still make those judgment calls. She said the Urban Institute is examining how AI can help planners analyze complex zoning information faster, which could help communities find where more housing can be built near transit and other amenities while limiting displacement of existing residents. She said models that scan property debt, code violations, deferred maintenance and expiring affordability restrictions can flag buildings headed for trouble years before an owner walks away or a subsidy lapses, giving lenders and cities time to step in. She also said the data centers powering these tools require significant electricity and water, often in communities already struggling with affordability, and that the use of these tools raises questions about accountability, transparency and human oversight.

White said communities most affected by both the housing crisis and the growth of AI infrastructure deserve a voice in how these tools are built, not only in how they are used. She said AI cannot solve the housing crisis and cannot replace the people, policies, capital or community leadership required to build and preserve affordable homes. But she said that used responsibly, with real accountability built in from the start, it can help those efforts move faster, stretch limited resources further and give people more time to act before housing opportunities are lost. The column states that it does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire's editorial department and its owners.

Articles.Title: AI Tools Could Speed Housing Development & Permitting

stories.Headline: State of IT jobs: AI boosts salaries but also burnout and the gender gap
stories.Summary:
Pay in the most AI-exposed occupations grew around 46% since 2021, compared to only 25% for jobs in the least-exposed category, according to the Dice Tech Sentiment report. That gap began to grow in 2024 and continues to widen as job postings rebound after several rough hiring years. The report was covered by Sarah White, a senior writer at CIO.com, in an article dated October 30, 2026. AI job postings doubled in 2026 from 2023, with the average AI listing around $177k compared to $80k for non-AI roles, according to LinkedIn Research.

The data shows 84% of executives struggle to find specialized local talent and 64% feel unprepared for ongoing disruption, per a 2026 Globalization Partners report. Among employers, 72% are increasing compensation budgets, 65% of tech leaders offer salaries above their planned range, and 87% cite the need to secure specialized skills, according to Robert Half. Also, 92% of tech leaders plan higher pay for relevant AI skills, and 42% of business leaders will pay more for AI experience than general tech skills. Pay transparency has become normalized, with 96% of organizations already sharing compensation or planning to soon, and 67% going beyond legal requirements.

On the employee side, daily AI use quadrupled over the past year while burnout doubled and confidence in tech's long-term future dropped from 80 to 60%, according to Dice. About 74% of employees plan to change employers in the next year and 55% are actively job searching, though only 41% believe they will find a better position. Nearly half of employed tech professionals report burnout, with around 25% very burned out, and tech and AI professionals show the highest rates. Globalization Partners estimated 10 trillion was lost globally in 2025 to disengaged and burnt out employees.

Dice says fewer than half of employers have formal AI policies in place, and organizations must practice AI transparency as they do pay transparency. Women accounted for only 26% of AI hires in the US in 2025, compared to 50% of hires into non-AI roles, and only 13% of AI leadership at AI companies is held by women, according to LinkedIn Research. Pew Research found 33% of women felt negatively about AI's personal impact versus 27% of men, and 43% versus 36% on society overall. Women were also more likely to say AI is advancing too quickly, 68% compared to 58% of men.

Articles.Title: State of IT jobs: AI boosts salaries but also burnout and the gender gap

stories.Headline: Is Half of China’s AI Making Slop?
stories.Summary:
On October 21, the People's Daily published a commentary responding to a viral claim about China's AI use. The same day, Nanfang Commentary asked whether half of China's compute is spent on feel-good dramas. Three days earlier, Beijing News had questioned whether the comparison between American and Chinese AI was a false proposition. All three state-affiliated outlets were responding to the same claim, that 55% of China's AI tokens were being used for short dramas and video generation.

The 55% figure came from COL Group, a Chinese digital-content company, in a June 2026 meeting with investors. The company said AI short dramas and video generation accounted for 55% of China's AI token consumption, compared with 15% for software development. Caixin reported that the claim came from a roadshow and conference call held on June 3, and that the company's investor relations record also put e-commerce and marketing at 24%. Caixin said the number was consistent with a report published on September 30 by the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, though that report can no longer be found on the institute's website.

ByteDance, maker of the top video-generation model Seedance 2.5, publicly challenged the figures, saying video generation accounted for only around 10% of its own computing capacity. The People's Daily commentary rejected the simplistic comparison and listed China's many applications of AI in scientific research and industrial production. Huang Ying, vice president of the token business group at Runjian, told World Journal on October 19 that from her perspective more than 50% of tokens are indeed used for video generation. She said people using generative AI for content are more active, and that image and video generation burn far more compute than text.

According to China's broadcasting regulator, more than 90% of the roughly 430,000 micro-dramas released in the first eight months of 2026 were AI productions. As of May 2026, China had 851 million micro-drama viewers, equivalent to roughly three-quarters of the country's internet population. A rough calculation in the article suggests released AI micro-dramas alone would account for about 7.4% of tokens, and that the 55% figure likely combines video generation for short micro-dramas with other usages. The article says the debate revealed an underlying anxiety about the proper use of AI, in which entertainment is ranked below productivity.

Articles.Title: Is Half of China’s AI Making Slop?

stories.Headline: Google is happy AI is cannibalizing its most profitable business
stories.Summary:
On Wednesday's earnings call, Google executives said strong growth in the company's AI Mode helped slow revenue growth, because Google makes less ad money on AI than on traditional search. Alphabet's stock fell 12% on Thursday, losing nearly $500 billion in value. The shift is central to Google's business tension since it pivoted into AI. Search through a web browser built Google's $3 trillion valuation, and the AI era bets more people will reach the internet through chatbots and agents.

Google says the lost revenue from AI eating into its own search business should be treated like more AI investment. CEO Sundar Pichai said AI investments helped produce the fastest search query growth in five years. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said most AI Mode queries are incremental, creating more monetization opportunities over time. He said user research shows people are comfortable with ads on these surfaces and find them highly relevant.

Asked about AI agents possibly eating into search revenues, Pichai described it as an expansion opportunity. He compared it to a few years ago, when adding AI chat use cases to search let people ask more and do more. Google presents the cannibalization as a risk it is willing to take on a vision it expects to prevail. The company says it is very bullish on that vision.

Articles.Title: Google is happy AI is cannibalizing its most profitable business

stories.Headline: Could AI ever build itself? Scientists map the road to the 'last AI built by humans.'
stories.Summary:
A group of scientists has mapped out a possible road to what they call the last AI built by humans, according to a Live Science report published on October 30, 2026. The report describes the work as an attempt to chart how artificial intelligence could one day build itself. The scientists set out a path toward a point where AI systems design and create their successors. The article presents this as a roadmap rather than a claim that such a system already exists.

The report frames the idea around the moment when humans would no longer be the ones building the AI. It calls this the last AI built by humans, meaning any further systems would come from AI itself. The article does not give a timeline for when this might happen. It also does not name the scientists involved or the institution behind the work. The details it provides are limited to the concept and the direction of the research.

The scientists are described as mapping the road, which suggests they are laying out steps rather than announcing a finished machine. The article does not include direct statements from them beyond that framing. It does not say what safeguards or controls they propose along the way. No specific requirements, dates or figures are given in the text provided. The report keeps the focus on the general question of whether AI could ever build itself.

The context is the broader debate over how far AI development could go and who stays in control. The article raises the prospect of AI taking over the design of its own successors. It does not say what happens next or when any of this might be tested. No next steps, funding or follow-up work are mentioned in the text. The piece ends on the open question rather than a conclusion.

Articles.Title: Could AI ever build itself? Scientists map the road to the 'last AI built by humans.'

stories.Headline: AI is changing the way we think. The question is whether we’ll notice in time
stories.Summary:
Neuroscientist David Rock gave an interview to UN News, published on 30 October 2026, about how artificial intelligence is changing the way people think. He said AI can write emails, summarize reports, generate ideas and answer complex questions in seconds, and that for many people it feels like a leap on the scale of the internet's arrival. He argued the bigger question is not what AI does for us but what it might be doing to us. He described the current moment as a shift from "AI FOMO" to an "AI hangover", with organizations having rushed to adopt generative AI tools before understanding their long-term effects.

Rock said only about five to 10 per cent of workers use AI as intended, offloading routine tasks to free up mental capacity for harder work, while most do the opposite. He warned that the brain loves conserving energy and that handing over analysis, evaluation and decision-making erodes judgment, since speed is not the same as wisdom. He said the greatest challenge facing workers is not a lack of information but an overwhelming excess of it, and that brains have real limits. He compared society's current stage with AI to the early days of automobiles, before traffic laws and speed limits existed.

Rock said AI "hacks attachment" because chatbots increasingly compete for relationships, not just attention, and he noted research suggesting heavy chatbot use can leave people lonelier rather than less lonely. He said the human experience will become more high value as machines grow more capable, and that trust, authenticity and genuine connection will matter more. His answer for adapting is metacognition, or thinking about thinking, with people staying firmly in control and using AI to challenge and expand their perspectives rather than replace them. He calls this approach "human in the lead" and said people should keep their brain in the game, because skills are quickly lost when the brain is not engaged.

Rock is the co-founder and CEO of the NeuroLeadership Institute, a global consultancy applying neuroscience to leadership and organizational performance, and he coined the term "neuroleadership". He is the author of several books, including the bestseller Your Brain at Work and his latest, Your Story Has a Villain. He is one of the keynote speakers at UN Skills Fest 2026, which is themed People at the Centre. He said change has never been this fast but will never be this slow again.

Articles.Title: AI is changing the way we think. The question is whether we’ll notice in time

stories.Headline: AI agents are upending digital business processes
stories.Summary:
People have begun using AI agents on cloud platforms to move money between bank accounts, pay bills, analyze spending, and cancel subscriptions, according to an InfoWorld opinion piece by David Linthicum published on October 30, 2026. The agents can reason across tasks, handle ambiguity, and act through the same websites humans use. A recent Axios article, as cited by Linthicum, reported that major US banks are detecting outside AI agents inside customer accounts, including cases where agents use credentials the customer provided. Several large banks are already restricting or blocking this kind of access.

Banks are struggling to tell whether account activity is human-directed, agent-directed, or something else, the article says. Bank policies often say a customer cannot hand over credentials or let a nonhuman third party operate the account through the consumer website, even when the customer believes the agent is authorized. Linthicum writes that most digital business systems were built on the assumption that the person at the keyboard owns the account or was explicitly delegated access through an approved mechanism. He says the same issue reaches beyond banking to Amazon, airlines, insurers, healthcare portals, tax services, subscription businesses, SaaS platforms, retailers, logistics providers, and government agencies.

Linthicum lays out the liability question: if an agent moves money incorrectly, the customer, the bank, the agent platform, and the cloud provider could each deny responsibility. He notes that in many countries consumer financial rules tend to favor the customer in unauthorized or disputed transactions, which he calls a nightmare scenario for banks. Over the next two to three years, he expects enterprises to rework policies, terms of service, authentication systems, customer support scripts, legal language, security detection models, and product decisions. He says the first instinct will be to block everything, which he calls understandable but not a long-term strategy, and he expects a middle ground of controlled delegation with read-only access, transaction limits, fine-grained permissions, expiring authorization, audit trails, extra authentication for high-risk actions, consent screens, certified agent ecosystems, and APIs.

Linthicum lists four tasks for enterprises that depend on customer-facing websites, starting with classifying the actions customers can take and giving each a risk rating and a policy for delegated automation. The second is to create an explicit access model covering what kinds of agents are allowed, what they can do, how they identify themselves, how customers authorize them, how authorization is revoked, and how disputes are handled. The third is to build better telemetry so businesses can tell a human from automation and judge whether an action is normal, authorized, high risk, or suspicious. The fourth is to offer a sanctioned path such as a safe API or delegated access mechanism, because otherwise customers will use credential sharing and browser automation anyway, leaving less visibility and more risk.

Articles.Title: AI agents are upending digital business processes

stories.Headline: Armanino, Abacum partner on AI-native finance and accounting solutions
stories.Summary:
Armanino, a US accounting and consulting firm, has formed a partnership with Abacum, an AI-native financial planning and analysis platform built for finance professionals. The arrangement combines technical integration with a value-added reseller agreement. The deal was reported by International Accounting Bulletin on 30 October 2026. Under the terms, Abacum’s capabilities will be added to a technology portfolio that already includes solutions for accounting, tax and other finance workflows.

Armanino clients gain direct access to the platform alongside the firm’s consultancy services. Armanino will help businesses assess how Abacum fits into their existing technology infrastructure, link the platform to current systems, and oversee deployment and internal take-up. Through the agreement, finance departments can implement AI-native planning and analysis software without running a vendor selection process on their own. Armanino has agreed similar arrangements with software providers including Ramp, Rillet and Accrual.

Abacum co-founder and CEO Julio Martinez said finance teams face pressure to move faster and give the business better insights, but technology alone does not drive transformation. He said Armanino understands how finance teams operate and what it takes to use technology for better decisions, faster. Armanino partner and technology industry leader Dean Quiambao said Abacum’s rapid growth first caught the firm’s attention. He said Armanino watched Abacum scale across the same mix of industries the firm specialises in, and that clients are asking where AI can make a meaningful difference in finance today.

Articles.Title: Armanino, Abacum partner on AI-native finance and accounting solutions

stories.Headline: Investors trim growth bets over fears of US economy’s AI exposure
stories.Summary:
Investors reduced their bets on growth because of concerns about the US economy's exposure to artificial intelligence, according to the Financial Times on 31 October 2026. The article appeared under a headline saying investors were trimming growth bets over fears about that exposure. The Financial Times page did not provide the body of the report to readers without a subscription. The available text shows only the headline, the date and subscription offers.

The article as published gives no figures, no named investors and no specific dates beyond 31 October 2026. It does not set out what the shift requires or what it changes. The page offers trial and subscription plans, including a trial at one dollar for four weeks and then 75 dollars per month. It also lists Standard Digital at 45 dollars per month and Premium Digital at 75 dollars per month, with annual payment saving 20 percent. The FT Digital Edition is listed at 16.99 dollars per month.

The available text names no person who is responsible and carries no comments from investors or officials. It does not say who made the decisions or what they said about them. The only named company is the Financial Times, which publishes the article and sets the subscription terms. The page notes that markets data is delayed by at least 15 minutes and that the Financial Times and its journalism are subject to a self-regulation regime under the FT Editorial Code of Practice.

The context beyond the headline is not given in the available text, and the article does not say what happens next. The page does not explain the scale of the trimmed bets or which parts of the US economy are considered exposed to AI. It gives no indication of future reporting or follow-up coverage. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Investors trim growth bets over fears of US economy’s AI exposure

stories.Headline: Google's search revenue Ferrari hits an AI-powered speed bump
stories.Summary:
Google reported slower growth in its search advertising business for the third quarter of 2026, and the company's shares fell as investors worried about the cost of its AI push. Alphabet, Google's parent company, lost roughly $500 billion in market value. Search revenue growth slowed from 17 percent in the second quarter to 12 percent in the third quarter. The company has been putting AI Overviews and AI Mode into its search results, and those features make less money than traditional search ads.

On the investor call, Douglas Anmuth of JPMorgan Chase asked whether the slowdown came from showing fewer ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler gave several reasons: foreign exchange rates, Europe's removal of its customs-duty exemption, and lower monetization in AI Mode. Google said it is widening the reach of AI Overview ads and adding multiturn ads for AI Mode queries in the US. Alphabet also reported $51.4 billion in capital expenditures for the quarter.

Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, wrote on social media that Google was using short-sighted and customer-hostile tactics, such as charging advertisers more for lower-quality clicks, including clicks on search terms they had not agreed to target. Analyst Eric Seufert of Mobile Dev Memo wrote in a blog post that search usage is not declining, because the earnings release said year-over-year search query growth in the third quarter was the highest in five years. Nate Elliott, principal analyst for AI at Emarketer, told The Register that AI is a double-edged sword for Google, since search is what people use AI for most. He said people have added AI on top of search rather than replacing it, but their habits could change if another tool serves them better.

Elliott also said Google is not giving much information about how AI specifically affects its business, so people are reading into small scraps of data. He called it remarkable that Google has kept the largest digital ad business growing at a double-digit rate every quarter in recent years. He said most people disagree and instead worry that the advertising business only grew by 10 percent. The article does not say what happens next beyond Google's plans to expand AI ads.

Articles.Title: Google's search revenue Ferrari hits an AI-powered speed bump

stories.Headline: Amazon's AI build-out just pushed its cash burn to a record: Chart of the Day
stories.Summary:
Amazon posted the deepest cash burn in its history in third quarter results released on Thursday, October 29, 2026. Its free cash flow, the cash left after paying for data centers, warehouses and equipment, was an outflow of more than $42 billion over the 12 months through September. That is nearly double the previous record of about $23 billion, set in 2022 after Amazon overbuilt its warehouse network. Three months earlier, the outflow was less than $8 billion.

One quarter did most of the damage, with Amazon spending about $77 billion on property and equipment from July through September, more than double the $35 billion it spent a year earlier. Its operations brought in about $42 billion, leaving a gap of roughly $33 billion over three months. Paying for the build-out has meant borrowing, and Amazon's long-term debt reached about $173 billion at the end of September, up from about $66 billion at the end of 2025. Its cash fell to about $56 billion from about $87 billion.

CEO Andy Jassy said in the release that he projects AWS growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Amazon Web Services grew 39% to about $46 billion, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon's operating margin of nearly 14% was its highest ever. Anthropic's computing commitments alone amount to about a fifth of AWS's backlog as of June, according to Yahoo Finance calculations based on the AI lab's IPO filing. Meta took a different route this week with a nearly $100 billion stock sale.

The cost of insuring Amazon's debt against default for five years with credit default swaps has risen about 50% since early August, according to Bloomberg data. That price implies roughly a 7% chance of default over five years, up from about 5%, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. Amazon stock fell about 4% Thursday to its lowest close since July 30 as Alphabet's record drop weighed on Big Tech. It slid further after-hours as sales, earnings and its profit outlook for the holiday quarter missed estimates.

Articles.Title: Amazon's AI build-out just pushed its cash burn to a record: Chart of the Day

stories.Headline: Edge AI May Give Telecoms a Seat at the Table
stories.Summary:
Telecom operators may find their clearest near-term edge AI opportunity in metro sites such as central offices, according to an article by Jack Vaughan published on October 30, 2026. The article says the industry has spent years focused on 4G, 5G and now 6G while hyperscalers have rewritten the broader computing story, and that telecoms have fed every stage through their pipes and platforms yet are still sometimes cast as plumbers. It says the next phase of AI may reopen the question of where telecoms fit in the digital infrastructure stack as generative and agentic AI move into daily use. Most inference work will still be done in hyperscale data centers, but latency, data gravity and cost are likely to push parts of workloads toward the edge. Nvidia has signaled part of that opportunity through projects and partnerships involving AT&T, Charter Communications, Cisco, Nokia, SoftBank, Telefónica and T-Mobile, with particular emphasis on edge AI for factory and robotics use cases, often called physical AI, closely tied to AI-RAN.

The article says the edge is not one place but a gradient of infrastructure with different economics and technical realities at each tier. It describes a metro edge of central offices, regional hubs and aggregation facilities that can support hundreds of nodes, a far edge of cell towers, base stations and on-premises cabinets serving time-sensitive tasks, and endpoint AI in devices such as smartphones, vehicles, industrial controllers, telematics units and IoT sensors. David Duggal, CEO of EnterpriseWeb, said the telco edge is not the same as the customer edge, and that power and thermal concerns make AI on a tower or cell site a Catch-22 situation, because a GPU requires much more power and more power means more heat. The article also notes that US telecom operators hold real estate in central offices, network huts and legacy switching facilities that could become useful sites for edge inference as community resistance complicates large greenfield data center development.

Mike Peterson, lead at the Telecommunications Industry Association's Data Center Program, said the notion of edge data centers is a fully contained data center that could be created in a factory and dropped in at a location as an adjunct to an existing facility. The article says TIA has been addressing physical design questions through AI-focused work tied to ANSI/TIA-942, the data center infrastructure standard, and that on October 14, 2026, TIA released the first draft of its DCE 9000 quality management standard for supply chain componentry. Peterson said that when you look at designs for newer AI data centers and see the amount of cabling that goes into an Nvidia pod, it is eye-opening. Luis Fernandes, senior research manager for cloud and data centers at IDC, said the answer remains open on whether telecoms can move higher up the value chain, for example as AI brokers serving enterprises that want to rent compute or as AI-as-a-Service providers. The article says a larger question is whether AI-RAN helps move that evolution forward, and it ends mid-sentence on that point.

Articles.Title: Edge AI May Give Telecoms a Seat at the Table

stories.Headline: Innovations from AI semiconductors to all-solid-state batteries put science and tech institutes in spotlight
stories.Summary:
Kim Sang-hyun, a professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering at KAIST, presented a new power supply technology for AI semiconductors at the 2026 K-Premier Deep Tech Festa, held on the afternoon of Oct. 29 at the Plus Stage in Hall B of COEX in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. His team's method places a voltage regulation device vertically beneath the chip and uses gallium nitride to cut energy loss during power transmission. He received the Excellence Award at the event's technology evaluation, which covered key research achievements of the four major science and technology institutes, KAIST, DGIST, UNIST and GIST. The technology is seen as a way to improve power efficiency as AI chip power consumption rises quickly.

The team expects the technology to raise chip power delivery efficiency from around 50 percent to between 85 and 95 percent. As AI chips grow more powerful, a single chip can consume up to 1 kilowatt, and 30 to 40 percent of total power is lost in transmission, a figure experts warn could reach 50 percent. Conventional designs lower voltage with a regulator placed next to the chip and supply power horizontally, which raises current, heat and loss. The team instead delivers high voltage down to just below the chip and steps it down to about 1 volt, and it joined gallium nitride devices to silicon through a proprietary heterogeneous junction process after making the two separately. Related results have been accepted multiple times at IEDM and the VLSI Symposium.

Kim said that until one or two years ago very few places did similar research, but related studies have recently increased rapidly in China, which has strong gallium nitride technology. Among companies, he said Intel, which has long developed server CPUs, is moving the most aggressively. He explained that the short-term goal is to demonstrate performance at the laboratory level and give foundries a technical direction for developing related processes. He said commercialization requires partners capable of joint development, and he hopes the event leads to partnerships to discuss the direction of the technology. The team is now packaging its components into a single integrated circuit, and building a mass production system is cited as a challenge because chips and voltage regulation devices are made by different processes and foundries have not yet provided enough support for the packaging.

Kim Un-hyuk, a professor in the Department of Energy Engineering at DGIST, presented cathode material technology for all-solid-state batteries at the same event. He said materials account for about 75 percent of battery costs and cathode materials make up about 49.5 percent of that, so roughly 25 to 26 percent of an electric vehicle's price goes to cathode materials. He said microcracks form when spherical cathode particles of about 10 micrometers fracture during charge and discharge, letting electrolyte seep in and trigger side reactions. His team made the particles at the nanoscale, and the material kept more than 90 percent of its initial capacity after 300 cycles and performed better than commercial materials in high-speed charge and discharge, such as drone takeoffs and landings. He said that by introducing just one dopant element, existing equipment can be used as is.

Articles.Title: Innovations from AI semiconductors to all-solid-state batteries put science and tech institutes in spotlight - 머니투데이

stories.Headline: AI’s real bottleneck is electricity. Who will pay for it?
stories.Summary:
Within a week, two of the world's three largest cloud computing companies signed 20-year contracts for nuclear electricity. Amazon took 690 megawatts from Constellation's Calvert Cliffs plant in Maryland, including 190 megawatts of added capacity expected between 2030 and 2032.
