Google signed an agreement bringing 890 megawatts of additional nuclear capacity into the United States. Constellation is investing more than $4.3bn to upgrade 11 reactors across Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Neither deal involves building a new reactor, and both pay for more output from reactors that already exist.

The US Department of Energy is providing up to $4.4bn in loans to restart three shuttered plants, aiming to restore about 2.25 gigawatts. Palisades in Michigan, closed in 2022, is contracted to generate again by March 2027 and would be the first US commercial nuclear plant to restart after decommissioning. The International Energy Agency estimates global data centre electricity demand will more than double to around 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, even with continued efficiency gains. Most of these deals sit inside PJM, which serves roughly 67 million people across 13 states and Washington, DC, and passes capacity auction costs to consumers. Capacity prices hit the regulatory cap in three consecutive auctions, and PJM's independent market monitor attributed about $29.4bn in capacity costs across the four most recent auctions to data centre demand.

The Natural Resources Defense Council estimates the typical PJM household could face an additional $70 per month by 2028 if current trends continue. Virginia has created a separate electricity rate class for data centres, Ohio has introduced minimum billing requirements, and Illinois is debating legislation. In October 2026, US federal regulators rejected most of PJM's proposal to require large new consumers to provide their own generation capacity. The article says the Google agreement aims to answer objections by having major new consumers bring additional generation rather than compete for constrained supply, but the arrangement remains voluntary.

Qatar's sovereign fund has committed to a $20bn joint venture with Brookfield for AI infrastructure, starting at roughly 300 megawatts and potentially reaching near 1.5 gigawatts. Abu Dhabi is pursuing up to five gigawatts of AI data centre capacity, and Saudi Arabia is targeting almost two gigawatts through HUMAIN. The article says a completed 1.5-gigawatt build-out in Qatar would equal about 12 percent of the country's installed generating capacity. It says the Gulf can settle first what the industrial tariff is, who funds new generation, what happens to contracts when hardware ages, and what long-term benefits follow beyond energy revenues and limited jobs.

Articles.Title: AI’s real bottleneck is electricity. Who will pay for it? - Al Jazeera

stories.Headline: A Look at AI, a Lens on Aging
stories.Summary:
Belfast Senior College will hold two free public events on Nov. 9 and Nov. 10, pairing a technology talk with the world premiere of a locally made film. The first event, “First Look at AI,” will be presented by Doug Chamberlin on Monday, Nov. 9, from 4 to 5:30 p.m. in the Abbott Room at the Belfast Free Library. The talk is co-sponsored by the library and will examine artificial intelligence from the average person’s perspective. It will address what AI is, how people can use it and how they can protect themselves from its risks.

Chamberlin will also consider whether AI is as dangerous as some suggest, drawing on four decades of technology experience. During his career as a software developer, systems analyst and database designer, he saw technology deployed both appropriately and in ways that missed the mark. He now assists Belfast Senior College with technical challenges and teaches technology courses. Registration for the library presentation is encouraged but not required at belfastseniorcollege.org/events.

The following day, “Growing Old Together in Belfast” will have its world premiere at noon Tuesday, Nov. 10, at the Colonial Theatre. The film was written and directed by Jeff Edwards and grew out of his Belfast Senior College class, “An Experiment in Creating a Movie,” with technical support from Belfast Community Media. It follows eight characters coming to terms with aging, told as a whimsical tale with a hopeful view of transformation and connection in later life. The cast includes Jeff Edwards, Sarah Edwards, George Frangoulis, Kristin Frangoulis, Lisa Kushner, Ned Lightner, Tycelia Santoro, Linda Garson Smith and Joanna Young.

Ned Lightner, Alex Chaplin and Anne Sezak provided technical support, and Andrew Elijah Edwards edited the film. Music by Belfast-based artists Elsie Gawler and Ethan Stokes Tischler is featured throughout the production. The film runs one hour and 19 minutes, and admission is free, but seating is limited to 120. Reservations are optional and may be made at colonialtheatre.com. Together the events reflect Belfast Senior College’s emphasis on practical learning, creativity and community, and both November events are open to the public at no charge.

Articles.Title: A Look at AI, a Lens on Aging

stories.Headline: Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth
stories.Summary:
Google on Friday celebrated receiving a poem from its first experimental orbital AI datacenter satellite. The company's Suncatcher satellite was launched at the start of the month and put into low Earth orbit. It responded to a ground station prompt asking for a haiku from the perspective of a TPU orbiting Earth, with the world spinning beneath it. Travis Beals, senior director of Google's interdisciplinary Paradigms of Intelligence research team, said the onboard Gemma 4 model achieved its "Hello World" milestone by sending an inference response from orbit. The satellite sent its reply as it passed over Svalbard, Norway, and the roughly 20 tokens would cost about $0.000012 through the Google Cloud API, based on Gemma 4 26B's pricing of $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens, excluding input costs.

Google's calculations suggest that if launch costs fall to $200/kg, the amortized launch cost of about $810 to $7,500/kW/year could be comparable to current US terrestrial datacenter electricity spending of about $570 to $3,000/kW/year. Google predicts SpaceX could reach that by 2035, more or less, and considers it strategically beneficial to prototype well in advance. Laboratory testing of the Trillium Cloud TPU and AMD host server showed high-bandwidth memory is the most sensitive part, showing irregularities after a cumulative dose of 2 krad(Si), about 3× Google's minimum requirement of 750 rad(Si). Beals said that after the haiku, the team tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the technical status of the payload systems. Google researchers said that for typical transformer workloads, the observed silent data corruption rate of about one event per 17 rad, at an estimated orbital dose of 150 rad(Si)/year, translates to a very low failure probability on the order of one per 3 million inferences, assuming one inference per second.

They added that while this error rate is likely acceptable for inference, the impact of single event effects on training jobs and the efficacy of system-level mitigations requires further study. Next up are tests for evaluating how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation. Next year, the plan is to test a pair of interconnected satellites. Rather than lofting large satellites into orbit, Google anticipates sending a constellation of many smaller satellites that communicate with one another.

Articles.Title: Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth

stories.Headline: Fayetteville School Board members review potential updated AI policy at October board meeting - Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
stories.Summary:
Fayetteville School Board members got their first look at a proposed updated artificial intelligence policy at their October meeting, held Thursday night. The draft was introduced as new business, so no vote was taken. The board will be asked to review the policy again at its November meeting, when approval or denial will be considered. District leaders spent the past year drafting an AI policy that the board had previously adopted.

The policy is meant to ensure safe and responsible use of AI, encourage innovation in teaching and support efficient operations, with clear expectations for how the technology is used. Act 848, passed in 2025, requires all Arkansas public entities to set policies and training requirements for employees who use AI and automated decision tools. The draft merges the district's own policy with a longer policy from the state Department of Elementary and Secondary Education that districts were required to adopt. It also covers privacy, saying confidential student or personnel data cannot be entered into public or unapproved AI tools, and that those tools cannot be the only basis for decisions that significantly affect students, such as grades.

Claire Wilkinson, the district's general counsel, told the board the goal was to combine the required state policy with the one custom made for the district. She said she still has questions about the state's policy, particularly around requirements for contracts with companies that provide AI software. She noted the Arkansas School Boards Association is working on its own model policy that the district could use for guidance. Wilkinson also acknowledged the district is in uncharted territory and said board members will likely have questions before the policy is put in place.

The draft says AI must support student learning and not replace instruction, and that software must not limit students' ability to complete assignments. Any chosen program must let teachers disable AI features for specific assignments, include moderation to detect unsafe interactions and block inappropriate content. It also says tools must limit unnecessarily human-like behavior, avoid personal or emotional relationships with students and not use manipulative practices to encourage excessive use. The articles cite research on children's AI use and lawsuits against OpenAI over alleged harm, and note that public entities are left to write their own rules to protect students while exploring how the tools can help.

Articles.Title: Fayetteville School Board members review potential updated AI policy at October board meeting - Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette

stories.Headline: Aera bets on decision governance, not just AI
stories.Summary:
Aera Technology used its AeraHUB NY event this week to launch six innovations and give an update on its decision-intelligence solution. CEO Fred Laluyaux used the event to stress the need for governance and controls. The six announcements strengthen the company's position in the AI decision-making market. Each one adds more control, lets users develop new skills and gives them access to their AI of choice.

Laluyaux said effective use of AI needs more than basic automation and requires a complete rethink of how businesses operate. He said the answer is to move from personal productivity to enterprise productivity. He said Aera saves two and a half hours per information worker, about two weeks a year, but the workload is growing faster, so the impact on the bottom line is not necessarily visible. He said the answer is to leverage AI's reasoning power to solve problems. The company's Decision Cloud uses a Decision Data Model to pull data from across the enterprise, bringing in business rules, optimisation, simulation and machine learning, and orchestrating agents.

Laluyaux said Aera can build intelligent skills that learn, and that it is building and maintaining the skill. Shariq Mansoor, Co-Founder and CTO, framed it as ownership, saying every skill becomes another digital asset they own. Jeremy D'Hoinne, Vice President Analyst at Gartner, said these shadow AI agents take multiple forms, including embedded in existing enterprise software, consumed directly from the Internet or created by employees using recent technological progress and "vibe coding" to improve productivity. Laluyaux said intelligence without memory is not intelligence, and asked where the memory of all the decisions made every day is, saying the answer is usually in our heads and that is fundamentally the problem.

Policy Studio lets users upload a policy document that Aera uses to draft machine-readable rules, and Aera says these are not applied without human review. Laluyaux said organisations struggle to know where their policies are, which documents carry them, which systems are impacted and whether there are conflicts between the rules. He said when a policy change is wanted, people write a memo and send emails and hope it is all good, which is a problem at the scale of a large enterprise across 100 or more countries. The Decision Ledger records context, reasoning, policies evaluated, actions and outcomes for decisions made inside Aera or submitted from other systems through its APIs. The EU AI Act is now being implemented and enforced, with provisions such as traceability and governance in force in 2026, other provisions for high-risk systems from December 2027, and embedded systems in August 2028.

Aera is connecting to Microsoft Copilot Studio and other sources, will connect external agents using the Agent2Agent protocol, and will use its own Model Context Protocol server to integrate other external tools. The new Dynamic UX allows users to build their own environments using natural-language prompts and publish them as a skill. Command Center provides visibility into decision-making across the enterprise and lets teams see performance and business impact across their decisions. Laluyaux pointed to Gartner, which forecasts that 50% of business decisions will be augmented or automated by AI agents within the next 15 months, and that a quarter of digital officers will shift from a data-driven to a decision-centric model by 2028.

Articles.Title: Aera bets on decision governance, not just AI - - Enterprise Times

stories.Headline: DARPA Backs Project to Measure AI Energy Use at Every Stage of the Workflow
stories.Summary:
DARPA will put $1.83 million over two years into a project called E-CALC, which stands for Energy Calculus for ML Lifecycle Optimization. The work is led by Michigan Engineering, working with the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and the defense contractor BAE Systems. The goal is to estimate how much energy artificial intelligence uses at every stage of a workflow, from data processing and model training to real-world deployment. Michigan Engineering says misalignments between software and hardware can waste up to 30% of the electricity used in AI model training alone. The project is funded by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.

The backdrop is that researchers still cannot say precisely how much energy AI uses today. The International Energy Agency forecasts that data center power use will more than double by 2030 from its 2024 level, which was about 420 terawatt-hours. The new system is meant to let developers estimate energy usage without relying on expensive, time-consuming trial-and-error testing across thousands of hardware and software configurations. Michigan Engineering says more energy-efficient AI would bring down electricity demand, cut the cost of AI and extend battery life for AI-enabled devices. The technology could matter especially in military and defense settings, where field equipment and remote computing systems must run complex AI algorithms under strict battery and power limits.

Mosharaf Chowdhury, a University of Michigan associate professor of computer science and engineering and the principal investigator for E-CALC, said AI is becoming part of everyday life, business, science and national security but requires enormous and rapidly growing amounts of electricity. He said that if that energy use continues to rise unchecked, it could increase costs, strain power infrastructure and make advanced AI harder to deploy. He described the project as tackling a practical question, which is how to get widespread benefits of AI with minimum energy. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the two years of DARPA funding.

Articles.Title: DARPA Backs Project to Measure AI Energy Use at Every Stage of the Workflow

stories.Headline: Agentic AI for Immune-Related Adverse Event Detection in Cancer Immunotherapy
stories.Summary:
A study published in Nature Cancer on October 31, 2026, led by Jack Gallifant and colleagues, developed an agentic artificial intelligence system to detect immune-related adverse events in cancer immunotherapy. The system used large language models to extract from clinical notes whether an irAE was documented, whether it was current or historical, its severity grade, its attribution to checkpoint inhibitor therapy, and the clinician's certainty about that attribution. It was tested in three phases: retrospective testing on 289 expert-annotated notes, prospective silent deployment, and a randomized study of AI-assisted human review. The best performance came from GPT-4.1-mini within the agentic architecture.

The retrospective test set had 263 held-out notes after 26 were used for development. The system reached a temporality-agnostic macro-averaged F1 of 0.93 for note-level detection, with 0.92 for current events and 0.91 for past events. Exact multiclass CTCAE grading was harder, with an overall macro F1 of 0.66 for current events, highest for dermatitis at 0.73 and thyroiditis at 0.72, and lowest for colitis at 0.51. Removing the three-run self-consistency step dropped detection F1 from 0.92 to 0.78, while cost rose from about US$0.011 to US$0.021 per note. A rule-based system with 779 terms performed reasonably for simple binary detection but could not extract severity, attribution, certainty, or supporting evidence.

In the prospective phase, the system ran silently for three months between May and July 2025, evaluating 884 clinical notes and generating 31,824 label adjudications. Performance fell: binary F1 was 0.72 for current events and 0.79 for past events, and note-level predictions matched human review in 62% of cases for grade, 87% for attribution, and 83% for certainty. The authors attributed the decline to a broader case mix and evolving EHR templates, terminology, and documentation practices, and argued that clinical AI systems need continuous monitoring and periodic recalibration rather than one-time validation. The randomized 2 × 2 crossover study compared manual annotation with AI-assisted review, with 17 participants, 16 clinical research coordinators and one clinical research nurse, producing 316 evaluable timing observations.

The authors note that irAEs affect up to 40% of patients receiving checkpoint inhibitors and can involve almost any organ system, with myocarditis and pneumonitis among the potentially life-threatening events. Much of the evidence needed to identify these toxicities sits in free-text notes rather than structured EHR fields, and even ICD codes have limited sensitivity for hospitalization-associated events. The system covered six toxicities: pneumonitis, hepatitis, colitis, myocarditis, thyroiditis, and dermatitis. The study raises the question of whether AI can improve immune-toxicity surveillance without replacing the clinical judgment needed to interpret complex adverse events.

Articles.Title: Agentic AI for Immune-Related Adverse Event Detection in Cancer Immunotherapy

stories.Headline: Wikimedia Foundation Seeks to File Amicus Brief in OpenAI Copyright Case
stories.Summary:
The Wikimedia Foundation announced on October 30, 2026, that it has asked the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York for leave to file a friend-of-the-court brief in In re: OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation. That case consolidates 12 lawsuits against OpenAI, and its best-known member is The New York Times’ case against OpenAI and Microsoft. The Foundation’s filing is dated October 29, 2026, and is addressed to Judge Sidney H. Stein. It is a letter motion for leave to file, with the proposed brief attached as an exhibit and styled as supporting neither party.

The motion was submitted under the court’s local rules and an August 7, 2026 order governing amicus participation, as modified on September 24, 2026. Because that order directs prospective amici to move for leave, Wikimedia did not seek the parties’ consent. The proposed brief contains 5,831 words, within the 6,000-word limit the court set for amicus briefs. Rhett O. Millsaps II of Lex Lumina LLP is counsel of record, alongside the Foundation’s General Counsel Stephen LaPorte, Associate General Counsel Jacob Rogers, and Legal Counsel Aly Marino.

The brief argues that each distinct use of copied works across the stages of developing and operating a chatbot requires its own four-factor fair-use analysis, grounded in the Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts v. Goldsmith. It contends that scraping is acquisition rather than a copyright use, and that only what is done with the copies afterward should undergo fair-use analysis. On pre-training, the brief argues the use is likely fair, and it asks the court to rule that the pre-training of ChatGPT’s general-purpose model was fair use. It argues that retrieval-augmented generation likely fails the four-factor test and that OpenAI’s use of copies in that feature is not fair and must abide by licenses such as the Creative Commons license for Wikimedia Project content.

CEO Bernadette Meehan said the Foundation is taking a position to defend the free and open human knowledge that Wikipedia depends on. General Counsel Stephen LaPorte said the fair-use conversation cannot be limited to for-profit organizations, adding that a ruling that does not apply fair use principles carefully could threaten the sustainability of free knowledge and stifle open-source technologies. The Foundation said scraping of its projects must respect its public API rate limits or go through its Wikimedia Enterprise API offerings. It also said machine-learning tools already help volunteers fight vandalism, detect copyright violations and inappropriate personal information, and prioritize articles most in need of improvement.

Wikipedia holds more than 67 million articles across 300 languages, with nearly 250,000 volunteers contributing each month, and the Foundation describes it as one of the highest-quality datasets used to train LLMs. The brief states that more than 260,000 volunteer contributors per month, as of January 2025, create and moderate content across the Foundation’s thirteen free-knowledge platforms. Docket entries show that on October 28 and 29, 2026, Engine Advocacy, the Authors Alliance, Public Knowledge, Professor Matthew Sag, Brian L. Frye, Digital Content Next, and a group of publishing organizations including the Association of American Publishers moved to file their own amicus briefs. Summary-judgment briefing between the news publishers, OpenAI, and Microsoft continued, and Judge Stein must grant the Foundation leave before its proposed brief is formally accepted.

Articles.Title: Wikimedia Foundation Seeks to File Amicus Brief in OpenAI Copyright Case - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: The AI trade's trick-or-treat earnings season
stories.Summary:
The latest earnings reports from big tech companies unsettled Wall Street, as the results offered conflicting signals about the AI boom. The tech-heavy Nasdaq briefly fell into correction territory, dropping 10% from its prior peak and losing $1.2 trillion in value during October. The declines followed a series of earnings reports that highlighted major risks in the AI trade. Investors found evidence in the same reports to support both optimistic and pessimistic views.

Google lost more than $500 billion in market value after its earnings, as AI overviews eat into ad revenue from search. Search queries are up, but results in AI mode carry lower margins. On the other hand, Google Cloud is closing in on Microsoft's Azure cloud revenue, a striking change for a company that was an also-ran in cloud a few years ago. Much of that success is tied to demand for Google's TPU chips, which analysts expect to grow sharply in coming quarters.

Microsoft and Amazon both posted explosive cloud growth, though the market was disappointed Amazon's was not higher. Amazon's net income fell even as operating profits soared, because it did not repeat the pretax gain from its Anthropic investment that had boosted earnings a year earlier. Microsoft's OpenAI investment lifted its net income slightly and raised its profit growth. Some asset-light tech companies have turned free cash flow negative to fund AI ambitions, saying demand is outstripping supply.

Jeetu Patel, President and Chief Product Officer at Cisco, told Axios he is bullish but said a major cyber event hitting the core of AI demand could be a downside risk. DeepWater partner Gene Munster said the street is waking up to the risks of an agentic world, asking how Google makes money without ad search revenue and how Amazon makes money if shoppers use bots. Tech stocks are broadly under pressure following these results. Those existential questions are not stopping the AI capex spending spree, for now.

Articles.Title: The AI trade's trick-or-treat earnings season

stories.Headline: The $10 trillion AI buildout so far isn't stopping
stories.Summary:
A powerful backlash against AI and data centers has been building for months, and it has fueled local moratoriums and political opposition. The pushback has also raised fears that the $10 trillion infrastructure buildout could hit a wall. Despite more than 300 local moratoriums, U.S. data center development is moving at a blistering pace. The industry may add more than 50 gigawatts of capacity in 2027, according to research firm SemiAnalysis.

Construction on nearly half of that capacity is already at an advanced stage, and developers have signed $1 trillion in leases to support the expansion, SemiAnalysis says. The buildout is far from friction-free, and political, regulatory, supply and environmental hurdles are delaying some major projects. In New Mexico, Oracle took steps to protect itself from steep costs tied to delays of the $165 billion Project Jupiter stemming from local opposition, permitting roadblocks and power supply challenges. In Texas, an audit ordered by Gov. Greg Abbott is adding months of delays for projects seeking to connect to the state's electric grid. In New York, an executive order pausing environmental permits for larger facilities has delayed nearly 1 gigawatt of capacity, according to SemiAnalysis.

Local opposition and mounting regulatory scrutiny are creating isolated bottlenecks, but they have yet to derail the broader infrastructure boom. The stakes extend far beyond the U.S., and any backlash that slows the AI boom could have global consequences. The futures of politicians, economies and nations are increasingly tied to the race for technological supremacy. The midterm elections will offer an early test of whether growing voter resistance could become a more formidable obstacle.

Articles.Title: The $10 trillion AI buildout so far isn't stopping

stories.Headline: Microsoft’s big buyout, Amazon’s trillion-dollar future, and an AI wearable reviews our show
stories.Summary:
Microsoft is offering buyouts to about 60,000 employees, about a quarter of its workforce, including some executives. The offer was reported by GeekWire in an episode published on October 31, 2026. Unlike the retirement program Microsoft offered in the spring, this one has no age or tenure requirement. Business leaders decide whether their groups take part. The buyout comes as Microsoft reports a blockbuster quarter, including $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI, more than the company made from Xbox or Bing.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy predicts that AWS and Amazon’s stores business could each reach $1 trillion in annual revenue in the next five to 10 years. AWS grew 39% in the third quarter, its fastest pace in nearly five years. Amazon’s profit fell short of expectations as the cost of its AI buildout and growing debt cut into earnings. On the GeekWire Podcast, Todd Bishop and John Cook discuss what is behind the offer and why buyout stories draw so much interest from readers. Todd also tests Amazon’s new Bee AI wearable, which listens to the first part of the show, summarizes the conversation and offers a critique of its own.

The hosts talk about what it is like to wear a device that records the people around you, a concern raised by a former AWS security engineer. John starts to come around on the device, with reservations about its shopping features. The episode also includes the hosts’ Halloween costumes and a Trivia Challenge inspired by T-Mobile’s new T-Mix plans. The show was edited by Curt Milton, with music by Daniel L.K. Caldwell. Listeners are directed to listen above and subscribe in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever they listen.

Articles.Title: Microsoft’s big buyout, Amazon’s trillion-dollar future, and an AI wearable reviews our show

stories.Headline: Who pays for the AI power boom?
stories.Summary:
Data centers are currently paying for the electricity they consume and generally must cover the costs of connecting to the grid, according to Axios. The rules get murkier when it comes to building new power plants and upgrading the broader electric system. Those costs can be spread among customers, potentially raising household electricity bills. Under longstanding federal rules, data centers and other large power users generally do not have to pay both for their share of the existing grid and the new transmission infrastructure built to serve them.

More than half of states have taken or considered steps to protect residential customers, including special electricity rates and requirements that data centers pay for infrastructure built on their behalf. The issue is surfacing in key midterm races, with candidates in both parties calling for stronger protections against higher power bills. Congress is considering bipartisan legislation that would require large data centers to cover more infrastructure costs, even if projects are canceled. Who ultimately pays depends on where a data center is built, how its utility charges customers and whether new protections take effect.

Policymakers increasingly want technology companies, not everyday electricity customers, to shoulder more of the costs of the AI-driven buildout of electricity infrastructure, Axios reports. Decisions being made now about who pays for new power infrastructure could affect Americans' electricity bills for years to come. Data centers are becoming a major political issue as costs climb and communities push back against paying for the industry's expansion. The article does not say what happens next beyond the pending legislation and the state actions already taken or considered.

Articles.Title: Who pays for the AI power boom?

stories.Headline: Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims
stories.Summary:
Cisco Talos researchers have found a new strain of infostealer malware that adds AI analysis to its theft, according to research shared exclusively with WIRED's Kernel Panic newsletter. The malware calls itself Volta-Autodoxer internally, and the researchers flagged it using their new CAIRN framework, which is built to identify hacking tools that use AI. Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild. The finding shows how commercial LLMs are being used to enhance established types of malware.

Infostealers hide in counterfeit software and grab usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, credit card data and more from infected machines. Volta sweeps for passwords stored in browsers, Microsoft OAuth tokens, cookies, payment cards and crypto wallet seed phrases, and also for active Discord, Telegram, Steam and Roblox sessions. It then does a deeper second sweep, using a target's Gmail or another central account to build a picture of the victim, their location and habits, including receipts and order history from services such as UberEats and DoorDash. It feeds the results to AI tools through OpenRouter, defaulting to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, with fallbacks to Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and then Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash in case guardrails block the requests. Its creators included a 240-word prompt telling the model to act as a forensic intelligence analyst and produce a structured, citation-backed assessment of the victim, covering an executive summary, what the person does, what they are worth and their opsec.

Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos, said Volta is mature as a stealer and casts a wide net for what it collects, compiling everything into a serialized dossier for the models. He said the prompt is carefully crafted not to imply anything overtly malicious, and that the creators built in the expectation of model refusals, planning failover to more permissible models down the chain. He added that the implant still works without the AI, and that the AI calls are above and beyond. He also said Volta contains clues it may have been built to sell to a range of attackers rather than for one actor's campaigns.

Fetterman said that identifying high-value targets faster probably gives attackers a better chance of using stolen credentials or tokens before they expire or passwords are changed. He said more advanced capabilities are becoming accessible to lower-level attackers, which he called interesting and disturbing. Researchers at Crowdstrike recently told WIRED they had seen four distinct hacking groups, operating in Chinese, Spanish and English, Indonesian, and Russian, use AI tools to compromise dozens of targets around the world, including government entities and businesses in health care, retail and travel. The article says the AI expansion foreshadows more invasive and sinister activity in the future.

Articles.Title: Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims

stories.Headline: Why unions are split over AI as data centers take off
stories.Summary:
Unions are divided over artificial intelligence and data centers, according to an Axios report published on October 31, 2026 by Nathan Bomey. Trade unions like the electrical workers and plumbers like the construction work that data centers bring. Other groups, including the Teamsters, want policies that restrict AI because it might replace jobs. The split has complicated labor's political alliances as both parties court union voters.

Trade unions have formed a new partnership with OpenAI and the real estate and financial firm Blackstone to fight moratoriums on data center construction. The AFL-CIO is pushing state legislatures to adopt restrictions on AI, including rules to prevent it from surveilling workers and making health care decisions without human oversight. Teamsters president Sean O'Brien is leading a charge to keep robotaxis and autonomous trucks off the streets unless they have a safety operator. The report gives no specific dates, vote counts or other numbers beyond the October 31, 2026 publication date.

Arthur Wheaton, director of labor studies at the Cornell ILR Buffalo Co-Lab, said it has always been a misnomer that labor must agree on everything, and that when one union loses another might gain. He said many unions will support technology if there is training for it and it does not replace jobs, but they want nothing to do with it if it replaces people. UAW president Shawn Fain criticized what he called a corporate narrative that technology should reduce jobs and make more profits, saying it does not have to be that way. Teamsters vice president at-large Peter Finn said labor has a duty to shape how AI is rolled out so it puts people first, and he criticized robotaxis as designed to get rid of the driver. Aurora CEO Chris Urmson told Axios that trucking is a very dangerous job with many health issues and that the Teamsters' effort to thwart self-driving vehicles is misguided.

The report says the advent of self-driving vehicles is a major flashpoint, pitting the Teamsters against Tesla, Waymo, Zoox and the self-driving truck startup Aurora. Autonomous-driving companies argue that too many people die or are injured in vehicle accidents to justify keeping human drivers once the technology is safer. Wheaton said labor is not one identifiable thing and has no single voice. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Why unions are split over AI as data centers take off

stories.Headline: The AI boom's political reckoning
stories.Summary:
Opposition to AI data centers became a defining issue in the 2026 midterm elections, with data centers serving as a target for public anger. Voters in 10 states will decide on 41 data center ballot measures on Election Day, ranging from new requirements for developers to outright bans on construction. All six data center measures already decided this year, in New Hampshire, Wisconsin, Michigan and California, went against development, according to Ballotpedia. In Texas, incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott reversed course after years of courting the industry, halting new approvals pending an audit of projects after a backlash in rural communities. Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa supports a moratorium on new data centers until tougher rules are established.

In Utah, a coalition of state leaders, local residents and environmental groups opposed a data center project backed by Kevin O'Leary. In Ohio, incumbent Sen. Jon Husted is on the defensive over past support for data centers in a race that could help decide Senate control, and the state has 21 data center-related measures on the ballot Tuesday. Local activists galvanized by data center fights are running for office across the country. President Trump declared at a rally in Ohio that "we want them," forcing the Husted campaign to distance itself from his remarks. Trump said data centers were designed in a "very beautiful way" and called them a "Golden Goose" for the U.S. economy.

Tatishe Nteta, a political science professor at UMass Amherst and director of the UMass Poll, said the backlash reflects tech giants and AI becoming an easy target, and that the country is close to the largest wealth gap in its history. He called it a failure of marketing on the part of the AI companies themselves and said they need to make a clearer, stronger case for why there are benefits for communities. Trump has praised Mark Zuckerberg for Meta's financial contributions to local communities, including $50,000 bonuses for teachers in Louisiana. Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy has called on companies to provide free electricity to residents living near data centers.

Many communities are skeptical of promises of economic revitalization after watching factories open and later abandon their towns and jobs materialize and then disappear, and residents face nondisclosure agreements that limit transparency around new projects. Some companies such as Microsoft have decided to end data center NDAs with local governments, but these efforts could be viewed as the result of public pressure and may be coming a little too late. Candidates caught flat-footed may survive the 2026 midterms with the right talking points, but as the AI industry's infrastructure demands soar and the economic stakes grow with record-breaking IPOs, messaging alone won't cut it. Politicians will increasingly be forced to stake out concrete policy positions and decide whose interests come first.

Articles.Title: The AI boom's political reckoning

stories.Headline: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
stories.Summary:
A new Windows infostealer called VOLTA-AUTODOXER was surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, according to a Cisco Talos blog published on October 31, 2026. The malware is self-deleting and has no attacker-owned infrastructure, with all observed endpoints controlled by third parties. After stealing data, it sends a structured evidence bundle to a large language model to rank the victim's assets by monetization value. If a model refuses, it fails over to a chain of up to three models.

The stealer harvests browser passwords, cookies, payment cards, cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases, Discord, Telegram, Steam and Roblox sessions, Microsoft OAuth tokens, SSH and cloud-provider keys, Wi-Fi profiles and screenshots. It builds a bundle containing geolocation, home address, employer, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen sessions to search Gmail for purchase receipts, pull UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enrich Discord accounts. The bundle is POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt asking the model to act as a forensic intelligence analyst, with output sections titled "WHAT THEY'RE WORTH" and "THEIR OPSEC."

The prompt tells the model to go deep, not wide, and to be blunt, specific and accurate. A hardcoded temperature of 0.2 suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency, and the fallback chain runs from Claude to kimi-k2 and then gemini-2.5-flash. The blog says the multi-model design suggests the operator anticipates refusals and pivots to smaller, more permissive models. The system prompt asks for a concise assessment of the victim's suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations, and encourages connections between sparse data such as names, addresses or universities and patterns in passwords.

Collected data is assembled locally in a file called Identity_Report.txt, serialized as JSON and sent to OpenRouter, with the reply received as AI_Analysis.txt. Both files exfiltrate together in volta_dox.zip, and exfiltration can happen in three stages: volta_log.zip after the stealer runs, volta_dox.zip after the AI call, and volta_doxnet.zip if network enrichment produces anything. The inference round-trip happens through the victim's own network connection on their own machine before the result is exfiltrated. VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots filled in at build time, which the blog says suggests a builder model where the author sells access and compiles a custom binary for each customer.

Much of the token-stealing relies on bypassing App-Bound Encryption in Chrome, and an application control policy restricting which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block that decryption path. Users should try to preserve the APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt file, a timestamped harvest log recording what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Compromised tokens should be revoked and passwords changed, and a wallet whose seed phrase was in plaintext on disk should be treated as fully compromised, with funds moved to a new wallet generated on an air-gapped device. The blog says the question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere but which phase it touches next, and that refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement as AI integration in malware matures.

Articles.Title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer

stories.Headline: Azeem Azhar on the Explosion of Hacking and Other AI Issues
stories.Summary:
Azeem Azhar, a writer, researcher and investor with Exponential View, spoke with Paul Krugman about a PHP hack and the wider spread of AI-driven hacking. Azhar said AI models have become good enough to be used in code and directed to find vulnerabilities and bugs in software. Because AI systems are tireless and can be spun up in large numbers, they can find many vulnerabilities quickly and chain them together. He called the PHP hack a "Wuhan moment," comparing it to an infectious disease that has a much bigger impact than others circulating.

PHP is a programming language that 70% of websites run on, Azhar said. It was easy to use and cheap, and it got extended and extended, and Facebook used it a lot, so it became part of the internet's architecture. He said AI models crossed a threshold at the start of this year when Anthropic had a model called Claude Mythos, which he called the best cybersecurity model in the world. It was not made widely available, and only a small number of organizations got access to it. Over the summer, open-weight models started to approach Mythos's capabilities, and there has been a rapid increase in the number of vulnerabilities being discovered.

Azhar said the bad guys move more quickly in general, because they only have to find one vulnerability at one place, while the good guys have to defend every vulnerability all the time. He said the Deputy Chief Information Security Officer at Anthropic said it is going to be quite a rough 18 months. He said there are billions of computers connected to the internet and trillions of lines of code and systems that have not been updated for years. He said things can spread faster than we can figure out what to do about them, as happened with the virus first called 2019-nCoV before it was called SARS-CoV-2.

Azhar said many people already spend a lot of time in walled gardens, and he expects the number of AI agents to rapidly exceed the number of humans. He said the amount of browsing done by bots is now higher than by humans, and that will tilt enormously toward machines over the coming few years. He likened the change to Fifth Avenue in 1895, when more people strolled in the middle of the street than there were automobiles, but by 1920 people did not stroll down the middle of the street. He said the internet would need to start to filter out what AI systems need, because they move in milliseconds and have completely different technical requirements. He said people who want to be really secure might choose to stay in a safe enclave, and he gave Apple's App Store as an example.

Articles.Title: Azeem Azhar on the Explosion of Hacking and Other AI Issues

stories.Headline: Avenged Sevenfold’s Zacky Vengeance Defends AI Art, Calls Majority of Designers He’s Worked With "Lazy"
stories.Summary:
Avenged Sevenfold guitarist and vocalist Zacky Vengeance defended the band's use of artwork that some fans believe was AI-generated, according to Metal Injection. The dispute arose from the band's annual Misfits tribute, for which they recorded a cover of "Horror Business" for their Deathbats fan club. The artwork chosen to accompany that release drew criticism, and Vengeance responded on social media rather than backing down. The article was published on October 31, 2026, and his comments were posted on October 29, 2026.

Vengeance wrote that he fully embraces AI and that he loves physical art and the talented people who create it, calling himself one of them. He said the majority of designers he has worked with over the past 20 years are lazy and allowed themselves to be replaced through complacency and greed. He said he prefers his prompts and the collective hive mind and efficiency of the future, and added that AI will absolutely kill us all. He also likened the debate to arguments about tools, saying the problem is not the technology but how people choose to use it.

In replies to fans, Vengeance said AI cannot replace artists such as Wes, Cam and Micah, whom he said he deeply values and has long friendships with, but it can replace anyone replaceable. He said he has purchased artwork by someone named Eddie and praises him constantly, so he has put his money where his mouth is in support of real artists. He also criticized people who scream against AI while consenting to terms of service that give away their personal data. The articles do not say what response the band or anyone else gave, or what happens next.

Articles.Title: Avenged Sevenfold’s Zacky Vengeance Defends AI Art, Calls Majority of Designers He’s Worked With "Lazy"

stories.Headline: Anthropic's path to the Nasdaq just got a lot bumpier
stories.Summary:
Anthropic released its IPO prospectus on Monday, and within days its key partners Microsoft, Google and Amazon reported quarterly results that deepened market worries about the AI buildout. The prospectus disclosed a net loss of $80 billion for the first half of the year, hundreds of billions of dollars in compute commitments and more than 90 pages of risk factors. Investors are still waiting for Anthropic's third-quarter financials. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.9% on Friday and posted its first three-week losing streak since March.

Microsoft lowered its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, Alphabet kept guidance of up to $205 billion and Amazon repeated its roughly $220 billion forecast. Amazon reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion for the trailing 12-month period, its second straight quarter of negative free cash flow, and Google reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion, with its stock falling almost 13% on Thursday, its worst day ever. Microsoft kept positive free cash flow of $18.6 billion, down for a second straight quarter, and said Thursday it plans to raise $25 billion in bonds. Oracle said at its investor day on Wednesday it will limit additional fundraising to $20 billion and turn cash flow positive in the second half of next fiscal year.

Daniel Newman, CEO at Futurum Group, said everyone is still full steam ahead on AI but the things around it took an interesting turn, and the hyperscalers' results raised eyebrows and added doubt about capital structure. He said the worry is that no company can now fund this from its own cash flow, and that Anthropic is the IPO market at this point, with real fear of missing out on a potentially generational company. David Hsu, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania Wharton School, asked how the technology translates into a viable business. Jonathan Krinsky, managing director at BTIG, wrote that it has been an ugly reporting season for tech. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Cloud growth stayed strong, with Microsoft, Google and Amazon all topping analysts' estimates on cloud revenue and Google's cloud business more than doubling from a year earlier. Citizens analysts wrote that Oracle's announcement put the biggest investor fear to rest, that funding its AI buildout would require an open-ended increase in debt and equity issuance. The IPO market has largely been frozen since SpaceX's record offering in June, and Oura, Firmus and SK Hynix's Solidigm subsidiary have recently postponed or abandoned IPO plans, while Nscale and SoftBank's SB Energy have not updated their prospectuses in weeks. Attention now turns back to Anthropic as investors assess how much risk they will assume and at what price.

Articles.Title: Anthropic's path to the Nasdaq just got a lot bumpier

stories.Headline: Texas A&M to open fully automated metallurgy lab, using AI and robotic workers to develop metal alloys
stories.Summary:
Texas A&M University announced a new Aggie AI Foundry, a laboratory created by A&M professors Raymundo Arróyave and Ibrahim Karaman. The College Station-based university said the lab will include a fully automated system to develop metal alloys using artificial intelligence and robotic workers. The announcement was reported on October 31, 2026. The university said this would increase the rate at which metal alloys are developed from months to just days.

According to the university, robots will mix, melt, and test materials using computer-controlled arms along an assembly line. AI could ultimately test as many as a trillion different combinations of periodic elements. The Aggie AI Foundry is supported by the WoodNext Foundation, a philanthropic organization founded by Roku CEO Anthony Wood and his wife Rusan, both of whom are university alumni. The WoodNext Foundation did not return a request for comment.

Arróyave said the move has not been without pushback, and that students, researchers, and others have raised concerns with him that a laboratory relying on artificial intelligence and robots rather than humans would dilute the profession of metallurgy. He said he may sound like one of those tech bros who minimize the impact of their frontier models on the workplace, and he gave his personal experience of learning to polish samples as a grad student at MIT, when his fingertips ended up bloody because his fingers were catching the polishing wheel. He said it was not that fun and he did not learn that much, and that he wished they had an automated polisher back then. He said there are parts that are not that romantic to the work of a researcher, and that an automated system can make it easier.

Arróyave argued that an AI-powered laboratory is like a skip-the-line fast pass at a theme park or getting to the Grand Canyon without having to drive there. He said what they are trying to do is get to the cool, fun part faster, but that is not going to negate the careful, detail-oriented process of investigation that happens once you find a really cool material. Though the lab is automated, students and humans in general will still play a role in the laboratory, and part of the creative vision is to enable students to focus on higher-level research instead of laboratory work. Arróyave called humans fundamental to the process and said they are going to train a new kind of scientist, who has to learn many more things than what they learned when they were students themselves.

Articles.Title: Texas A&M to open fully automated metallurgy lab, using AI and robotic workers to develop metal alloys

stories.Headline: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom?
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence buildout is a large bet on what businesses will pay for intelligence, and research this summer argued that productive use by enterprise customers is a key indicator to watch. The research said the risk of a bubble popping rises if infrastructure supply catches up before productive monetization appears. It forecast that supply constraints and healthy funding appetites could allow a soft landing, and it named 2029 as the highest-risk year. The discussion also drew on Michael Burry’s analysis of Anthropic PBC, Apollo research by Torsten Slok, and the history of the personal computer and internet eras.

As of the recording, the Nasdaq was down 937 points after earnings from the big hyperscalers were not well received, with Google’s advertising disappointment and AWS capex spend and negative cash flow named as culprits. Anthropic’s S-1 showed revenue growth of 14x in the first half of 2026 to $16 billion, and the company reported $132 billion in liquid assets, with only Alphabet and Berkshire holding more cash among U.S. nonbanks. Anthropic had raised about $140 billion and burned $10 billion to reach a $32 billion revenue run rate. Burry’s diagram from the S-1 showed $537 billion of multiyear compute commitments across take-or-pay deals, minimum purchase agreements, lease deals and capacity conditioned on delivery.

Crawford Del Prete, former president of IDC and now senior adviser at PSG Equity, said early signs of productivity gains are appearing but not yet in the numbers. He said companies are automating workflows, starting with coding and customer service and moving into other tasks, and that this makes the impact uneven because work is not rewired. He described circular financing as a way to rebuild the stack around the world at the same time, and said demand depends on the customer. He said one customer would take all the capacity it could get from Lenovo, HPE and Dell, while others are matching models to workloads to manage token spend, and he said he is not seeing many customers pull back because competitiveness drives the spending.

Del Prete said there is no software company today that is not investing for AI, and that they must do it to make their product sets competitive. He said everybody is willing to spend and it comes down to the resources they have. He also raised whether a large adjacent platform using AI could absorb a company’s area, and whether customers can vibe code and create software instead of licensing it. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the discussion of these questions.

Articles.Title: Can enterprise AI pay for the boom?
